en: The Scripture of the Prajñāpāramitā of the Victorious Heavenly King, Scroll One.
Translated by Prince Śubhakaravarman of the Kingdom of Ujjayinī during the Chen Dynasty.
Chapter One: On Thorough Penetration. Chapter One: On Thorough Penetration.
Thus have I heard:

At one time the Bhagavān was staying at the Great City of Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain, together with a great assembly of forty-two thousand bhikṣus—all of whom were arhats whose outflows were forever exhausted, who had accomplished what was to be done, laid down their heavy burdens, attained their own benefit, completely destroyed the fetters of existence, whose minds were well-liberated, and who had attained mastery like great dragons;
the only exception being Ānanda, who was still on the stage of training and had attained the fruit of a srotāpanna. Their names were as follows:

The Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya, Mahākāśyapa, Gavāmpati, Bakula, Revata, Piṅgalavatsa, the Greatly Wise Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Subhūti, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Aniruddha, Mahākātyāyana, Upāli, and Rāhula—these and others, numbering forty-two thousand people, were all present together.

There were seventy-two thousand Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas present, all of whom had thoroughly penetrated the profound nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). They were well-tamed and easy to transform, practiced equanimity with excellence, and served as true spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) to all sentient beings. Having attained unimpeded dhāraṇīs, they were able to turn the irreversible wheel of Dharma. Having made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas in the past, they had come from other Buddha-lands for the sake of the Dharma; being in their final birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*), they protected and upheld the treasury of the Dharma, ensuring that the lineage of the Triple Gem would not be interrupted. As true sons of the Dharma King, they succeeded the Buddhas in turning the wheel of Dharma, penetrating the profound realm of the Tathāgata, and remaining unstained by worldly laws despite appearing in the world.
Their names were: Bodhisattva Ratnākara, Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi, Bodhisattva Ratnamudrā, and Bodhisattva Ratnacūḍa.
Bodhisattva Ratnaśikhin, Bodhisattva Ratnakūṭa, Bodhisattva Ratnasāgara, Bodhisattva Ratnārcis,
Bodhisattva Ratnadhvaja, Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, Bodhisattva Suvarṇagarbha, Bodhisattva Ratnagarbha, Bodhisattva Guṇagarbha,
Bodhisattva Viśuddhagarbha, Bodhisattva Tathāgatagarbha, and Bodhisattva Jñānagarbha.
Sāgaramati, Sūryagarbha Bodhisattva, Samudragarbha Bodhisattva, Padmagarbha Bodhisattva,
Vimukticandra Bodhisattva, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva,
Candravaloka Bodhisattva, Samantasvara Bodhisattva, Samantanetra Bodhisattva, Padmanetra Bodhisattva, and Vipulanetra Bodhisattva.
...the Bodhisattva Samantacārin, the Bodhisattva Samantavrata, the Bodhisattva Matimant, the Bodhisattva Padmamatī,
the Bodhisattva Jayamati, the Bodhisattva Uttaramati, the Bodhisattva Vajramati, the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrīḍita,
the Bodhisattva Siṃhanādin, the Bodhisattva Mahāghoṣarāja, and the Bodhisattva Susvara...
Sattva, the Bodhisattva Vimala, the Bodhisattva Candraprabha, the Bodhisattva Sūryaprabha, the Bodhisattva Jñānaprabha,
the Bodhisattva Jñānaguṇa, the Bodhisattva Bhadraguṇa, the Bodhisattva Puṣpaguṇa, and the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī.
Among the sixteen worthy men, the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla was the leader;
among the bodhisattvas of the Auspicious Aeon, the Bodhisattva Maitreya was the leader;
and among the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the four kings were the leaders.
In the Heaven of the Thirty-three, Śakra is the leader;
among the Yāma devas, Suyāma is the leader;
in the Tuṣita heaven, Santuṣita is the leader.
In the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations, King Skillful Emanation is the leader;
in the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations, King Mastery is the leader;
among all the Brahmā heavens, Great Brahmā King is the leader.
Among the Śuddhāvāsa devas, Maheśvara was the foremost.
Furthermore, there were various asura kings:
the asura king Sali, the asura king Rāhu, and so forth, including immeasurable hundreds of thousands of great asura kings.

Furthermore, there were various dragon kings—Anavatapta the Great Lake Dragon King, Mānasa Dragon King, Sāgara Dragon King, Vāsuki Dragon King, and Takṣaka Dragon King—each leading immeasurable hundreds of thousands of followers. Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, forty yojanas in length and breadth, was filled from the ground to the sky with no intervening space.
Devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others, with single-minded devotion, joined their palms and paid homage to the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded before and behind by an assembly of hundreds of thousands who made offerings, paid homage, revered, and praised him.

From the face of the Tathāgata, a great radiance was emitted, illuminating immeasurable worlds throughout the ten directions; it then returned to the Buddha’s presence, circled him three times to the right, and entered through his face.

To the east, passing from here through Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers, there is a Buddha-land named Adornment. There, the Buddha is named Samantaprabhāsa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. He currently dwells in the world, preaching the True Dharma of the One Vehicle for the sake of the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
In that buddha-field, even the names "śrāvaka" and "pratyekabuddha" do not exist, much less those who practice their respective dharmas.

All the bodhisattvas therein are non-retrogressive from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; the sentient beings of that land do not depend on food and drink, but are sustained solely by meditative concentration.
The light of the sun, moon, and stars all ceased to appear, and only the Buddha’s radiance illuminated that land.
It was devoid of mountains and hills, with ground as level as the palm of a hand.

A bodhisattva named Vighuṣṭaśabda, together with hundreds of thousands of other bodhisattvas, went to where the Buddha was. He bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, addressing him thus:
“World-Honored One!
By what causes and conditions does this radiance illuminate this land?
At that time, the Tathāgata Samantaprabha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vigatarāga, saying:

“Good son! To the west, passing from here through worlds as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers, there is a buddha-field named Sahā. There dwells a Buddha named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. He now wishes to preach the Mahāprajñāpāramitā for the sake of all bodhisattvas; it is for this reason that he has emitted this radiance.”
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimalaprabha addressed that Buddha, saying:
"I now wish to go to the Sahā world to pay homage and make offerings to Śākyamuni Tathāgata, and to hear and receive the True Dharma."
That Buddha replied,
"Good son, now is precisely the right time."

At that time, the Bodhisattva Free from Obstructions (Vigataraja), having received the Buddha’s permission, immediately came to the Sahā world accompanied by an immeasurable retinue of bodhisattvas. Arriving at Vulture Peak Mountain, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to sit on one side.

To the south, passing from here through worlds as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers, there is a buddha-land named Pure Flower; the Buddha there is named Sunlight, who is endowed with the ten titles, and his bodhisattva is named Sun-Treasury.

To the west, passing from here through worlds as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers, there is a land named Jewel Flower. The Buddha there is named Light of Merit, fully endowed with the ten titles, and his bodhisattva is named Treasury of Merit.

To the north, passing from here through worlds as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers, there is a land named Pure, where the Buddha is named Sovereign King and the bodhisattva is named Wide Renown.

To the southeast, passing from here through worlds as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers, there is a land named Flame, where the Buddha is named Nectar King and the bodhisattva is named Non-retrogression.

To the southwest, passing from here through worlds as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers, there is a land named Pure Merit; the Buddha there is named Wisdom Torch, and the bodhisattva is named Great Wisdom.

To the northwest, passing from here through worlds as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers, there is a land named Ramanīya; the Buddha there is named King of Wondrous Sound, and a bodhisattva named Guṇarāśi.

To the northeast, passing from here through worlds as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers, there is a land named Prajñālaṃkṛta; the Buddha there is named Jñānottara, and the bodhisattva is named Nityapramudita.

To the zenith, passing from here through worlds as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers, there is a land named Acala; the Buddha there is named Vajralakṣaṇa, and the Bodhisattva is named Ratnadhvaja.

To the nadir, passing from here through worlds as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers, there is a land named Candraprabhā; the Buddha there is named Vajraratnavyūharāja, and the Bodhisattva is named Ratnaprasāda.
It was the same for all of them.

At that time, there was a heavenly king among the assembly named Pāpāra. He rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, addressing him thus:
“World-Honored One!
"I now wish to ask a question; if I am granted permission by the Buddha, I shall venture to set forth my doubts.
At that time, the Buddha addressed King Śūra-deva, saying:
"Great King!"
“The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha shall explain according to whatever questions are asked.
At that time, King Śūra, filled with joy and leaping for gladness at having attained what he had never experienced before, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice and study a single dharma so as to penetrate all dharmas?
The Buddha addressed King Śūraṅgama, saying: “Great King!
Excellent, excellent!
You have asked well.
Listen attentively, listen attentively!
"Reflect upon this well.
As you have asked, I shall explain it in detail.
"Excellent, World-Honored One!"
"Indeed, we wish to hear it.
The Buddha addressed King Śūra-vīra, saying:
"Great King!"
The single dharma that the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices and studies to penetrate all dharmas is what is called the prajñāpāramitā.

When the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices and studies the prajñāpāramitā, they are then able to penetrate the dānapāramitā, śīlapāramitā, kṣāntipāramitā, vīryapāramitā, dhyānapāramitā, prajñāpāramitā, upāyakauśalyapāramitā, nidhipāramitā, brahmapāramitā, and jñānapāramitā.
“Great King!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, training in the *prajñāpāramitā*, practice the *dānapāramitā*?

A bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a pure mind free from expectations, teaches the Dharma to others without seeking fame or profit, but solely to extinguish suffering. He perceives neither a speaker nor a listener; there is no duality and no distinction because their intrinsic nature is detached. This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva training in the *prajñāpāramitā* while practicing the *dharmadānapāramitā*.”

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva studies the perfection of wisdom, they practice the perfection of fearless giving—regarding all sentient beings as their own parents, brothers, and relatives, causing all beings to feel intimate attachment toward them.
Why is this? Because throughout the beginningless succession of births and deaths, all beings wandering through the six realms have been one's own relatives.
If there are sentient beings in fear and distress, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva will even rescue them at the cost of their own life; how much less would they inflict harm upon them?
He does not perceive himself as bestowing fearlessness, nor does he perceive a recipient; there is no duality and no distinction, because their intrinsic nature is detached.

The bodhisattva-mahāsattva training in the *prajñāpāramitā* practices the *dānapāramitā* of providing the necessities of life—bestowing various kinds of material sustenance upon sentient beings according to their needs so that they may receive the ten wholesome paths of action. He does not perceive himself as bestowing goodness, nor does he perceive another as receiving the gift; there is no duality and no distinction, because their intrinsic nature is detached.

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva studies the perfection of wisdom, they practice the perfection of giving without expectation of reward. Whenever they practice generosity, they do not look for karmic fruition; it is the natural law of a bodhisattva that they should give spontaneously. They perceive neither the act of giving nor the reward of the gift, for these two are non-dual and undifferentiated, being devoid of intrinsic nature.

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva studies the *prajñāpāramitā* and practices the *dānapāramitā* of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), seeing sentient beings who are impoverished, aged, or diseased and without anyone to provide relief, they give rise to a heart of great compassion and make this vow:
"Once I have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I shall serve as a place of refuge for all sentient beings."

Dedicating even a small root of virtue toward enlightenment for the sake of sentient beings, they do not discriminate between themselves as the savior and others as those to be saved; for these are non-dual and without distinction, being devoid of intrinsic nature.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving with reverence while training in the perfection of wisdom—providing whatever others require, the bodhisattva mahāsattva personally takes up the objects and bestows them with a respectful heart so as not to weary the recipient—they do not perceive a self that can practice reverence, nor do they perceive another who receives it; there is neither duality nor distinction, for their intrinsic nature is detached.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva studies the perfection of wisdom, they practice the honored perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*). Toward all sentient beings, they conceive of them as teachers, preceptors, and parents; with a heart of reverence, they join their palms in respect. If they lack material wealth, they bestow kind words instead. They do not perceive a self that is capable of honoring others or anyone who is worthy of honor, for there is no duality or distinction, as all things are by nature detached from such constructs.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva studies the *prajñāpāramitā*, they practice the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) through offerings: if they see a temple or stupa, they should offer incense, flowers, lamps, oil, and perform sweeping and sprinkling; if they see a sacred image that is dilapidated or the True Dharma that is deficient, they should repair and restore them; if they see the monastic community, they should provide the four types of requisites, yet they do not perceive "I am the one who offers" or "that is the one who receives," for there is neither duality nor distinction, as their intrinsic nature is detached from such concepts.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving without reliance while training in the perfection of wisdom, they do not form such thoughts as:
"By means of this giving, may I be reborn in heaven or seek to become a celestial king; may I be reborn among humans or seek to become a human king."

"Even up to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, he does not seek to acquire it, because there is nothing to be obtained; this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s study of the *prajñāpāramitā* through which he penetrates the *dānapāramitā*."
“Great King!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) while training in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*), they reflect thus:

‘The Buddha has taught the *pratimokṣa* within the *āgama* teachings and the *vinaya*; a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in it, yet without perceiving the characteristics of the precepts or a self that can uphold them. They do not cling to the precepts, nor do they cling to views, nor do they cling to a self.’”
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva studies the *prajñāpāramitā*, they reflect as follows:

"Unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is not attained through the mere observance of precepts alone; rather, one should study the bodhisattva’s ethical conduct in its entirety. For the nature of the precepts is cool, tranquil, and non-arising, being by its very nature detached."
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva studies the prajñāpāramitā, they reflect in this way:
"How can the observance of ethical discipline sever the afflictions?
There are three kinds of afflictions:"
Greed, hatred, and delusion;
furthermore, each has three grades—namely, superior, middling, and inferior.
One must know their respective antidotes: for those in whom greed is predominant, one should cultivate the contemplation of impurity by fully observing the thirty-six components of the body.
Those with an abundance of hatred should cultivate the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion;
those with an abundance of delusion should cultivate the contemplation of dependent origination.
One does not perceive a subject that contemplates nor an object that is contemplated, for they are non-dual, undifferentiated, and devoid of intrinsic nature.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva studies the prajñāpāramitā, they further reflect:
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva remain free from improper mental attention?"
A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not give rise to this thought:
"I practice the conduct of tranquility, the conduct of detachment, and emptiness;
whereas all other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas remain amidst clamor and do not delight in the practice of emptiness."
"Seeing the non-duality of distinctions and knowing that self-nature is detached, one immediately extinguishes wrong thoughts.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva studies the Prajñāpāramitā, although they know all dharmas are detached, they still deeply fear sinful karma. As the Buddha has taught, they should maintain pure precepts and cultivate merits up to the Prajñāpāramitā; they do not dwell together with even a small amount of unwholesome dharmas.
As the World-Honored One said: "It is like a poisonous drug; whether much or little, it is harmful to all."
"When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva studies the Prajñāpāramitā, they constantly give rise to a sense of awe and remain in accord with faithful practice.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva wanders alone without a companion in a desolate place, and if there should be śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or others who bring gold, silver, lapis lazuli, pearls, agate, amber, coral, musaragalva, and white jade to entrust to the Bodhisattva, they do not give rise to greedy attachment nor have any intention to take them. They reflect thus:
'The World-Honored One has said:'"
"Rather than taking food by cutting flesh from one's own body, one must not take the wealth of others that has not been given.

Thus, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva trains in the perfection of wisdom with firm adherence to the precepts, even if Māra or his retinue should attempt to tempt the Bodhisattva with exquisite forms and appearances, their mind remains unshaken, and they reflect:
"The World-Honored One has said:"
"All dharmas are like dreams, illusions, and transformations;
they are non-dual and undifferentiated, for their intrinsic nature is detached.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva studies the Prajñāpāramitā, although he diligently maintains the precepts, he does not seek birth as a human or as a king of men, nor does he seek birth in the heavens or as a king of gods. His body is free from the three faults, his speech is devoid of the four transgressions, and his mind is exempt from the three errors.

Maintaining the precepts in this manner, one does not perceive a self that maintains them, nor does one perceive the characteristics of the precepts; there is neither duality nor distinction, because their intrinsic nature is free from such [dualities].
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s training in the *prajñāpāramitā* to penetrate the *śīlapāramitā*.
"Great King!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva studies the Prajñāpāramitā, they practice the Kṣāntipāramitā.
This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is always able to give rise to patience within their own mind, such that sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction do not follow them at all."
They also train in external patience (*bāhyakṣānti*), such that even if others strike or revile them, they never give rise to anger;
they also train in the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*), as the World-Honored One has said:
"The profound true nature is without person and without phenomena; non-arising and quiescence are precisely *nirvāṇa*."
Hearing these words, his mind was not startled or terrified, and he reflected:
"If I do not study this Dharma, how can I attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
He deeply contemplates the three poisons: from where do such greed and hatred arise?
By what causes and conditions are they produced?
By what causes and conditions are they extinguished?
Practicing such contemplation, one does not perceive birth nor any dharma that can be born; one does not perceive that which can extinguish nor that which is extinguished.

Thus, the mind of patience continues in an uninterrupted succession, without interval throughout the six periods of the day and night, and without discriminating among objects—whether it be parents, kings, or oneself toward whom one must be patient, or others toward whom one might employ force or even inflict harm.

A bodhisattva practices patience not for the sake of seeking recompense, fame, profit, benevolence, righteousness, shame, or fear; rather, it is the natural law for a bodhisattva-mahāsattva to practice patience, such that even if others inflict harm, beat them, or revile them, their mind remains unshaken.
If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva acts as a king or similar ruler and encounters a poor or lowly person who insults and humiliates him, he does not employ forceful punishment, saying:
"I am a king; by law, you ought to be punished and eliminated."
He then had this thought:
"In the presence of the various World-Honored Ones of the past, I made a great vow:
'I shall rescue and deliver all sentient beings, causing them to attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.'"
"If I were now to give rise to anger, I would violate my original vow.
It is like a skilled physician who makes this vow:
'I shall completely cure all those in the world who are blind and sightless.'"
"If one has lost one's own sight, how can one treat the illnesses of others?
Likewise, if a bodhisattva gives rise to anger while seeking to eliminate the darkness of ignorance for sentient beings, how can they possibly save them?"
Not perceiving a self that can endure, nor perceiving that which is to be endured— being without duality and without distinction because their intrinsic nature is detached—
this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s study of the prajñāpāramitā through the thorough mastery of the kṣāntipāramitā.
“Great King!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of vigor within the study of the perfection of wisdom, they cause those who have not extinguished [suffering] to extinguish it; they cause those who have not crossed over to cross over; they cause those who have not been liberated to be liberated; they cause those who have not been established in peace to be established in peace; and they cause those who have not yet studied to study.”
When a bodhisattva practices diligence in this manner, various evil Māras create obstacles for them, saying to the bodhisattva:
"Good son! Do not cultivate this dharma; you will labor in vain."

Why is this? In the past, I practiced this Dharma; yet, though it had not been extinguished, I sought to extinguish it; though I had not been delivered, I sought to deliver others; though I had not been liberated, I sought to liberate others; though I had not been established in peace, I sought to establish others in peace; though I had not attained learning, I sought to lead others to learn. Thus, I underwent diligent toil in vain, receiving no real benefit at all.
"Since long ago, I have seen many bodhisattvas who, while practicing and studying this path, have all regressed.
You should turn your mind away from it and instead take up the vehicles of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas to attain your own nirvāṇa."
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva immediately perceives this and says to the evil Māra:
"Depart by another way; my mind is like a diamond, which you cannot destroy."
"If you create obstacles, you will yourself suffer for a long night.
Thereupon, Māra vanished.

If other bodhisattvas practice the five pāramitās but have not yet attained the prajñāpāramitā, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who exerts such diligence can surpass them even in a hundred thousand kalpas, let alone those of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha vehicles.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they accomplish the Buddha-dharmas and become entirely free from all evils.
Although they practice diligence, they proceed neither too hastily nor too slowly, yet they make this great vow:

"May I obtain a body equal to that of the World-Honored One—with the white tuft of hair between my brows and the fleshly protuberance upon my crown—and just as the Buddha turns the wheel of Dharma, may I do likewise."

"Just as pure gold becomes magnificent and pure when adorned with various jewels, so too is the vigor of a bodhisattva: it remains far removed from defilements—namely, laziness, indolence, exhaustion, lack of self-awareness, and improper reflection. By being free from these defilements, one attains the adornment of pure wisdom and merit; the body does not grow weary, the mind feels no fatigue, and all unwholesome factors that obstruct the Path are entirely eliminated. All dharmas that assist the Path and lead toward Nirvāṇa are made to increase, such that even minor evils do not arise, let alone major ones."

Suppose that the worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, were filled with great fires like those of the Avīci Hell; if there were even a single sentient being outside these worlds who could be delivered and liberated, a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva would be able to pass through them, let alone many sentient beings.
One should form this thought:
"Unsurpassed Bodhi is not easily attained.
A Bodhisattva practices as if his head were on fire; such a heavy burden is difficult to carry for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas.
He reflects thus:
"All Buddhas of the past and present have cultivated this practice and thereby attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

I, too, must likewise cultivate it correctly; rather than abandoning sentient beings to swiftly attain *nirvāṇa*, I would prefer to remain in the hells for hundreds of thousands of kalpas so that these beings may cross over."

Practicing diligence in this way, one does not exalt oneself nor disparage others; one perceives neither "I" who can practice nor the dharmas that are practiced, for these are non-dual and undifferentiated, being by nature free from self-nature.
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s study of the prajñāpāramitā through which they penetrate the vīryapāramitā.

"Great King, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva studies the prajñāpāramitā and practices the dhyānapāramitā, they plant deep roots of goodness; in every successive birth within the Mahāyāna, they extensively cultivate sublime conduct and draw near to virtuous friends."
They will not be born into poverty or low status, but will always be born into great families of Brahmins or Kṣatriyas;
they will have correct faith in the Triple Gem,
and their wholesome dharmas will increase.
Due to their past roots of goodness, they form this thought:
"Sentient beings wander through the six realms for the long night; that the wheel of suffering does not cease is entirely due to craving.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives rise to a mind of weary detachment, knowing that [desire] arises from false discrimination. Within the sūtras, he skillfully explains in various ways the faults and afflictions of desire, likening it to a spear, a pestle, a sword, a snake, and a bubble—foul, impure, and impermanent.
How could a wise person be greedily attached to this dharma?
They would instead shave their hair and beard, leave the household life, and cultivate the Way.
They would cause what has not yet been seen to be seen, what has not yet been attained to be attained, and what has not yet been realized to be realized.

Having heard and accepted this teaching, one should practice in accordance with reality and contemplate according to the Dharma—namely, right view, right discrimination, right effort, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right mindfulness, and right concentration, whether in terms of conventional truth or ultimate truth.
Distant from clamor and bustle, seeking neither fame nor renown, one honors and respects [the practice], maintaining physical and mental diligence that never ceases.
One contemplates this mind to observe which objects it frequently engages with—whether they be wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral realms.
If one encounters wholesome objects, one should apply diligent effort to increase the roots of goodness, using the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment to counteract all evil and unwholesome states.
These evil and unwholesome states are greed, hatred, and delusion.
Greed has three grades: namely, superior, middling, and inferior.
As for the superior grade, upon merely hearing the name of sensual desire, one’s entire body trembles;
the heart leaps with joy, one fails to contemplate the faults of desire, detachment does not arise, and one is devoid of shame and remorse.
What is meant by lack of shame (*ahrīkya*)?
When wandering alone, one constantly dwells upon objects of desire with a continuous stream of thought, seeing only their excellence and failing to recognize their faults.

If one's parents or other elders reprimand such desires, one fails to perceive the gravity of the situation before those who are venerable and instead gives rise to contention; this is called lack of shame.
When such a person’s life ends, they shall be reborn in the evil destinies.
As for those of middling-grade desire, if they are separated from the objects of their attachment, the thoughts do not arise constantly.
As for those of inferior-grade desire, their lustful passion ceases as soon as they merely engage in conversation and laughter together.
Hatred is also of three grades.

As for those with superior-grade hatred, when their fury erupts, their minds become clouded and their vision disordered; they may commit the five heinous crimes or slander the true Dharma. Compared to such great and grave sins as the evils of the five heinous crimes, [the latter] does not even equal one-hundredth part of them.
Those with medium-grade anger commit various evils due to their resentment, yet immediately give rise to a mind of repentance.
Those with low-grade anger harbor no malice or hatred in their hearts; they merely revile and disparage others verbally, subsequently giving rise to remorse for their transgression.
Ignorance is also like this.
Although one performs such contemplation, knowing that all phenomena are like illusions, dreams, echoes, and cities of the Gandharvas—false, unreal, and seen due to inversion.

Having extinguished external objects, the internal mind is tranquil; one does not perceive a self that acts nor the dharmas that are acted upon, for they are non-dual and undifferentiated, being devoid of intrinsic nature.
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva training in the *prajñāpāramitā* and penetrating the *dhyānapāramitā*.
"Great King!

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva trains in the *prajñāpāramitā* and practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, they contemplate form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) with correct wisdom. They do not see the arising of form, they do not see the accumulation of form, and they do not see the cessation of form; it is likewise for feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness."
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature is entirely empty and lacks any reality; they are merely empty names.
Yet, while practicing the Prajñāpāramitā to transform all sentient beings, one never fails to explain that there are no karmic fruits and retributions.

All phenomena are like dreams and like illusions; they are without self, without person, without sentient being, without life-span, and without nourisher, yet it is said that there are karmic fruits and retributions.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this manner, evil Māras cannot find an opportunity.
Why is this? Because they draw near to spiritual friends and accomplish the factors that assist awakening which transcend the world.
They joyfully praise the profound and true Dharma of all Tathāgatas.
Whether gods, Māras, śramaṇas, or brahmins, none can equal the Bodhisattva except for the Buddha’s own perfect wisdom.
Not perceiving a self that practices nor the dharmas that are practiced— being without duality and without distinction because their intrinsic nature is detached—
is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s training in the *prajñāpāramitā* and thorough penetration of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
“Great King!

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva studies the Prajñāpāramitā and practices the Upāyakauśalyapāramitā, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva skillfully dedicates [the merit] toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. If they see flowers or fruits, they make offerings to the Buddhas and the assembly of Bodhisattvas six times throughout the day and night, dedicating these roots of goodness toward enlightenment;
the same applies to flowering trees and fruit-bearing trees.”

If one hears the profound meaning taught within the Tathāgata’s sūtras, believes in it with joy, accepts and upholds it, explains it for the sake of sentient beings, and dedicates these roots of goodness toward Bodhi.

If one sees the stupas, temples, or images of the Tathāgata and makes offerings of incense and flowers, it causes all sentient beings to leave behind the fragrance of broken precepts and obtain the pure fragrance of the Tathāgata’s discipline;
by sweeping, sprinkling, and plastering the ground, it causes all sentient beings to have their deportment perfectly orderly;
and by covering them with flower-canopies, it causes all sentient beings to be free from affliction and feverish distress.
Upon entering a monastery, one should make this vow: "May all sentient beings enter nirvana.
When leaving the monastery, one should vow: "May all sentient beings emerge from the realm of Māra.
As one opens the gate of the monastery, one should make this vow:
"By means of supramundane wisdom, may I open for all sentient beings the gates that have not yet been opened.
If I see them closed, may I, for the sake of sentient beings, close off the evil destinies and the three realms of existence.
When sitting, he should think:
"May all sentient beings sit upon the seat of enlightenment.
If lying on his right side, he should wish: "May all sentient beings attain nirvana."
When rising, he thinks:
"May all sentient beings arise free from all delusions.
When washing his feet, he wishes: "May all sentient beings be far removed from dust and defilement."
When prostrating to the Buddha and circumambulating the stupa, he made the vow that all sentient beings might become Teachers of Gods and Humans.
If there were followers of external paths with wrong views who were difficult to transform, he would think to himself:
"I am their teacher, yet they will certainly not believe."
Furthermore, he may become a fellow student or a disciple.

Although he dwells among that assembly, his observance of the precepts and his extensive learning surpass those of all non-Buddhists; consequently, they are subdued by him, revere him as their teacher, and invariably accept his words with faith.

He destroys their false teachings and preaches *nirvāṇa* for them, causing them to enter the true doctrine, cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*) with diligence, and attain various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and samādhi.

When he sees those with excessive desire, he transforms himself into a woman of supreme beauty to cause them to become attached; yet in an instant, he manifests impermanence by showing her form changing into a bloated, putrefying, and foul-smelling corpse, thereby increasing their sense of revulsion and inspiring in them a mind of weary detachment.
He immediately resumed his original form, appearing as a bodhisattva image and preaching the Dharma for them, causing them to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and attain the unsurpassed fruit.

Seeing Mahāyāna practitioners who have distanced themselves from virtuous friends, studying the path of the two vehicles without attaining its fruit, and thus vainly losing the Mahāyāna, he observes their faculties and natures and immediately preaches the Dharma for them so that they may enter the unsurpassed path.
Those who have not yet resolved to attain enlightenment are transformed so that they may resolve; those who have already resolved are instructed to make their resolve firm.

Seeing a person who upholds the precepts commit even a minor transgression, fail to perform repentance, and become weary, discouraged, and sorrowful such that they no longer cultivate the Path, he immediately expounds the Dharma for them as an antidote to enable them to repent and eliminate the offense, causing their progress on the Path to advance further.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva has few desires and is content, seeking only the benefit of the Dharma and preaching to sentient beings that they should make offerings to the Tathāgata, thereby accomplishing the six pāramitās through the offering of Dharma—this is the dāna-pāramitā.
To act without contradicting one’s words is the śīla-pāramitā.
That neither devas nor māras can disrupt or confuse them is the kṣānti-pāramitā.
The continuous succession of mind-moments without becoming weary is the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā);
focusing the mind on a single thought without being distracted by other objects is the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā);
preaching the Dharma and making offerings without perceiving a self or what belongs to a self is the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā).
One does not perceive a self that acts nor the dharmas that are acted upon; these are neither two nor distinct, for their intrinsic nature is detached.
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s training in the perfection of wisdom and the thorough penetration of the perfection of skillful means.
"Great King!

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva studies the *prajñāpāramitā* and practices the *nidhipāramitā*, the Bodhisattva makes a vow not to seek the path of the two vehicles for the sake of personal liberation from the triple world through the pursuit of [personal] bliss. He makes this great vow, saying:
'Only after all sentient beings—those comprised within the category of sentient beings—have entered *nirvāṇa*, shall my own body attain perfect enlightenment.'"

Those who have not yet resolved to attain enlightenment shall be inspired to do so; those who have already resolved to attain enlightenment shall be led to practice; and those who have already practiced shall be enabled to realize Bodhi.
Those who have realized Bodhi are requested to turn the Wheel of Dharma, and even to manifest emanated bodies and relics for the construction of stupas and offerings.
He further made this vow:
"In whatever world a Buddha attains enlightenment, may there be no celestial Māras at all.
May my own wisdom give rise to the unsurpassed mind, not depending on external conditions."
Furthermore, I vow that my body shall always remain in the world so that all sentient beings may achieve fulfillment.
I vow that those bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds, upon hearing the Tathāgata preach the most profound Dharma, shall not be startled or terrified.
May all sentient beings fully penetrate the boundless path of the Buddhas, the boundless realm of the Buddhas, and boundless great compassion.
Furthermore, may my own body always be born in impure lands and never in pure lands.
Why is this? It is like a sick person who requires medicine, whereas one without illness has no need for it.
I do not perceive a "self" that practices nor the dharmas that are practiced; these two are neither dual nor distinct, for their intrinsic nature is transcendent.
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s study of the *prajñāpāramitā* to master the *praṇidhānapāramitā*.
"Great King!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva studies the *prajñāpāramitā* and practices the *balapāramitā*, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to subdue the celestial Māras and crush all non-Buddhist paths, because they are fully endowed with merit, wisdom, and power."
There is not a single Buddha-dharma that they do not practice or realize through direct vision;
by means of their supernormal powers, they can lift Jambudvīpa, even the four continents, the trichiliocosm, and even immeasurable hundreds of thousands of worlds with a single hair;
they can take various kinds of jewels from the midst of space and bestow them upon all sentient beings.
In the infinite and boundless worlds of the ten directions, there is no teaching of the Buddhas that they do not hear and uphold.
They perceive neither a self that practices nor the dharmas being practiced; these are non-dual and undifferentiated, for their intrinsic nature is free from conceptualization.
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s study of the perfection of wisdom that penetrates the perfection of power.
“Great King!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva studies the perfection of wisdom and practices the perfection of gnosis (*jñāna*), the bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*): they see that arising is not truly arising, and that cessation is not truly ceasing. He reflects in this way:”
"These five aggregates are empty, without self, without person, without sentient being, without life-span, and without nourisher.
Yet ordinary beings falsely cling to a self."
The five aggregates are not the self; there is no self within the aggregates; the self is not the five aggregates; and there are no aggregates within the self.
Foolish ordinary beings, deluded and lacking knowledge of reality as it is, transmigrate through birth and death like a whirling firebrand.
All phenomena are by nature originally empty, neither arising nor ceasing; they are said to arise when conditions conjoin and to cease when conditions disperse.
Because their self-nature is not non-existent, they do not arise; because their self-nature is not existent, they do not cease.

For a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, there is not a single phenomenon among all objective realms that they do not thoroughly penetrate. By practicing such Prajñāpāramitā, they cannot be obscured by those of the Two Vehicles or the non-Buddhists; observing with wisdom, they clearly understand everything from their initial resolve until their entry into Nirvāṇa.
One is able to know all objects through a single dharma, for all objects are themselves that single dharma. Why is this?
Because suchness is one.
"One does not perceive a 'self' that practices nor the 'dharmas' being practiced; they are non-dual and without distinction, for their intrinsic nature is free from [such constructs].
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of the perfection of wisdom through the penetration of the perfection of knowledge.

Chapter 2: Revealing the Characteristics The Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra of the Victorious Heavenly King, Chapter Two: Revealing the Characteristics At that time, the Victorious Heavenly King rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee upon the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, bowed his head to the Buddha’s feet in salutation, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"This Prajñāpāramitā is profoundly deep.
What is the characteristic of this Prajñāpāramitā?
The Buddha addressed King Śūraṅgama, saying:
"Just as are the characteristics of earth, water, fire, and wind, so too are the characteristics of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
"World-Honored One!
What are the characteristics of earth?"
The Buddha said:
“It is all-pervasive and vast, difficult to measure; this is the characteristic of earth.
The characteristic of the *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise so.”
Why is this? Because suchness is universally pervasive and vast, and thus difficult to conceive.
Great King!
All medicinal herbs grow depending upon the earth;
likewise, all wholesome dharmas arise depending upon the Prajñāpāramitā.

Furthermore, just as the soil feels no joy when it is increased and no anger when it is diminished—because it is free from "I" and "mine" and lacks the two characteristics [of subject and object]; so too is this Prajñāpāramitā.
The Prajñāpāramitā is likewise: it does not increase through praise nor decrease through disparagement, for it is free from "I" and "mine," being devoid of dualistic characteristics.
In the world’s comings and goings, every lifting and placing of the foot depends entirely upon the earth;
likewise, if one seeks the path of goodness and aspires toward nirvana, one should rely upon this Prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, just as the great earth produces various kinds of jewels,
so too does the *prajñāpāramitā* produce various supramundane merits. Moreover,
just as the great earth cannot be shaken by the various sufferings of insects, ants, mosquitoes, and gadflies;
The Prajñāpāramitā is likewise: free from "self" and "what belongs to self," it cannot be shaken.

Furthermore, just as the great earth feels no alarm or fear upon hearing the sounds of lions, dragons, or elephants, so too the Prajñāpāramitā cannot be intimidated by celestial Māras or non-Buddhist heretics.
Why is this? Because one does not perceive a person, nor does one perceive phenomena, for their intrinsic nature is empty.
Furthermore, it is like the element of water, which flows from high to low.
All wholesome dharmas tend toward the Prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, just as the element of water can moisten grasses and trees so that they produce flowers and fruits, so too is the Prajñāpāramitā:

it moistens all samādhis, gives birth to the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma), brings the tree of omniscience to fruition, yields the fruit of the Buddha-dharmas, and benefits sentient beings.
Furthermore, just as the great element of water, when it drenches the roots of grasses and trees, can cause them to be uprooted and carried away by the current;
so too is the Prajñāpāramitā: all views, afflictions, and habitual tendencies are completely extinguished at their root, never to arise again.
Furthermore, just as the element of water is by nature fundamentally pure, stainless, and unclouded;

so too is the *prajñāpāramitā*: its essence is free from afflictions and is thus called "pure"; it is free from all delusions and is thus called "stainless"; and because it is of a single characteristic and not diverse, it is called "unclouded."
Just as a person in the heat of summer finds relief upon encountering cool water,
so too do sentient beings tormented by the fever of affliction find immediate cooling upon hearing the Prajñāpāramitā.
Just as a person suffering from thirst finds their thirst quenched only when they obtain water;
Seeking the supramundane Dharma, one attains the Prajñāpāramitā, and even the aspiration for further seeking comes to rest.
Furthermore, just as a spring of water is extremely deep and difficult to enter;
so too is the Prajñāpāramitā, for the realm of all Buddhas is extremely deep and difficult to enter.
Furthermore, just as water is level everywhere, even in places such as pits and hollows;
so too is the Prajñāpāramitā, for it is equal toward all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and ordinary worldlings alike.
Furthermore, just as water can wash the earth so that it becomes entirely pure,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who penetrates the Prajñāpāramitā becomes pure by being free from all afflictions.
Why is this? Because its intrinsic nature is pure and free from all delusions.
Furthermore, it is like the element of fire, which can burn all trees, shrubs, and medicinal herbs, yet does not form such a thought:
"I am able to burn things.
The Prajñāpāramitā is also like this: it can extinguish all afflictions and habitual tendencies, yet it does not form the thought, "I am able to eliminate them."
"Furthermore, it is like fire, which can fully ripen all things;
so too does the Prajñāpāramitā bring all Buddha-dharmas to fulfillment.
Again, it is like fire, which can completely dry up all moist things."
The Prajñāpāramitā is also like this: it exhausts all outflows so that they never arise again.
Even if a mass of fire were atop the Snowy Mountains, illuminating everything from one yojana to ten yojanas, it would have no such thought as, "I am able to illuminate what is distant."
The Prajñāpāramitā is also like this: it is able to illuminate all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, yet it does not form the thought, "I am able to illuminate them."
Furthermore, just as birds and beasts see a fire at night and, out of fear, flee far away;
so too do ordinary people of meager merit and those of the two vehicles feel dread upon hearing the Prajñāpāramitā and abandon it.
Even to hear the name of the Prajñāpāramitā is difficult, let alone to practice and study it.

It is like traveling a long distance at night and losing one’s way; upon seeing a light, one feels great joy, knowing that a village is nearby and hastening toward it. Upon arrival, one finds safety and is forever free from fear.

Likewise, in the wilderness of birth and death, those with merit who hear the Prajñāpāramitā will feel great joy, turning toward it for refuge and upholding it; they will forever be free from afflictions and their minds will attain peace and happiness.
Just as the fire of the world is common to both the noble and the lowly,
so too is the Prajñāpāramitā equally present for both ordinary beings and sages. Furthermore,
it is like how both Brahmins and Kṣatriyas alike offer worship to the sacrificial fire.
All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas universally make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, just as a small fire can burn a trichiliocosm, so too is the Prajñāpāramitā:
if one hears even a single phrase, it can incinerate immeasurable afflictions.

“Great King! The Prajñāpāramitā is free from defilement and unattached; it is tranquil and boundless, possessing infinite wisdom. It equally penetrates the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), being like the nature of space, having no place of abiding. It is a realm free from marks, transcending all discursive thought (vitarka-vicāra). Within the mind and mental factors (citta-caitasika-dharma), there is no discrimination; it is without arising and without cessation, for its self-nature is detached.”
“Great King!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, it is rare in the world;
they benefit sentient beings just as the sun and moon provide for all to enjoy.”
Furthermore, just as the moon can dispel heat and affliction, so too is the Prajñāpāramitā; it can eliminate the feverish poison of all afflictions (*kleśa*).
Moreover, just as the moon is pleasant for the world to behold;
The Prajñāpāramitā is likewise so: it is that which all noble ones delight in beholding.

Furthermore, just as the new moon increases day by day, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who draws near to the Prajñāpāramitā grows progressively from the first generation of the mind of awakening until the attainment of bodhi. Conversely, like the dark fortnight of the moon which wanes day by day, [those who distance themselves from it] gradually diminish.
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the Prajñāpāramitā, their afflictions and fetters are extinguished one after another.
Just as the moon in the world is praised by both Brahmins and Kṣatriyas,
so too are all sons and daughters of good family who draw near to the Prajñāpāramitā praised by all the worlds, including devas, humans, and asuras.
Just as the moon travels throughout the four continents;
so too is the Prajñāpāramitā: whether in form or in mind, there is nowhere it does not pervade.
Just as the worldly moon is ever self-adorned;
The Prajñāpāramitā is likewise: its nature is inherently adorned. Why is this?
Because it is neither born nor extinguished;
its nature is fundamentally pure, pervading all phenomena, for its self-nature is free from [all conceptualization].
Just as the sun in the world dispels all darkness, yet does not form the thought,
"I am able to dispel darkness," so too is the Prajñāpāramitā; it is able to destroy all afflictions from beginningless time, yet it does not form the thought:
"I have destroyed the afflictions.
Furthermore, it is like the sun that causes the lotus flowers to bloom, yet does not form the thought:
"I am opening the lotuses."
The Prajñāpāramitā is also like this: it can open the way for bodhisattvas, yet it has no such thought.
Furthermore, it is like the sun that shines universally upon the ten directions, without forming the thought:
"I am able to shine everywhere."
The Prajñāpāramitā is also like this: it can illuminate the boundless, yet there is no appearance of illumination.
Furthermore, just as when one sees the east turn red, one knows that the sun will rise before long;
so too, if one hears the Prajñāpāramitā, one should know that the Buddha is not far away.
Just as the people of Jambudvīpa experience great joy upon seeing the rising sun,
so too do all the noble ones experience great joy whenever the name of the Prajñāpāramitā exists within the world.
Furthermore, just as when the sun rises, the light of the moon and the stars all disappears;
so too, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, the virtues of the two vehicles and of outsiders do not appear.
Furthermore, just as one can only see the depressions, hollows, heights, and lowlands when the sun rises;
so too, when Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the Prajñāpāramitā, the world then comes to know the paths of the heterodox and the orthodox.
Why is this? Because the Prajñāpāramitā is equal in its own characteristics, neither arising nor ceasing, for its nature is one of detachment.
"Great King!

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the Prajñāpāramitā, they extensively cultivate the practice of emptiness, remaining free from all dwelling and attachment. They cultivate the Path to transcend all obstacles, distance themselves from evil associates, and draw near to all Buddhas. With every thought succeeding the next, they maintain uninterrupted mindfulness of the Buddha. They penetrate equality and accord with the Dharma-realm, sporting with supernatural powers throughout the lands of the ten directions, yet remaining utterly unmoved in their original place. Thus they perceive the teachings of all Buddhas as if they were right before them.
Though dwelling in the world, they are unstained by worldly dharmas, just as a lotus flower grows amidst the mud.
Although Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwell within birth and death, because of the power of skillful means (*upāya*) of the *prajñāpāramitā*, they remain unstained and unattached.
Why is this? Because the Prajñāpāramitā is neither born nor extinguished; its own characteristics are equal, it is neither perceived nor clung to, for its nature is one of detachment.
Furthermore, just as a lotus flower does not allow a drop of water to remain;
so too, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, not even a single unwholesome dharma can abide for a moment.
Furthermore, just as wherever a lotus flower is found, it is fragrant;
so too, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, whether in cities, towns, villages, or among humans and devas, they are everywhere endowed with the fragrance of the precepts.
Furthermore, just as the nature of the lotus is pure and it is cherished and honored by brahmins, kṣatriyas, elders, and householders;

so too, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they are loved and revered by devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, other bodhisattvas, and all buddhas.
Furthermore, just as a lotus flower beginning to bloom can delight the hearts of all,
so too the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practicing the Prajñāpāramitā always has a smiling countenance and never frowns, thereby able to gladden all sentient beings.
Furthermore, as it is for worldly people that seeing lotus flowers in a dream is an auspicious sign,
so too is it an omen of good fortune for all humans and devas— even to hear or see a bodhisattva practicing the *prajñāpāramitā* within a dream— let alone to behold them in reality.
Furthermore, just as when a lotus flower first emerges, it is cherished and protected by both humans and non-humans;
so too, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva first studies the Prajñāpāramitā, they are guarded and protected by all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śakras, Brahmās, and the various devas.

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, they give rise to such a mind: they penetrate all the pāramitās according to reality, fulfill the Buddha-dharmas, and transform sentient beings; they sit beneath the Bodhi tree and realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, turning the wheel of the true Dharma—which cannot be turned by any śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, māras, Śakras, or Brahmās in the world—and they deliver all sentient beings throughout the boundless worlds of the ten directions, impartially rescuing them from the ocean of birth and death, and establishing them all within the Prajñāpāramitā.
For those who are without refuge, without support, and without protection, he acts as their protection;
for those who wish to see the Buddha, he immediately reveals him to them;
and he utters the lion’s roar.
They sported with supernatural powers,
extolled the Buddha’s merits,
and caused the assembly to yearn with longing.

Their mind is pure and unwavering; their intent is free from flattery and crookedness, remaining far removed from perverse thoughts. That is to say, they do not dwell upon the teachings of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas. Having exhausted all defilements, they are no longer subject to afflictions. Their bodies are free from hypocritical conduct and they distance themselves from improper demeanor; their speech is devoid of artifice, speaking only according to reality. They are always grateful for kindness received and repay even small favors with great weight; their hearts harbor no resentment, and their speech is ever gentle.

Cultivating the mind in this way of purity, one perceives neither that which can defile nor that which can be stained; there is no duality and no distinction, for its intrinsic nature is free from them.
"Great King!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they are able to have faith in the three kinds of purity of the Tathāgata, reflecting as follows:
"The sūtras state that the Tathāgata possesses the Dharma-body, the tranquil body, the unequaled body, the immeasurable body, the unshared body, and the vajra-body."
Regarding this certainty, one’s mind is free from doubt.
This is called being able to believe that the Tathāgata’s body is pure.
Furthermore, one reflects:
"The Sūtra says: 'The Tathāgata’s mouth is pure; thus he bestows the prediction of Buddhahood upon ordinary beings, and likewise grants the prediction of attaining Buddhahood to Bodhisattvas.
To believe such words is to be without contradiction."
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has forever departed from all faults; he is free from all defilements, devoid of afflictions, tranquil, and pure.
It is impossible for anyone—whether a deva, a māra, a śramaṇa, a brāhmaṇa, or even Brahmā—to find any lapse in the verbal karma of the Tathāgata.
This is called being able to believe in the purity of the Tathāgata’s speech.
Furthermore, the Sūtras state that the Tathāgata’s mind is pure.
Regarding the matters contemplated by the minds of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, neither śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, nor bodhisattvas—nor any among gods or humans—are able to know them.

Why is this? The mind of the Tathāgata is profoundly deep and difficult to enter; it is beyond all discursive thought and observation, transcends the sphere of conceptualization, and is without limit or measure, being equal to the realm of empty space.
Thus believing and knowing, the mind is free from doubt.
This is called being able to believe in the purity of the Tathāgata’s intention.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they reflect as follows:
"As the Buddha has taught, the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva, for the sake of all sentient beings, bears the heavy burden without fear or weariness.

His mind is firm and never regresses; he practices the various pāramitās in succession, accomplishing the Buddha-dharma without obstruction. Possessing boundless, peerless, and unshared dharmas, his words are definitive, his nature is courageous, and he accomplishes the vast deeds of the Tathāgata."
Regarding these matters, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is without doubt or confusion, receiving them with deep faith.
As the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they reflect thus:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom and sits at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), they are able to attain the unimpeded, pure divine eye, divine ear, knowledge of the minds of others, knowledge of past lives, and knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya-jñāna); in a single thought-moment, they penetrate the wisdom of the equality of the three periods of time."

Thus he observes all the world as it truly is: "Such beings, possessing misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind, reviling the noble ones, holding wrong views, and performing unwholesome deeds, shall upon the dissolution of the body after death fall into the evil destinies."

Thus, those beings who possess good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind; who do not revile the noble ones; who hold right views and engage in right action—upon the dissolution of the body after death, they shall be reborn in a happy destination.
Having observed the realm of sentient beings as it truly is, he forms this thought:
"In the past, I made a vow to practice the bodhisattva path to awaken myself and to awaken others; this vow should now be fulfilled."
"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they do not doubt or become confused regarding such matters, but accept them with faith exactly as they are.
Great King!"

The place where a Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood is called the "site of awakening. Self-awakening is called "right awakening," and bringing sentient beings to maturity is called "right universal awakening.
"Great King!
In this way, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, they know with faith that a Tathāgata appears in the world."
“Great King!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, upon hearing the teaching of the One Vehicle (ekayāna), they immediately believe and accept it. Why is this?
What all Buddhas have spoken is true and not false; all various other vehicles emerge from the Buddha-vehicle.
Just as in Jambudvīpa, the various names for cities, towns, and villages all belong to this continent;
likewise, the various names by which these vehicles are described all belong to the Buddha-vehicle.
Again, he thought:
"The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, employs skillful means; all his various teachings of the Dharma are true and not false. Why is this?"

“The World-Honored One teaches the Dharma according to the faculties and natures of sentient beings; therefore, he distinguishes and speaks of three vehicles, though in reality there is but a single path.
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, he further reflects:
“The Dharma taught by the Tathāgata through his profound and far-reaching voice is true and not false.”

Why is this? Even Śakra, Brahmā, and the other devas possess profound and far-reaching voices through their meager merits; how much more so, then, for the Tathāgata, who has accumulated merit through the practice of immeasurable billions of kalpas?
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they form this thought:
"The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma does not conflict with the various faculties of beings; whether superior, middling, or inferior, it brings all to fulfillment."
"Sentient beings each think, 'The Buddha is speaking specifically for me,' yet from the very beginning, all Buddhas have neither spoken nor shown anything.
Regarding such matters, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has no doubt, but possesses faith and understanding.
“Great King!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, he attains a subtle state of mind and reflects thus:
‘The world is a mass of blazing fires: namely, the fire of greed, the smoke of hatred, and the darkness of delusion.’”
How should one cause all sentient beings to attain liberation?
If one can penetrate the equality of all phenomena, this is called liberation.
To know phenomena as they truly are, like illusory appearances, and to skillfully contemplate causes and conditions without making conceptual distinctions—this is liberation.
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, they reflect thus:

"All dharmas are without origin, yet there is karmic retribution. Whatever words the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas speak, I know their intent; having known the intent, I contemplate the meaning; having contemplated the meaning, I perceive reality; and having perceived reality, I deliver sentient beings."

“Great King! When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, he skillfully employs expedient means to preach the Dharma for the sake of the multitudes, saying: ‘All dharmas are entirely without self, without sentient beings, without nourishers, without persons, without agents, without perceivers, without producers, and without viewers; they are empty and non-existent, lacking an independent nature, and arise from the conjunction of false conceptualizations.’”
"Great King!

If one says that all phenomena are entirely without self, up to and including being without a viewer, this is a statement in accordance with reality regarding emptiness and non-existence; even the conditions for birth are likewise so."
“Great King!
When one’s preaching of the Dharma accords with the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa), it is called ‘conforming to principle.

Not contradicting the characteristics of phenomena, being in accord with the Dharma, attaining entry into equality, and manifesting the underlying meaning—this is called ‘skillful preaching of the Dharma.’”
“Great King!

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, they attain unimpeded eloquence—namely, unattached eloquence, inexhaustible eloquence, continuous eloquence, uninterrupted eloquence, undaunted eloquence, fearless eloquence, uncommon eloquence, eloquence honored by gods and humans, and boundless eloquence.”

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they attain pure eloquence, namely: eloquence that is not hoarse, eloquence that is not confused, eloquence that is without fear, eloquence that is without arrogance, eloquence fully endowed with meaning, eloquence fully endowed with phrasing, eloquence that is not clumsy or harsh, and eloquence that is timely.

"Great King! When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, he does not shout because he is free from the fear of the majesty of the great assembly; he is not confused because he firmly abides in fearless wisdom; he has no dread because the Bodhisattva dwells among the multitude like a lion king; he is not arrogant because he is free from all afflictions; he is endowed with meaning because he does not speak what is meaningless and thoroughly penetrates the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*); he is endowed with flavor because he is skilled in understanding writing, treatises, characters, and worldly knowledge; and he is not clumsy or harsh because he has practiced skillful speech for immeasurable eons."
He teaches the Dharma in accordance with the four seasons: as he speaks in spring, so he speaks in autumn and winter.

That which should be spoken first is not spoken in the middle or last; that which should be spoken last is not spoken first or in the middle; and that which should be spoken in the middle is not spoken first or last, for he is skillfully aware of the proper timing.
“Great King!

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, he attains eloquence that causes all beings to rejoice. This consists of loving speech; his countenance is always smiling and never frowning; his words are meaningful and accord with reality; what he says is definitive and he does not deceive others; and he delights in various forms of discourse.”

He gladdens the multitude with gentle speech; his countenance is broad and harmonious, causing others to feel drawn to him. He speaks in accordance with the meaning so that hearers may attain realization; he speaks in conformity with the characteristics of phenomena for the sake of their benefit. He teaches with impartiality, his mind free from favoritism; he delivers definitive teachings, free from false words. With various forms of eloquence, he accords with the faculties and natures of the assembly, causing them to attain joy.
“Great King!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, they achieve great majestic power. Why is this?
"Because those who are not vessels do not hear it.
At that time, King Śūraṃgama addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, their mind is equanimous; how then could they fail to teach those who are not vessels?
The Buddha said to King Śūra: "Great King!"
The nature of the Prajñāpāramitā is inherently equal; it perceives neither the worthy vessel nor the unworthy vessel, and it perceives neither the speaker nor that which is spoken.
Sentient beings, through their delusions, perceive speaking and non-speaking.
Why is this? Because the Prajñāpāramitā is neither born nor extinguished, devoid of marks or conceptual differentiation, and like space, it pervades all things;
sentient beings are likewise neither born nor extinguished.
It is the same for śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas.

To dharmas that have no names, one provisionally establishes names, saying "this is a sentient being," "this is prajñā," "there is one who can speak," "there is something spoken," or "there is a listener. Yet, within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), they are all of one single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness (*animitta*).
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, because their majestic power is so weighty, those who are not vessels do not hear it.

"Great King! The *prajñāpāramitā* is not taught to sentient beings who are not vessels; it is not taught to followers of external paths; it is not taught to those who lack respect; it is not taught to those who lack correct faith; it is not taught to those who seek to trade the Dharma; it is not taught to those who crave gain and offerings; it is not taught to those who are jealous; and it is not taught to those who are blind, deaf, or mute."

Why is this? When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, their mind is free from stinginess; they do not conceal the profound Dharma, nor is it that they lack great compassion for sentient beings, for they do not abandon sentient beings.
Sentient beings perceive the Tathāgata and hear the True Dharma due to the roots of goodness cultivated in their past lives.

The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have no inherent intention to speak for this person or that; rather, it is only because those with heavy karmic obstructions fail to see or hear [the Buddha], even though he is very near to them.
At that time, King Śūra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what kind of sentient beings are capable of hearing the Dharma preached by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas?”
The Buddha told King Śūra: "Great King!
To those who possess right faith, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas immediately preach the Dharma."

Their faculties and natures are fully matured, making them fit vessels for the Dharma; they have planted roots of goodness under past Buddhas, their minds are free from flattery and crookedness, their deportment is perfectly composed, they do not seek fame or profit, and they draw near to virtuous friends.
"Those of sharp faculties understand the meaning through the words; they exert themselves for the sake of the Dharma and do not contradict the Buddha’s intent.
Great King! It is for such beings as these that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas preach the Dharma."
“Great King!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, he is able to act as a Dharma teacher, skillfully expounding the Dharma.
In what way does he skillfully expound the Dharma?
For the sake of benefiting the Buddha-dharma, one speaks of the Buddha-dharma, yet ultimately the Buddha-dharma cannot be seen;
though one speaks of the pāramitās, the pāramitās are ultimately unattainable;
though one speaks of bodhi, bodhi is ultimately unattainable.
Although they have severed the afflictions, it is said that the afflictions are ultimately unattainable;
although they act for the sake of nirvāṇa, it is said that nirvāṇa is ultimately unattainable;

although they act for the sake of the stage of entering the stream, the fruit of entering the stream, and so on up to the stage of entering arhatship and the fruit of arhatship, it is said that these four fruits and their respective stages of entry are ultimately unattainable.
Although they attain the fruit of a pratyekabuddha, that fruit of a pratyekabuddha is ultimately unattainable;
although they eliminate the view of a self, that view of a self is ultimately unattainable;
yet they speak of the existence of karmic retribution.
Yet it is said that karmic retribution is ultimately unattainable. Why is this?
That which is obtained through names and designations is not a real dharma.
The Dharma is not names; it is not the realm of speech. The Dharma cannot be deliberated upon and is not measurable by the mind.

Names are not the Dharma, and the Dharma is not names; yet, based on conventional truth, one provisionally speaks of its existence through false designations, speaking of a nameless Dharma as having a name.

Names are empty; emptiness possesses nothing. That which possesses nothing is not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*); that which is not the ultimate truth is the delusive dharma of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
"Great King!
This is called the skillful teaching of the Dharma by a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, through the power of skillful means he attains unimpeded eloquence and teaches this profound perfection of wisdom according to the faculties and dispositions of sentient beings."
The Śrīdevī-rāja-prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll One.
The Śrīdevī-rāja-prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll Two.
Translated by Prince Yueposhouna of the Kingdom of Ujjayinī during the Chen Dynasty.
Chapter Three: The Dharma-Dhātu Chapter.

At that time, King Śūraṃgama rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva study the perfection of wisdom and penetrate the profound realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu)?
At that time, the Buddha praised King Śūra, saying:
"Excellent, Great King!"
"Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well.
Thus did Śikhi-deva-rāja address the Buddha.
“World-Honored One!
We would indeed wish to hear it.
The Buddha addressed King Śūraṅgama, saying:
“Great King!

Because Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas possess prajñā, they draw near to spiritual friends, diligently cultivate vigor, and remain free from all hindrances and delusions; their minds attain purity, and with reverence and respect, they delight in practicing the conduct of emptiness, distance themselves from all views, cultivate the path of reality as it is, and are able to penetrate the dharma-realm.”
“Great King!
Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess prajñā, they draw near to spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).

They rejoice in them and revere them as if they were the Buddha. By virtue of this close proximity, they do not fall into indolence; they extinguish all evils and unwholesome dharmas, and cause the roots of goodness (kuśalamūla) to grow and flourish.”
Having extinguished the afflictions and distanced oneself from obstructing dharmas, one immediately attains purity of body, speech, and mental action.

Because of this purity, reverence arises; with a reverent mind, one practices the conduct of emptiness. By practicing the conduct of emptiness, one distances oneself from all views; by distancing oneself from all views, one cultivates the right path; and by cultivating the right path, one is able to perceive the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
The Victorious Heavenly King addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is the dharma-dhātu?”
The Buddha said to King Śūraṅgama: "Great King!
It is precisely as it truly is."
“World-Honored One!
What is reality as it truly is? “Great King!”
"It is precisely unchanging.
"World-Honored One,
in what way is it not different?"
“Great King! It is what is called ‘suchness’ (tathatā).
“World-Honored One!”
"What is suchness? "Great King!
This can be known through wisdom; it cannot be expressed in words."
Why is this? Because it transcends all letters and is free from the realm of speech and the realm of the mouth.

It is devoid of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); there is neither "this" nor "that. It is free from characteristics and signless, far removed from deliberation, and transcends the sphere of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*). It is without ideation or signs, transcending dualistic realms and surpassing all ordinary beings.
