It is free from the sphere of the ordinary, transcends all demonic activities, and is able to leave behind hindrances and delusions. It is not known by consciousness; it abides in no fixed location.

The tranquil noble wisdom, which is subsequently the sphere of non-conceptual knowledge, is devoid of self and what belongs to a self, being unattainable through seeking; it is without grasping or abandoning, without defilement or impurity, pure and free from stain, supreme and foremost, and by nature eternally immutable.
Whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, its nature and characteristics abide eternally.
Great King!
This is the Dharma-realm.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the Prajñāpāramitā, they cultivate these hundred kinds of ascetic practices within this dharma-realm, causing all sentient beings to fully penetrate and understand them.
"Great King!

This is called the *prajñāpāramitā*, the suchness of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the markless state of non-discrimination, the inconceivable realm, true emptiness, and the non-dual realm of all-knowledge and the knowledge of all modes."
At that time, King Śūra devaputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how can one realize and reach this Dharma-realm?”
The Buddha addressed King Jayasena, saying: "Great King!
By means of the supramundane prajñāpāramitā as realization, the subsequent non-conceptual wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna) arrives."
The Deva-rāja Vijaya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is the difference between realization (prāpti) and arrival (gati)?”
The Buddha said to King Śūraṅgama: “Great King!
To see reality as it is through the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is called ‘realization’; to penetrate it through knowledge is called ‘attainment.’”
The Victorious Heavenly King addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation that penetrate the Prajñāpāramitā are not the supramundane non-conceptual wisdom that follows [the path].”
The Buddha said to King Śūraṃjaya:
"It is not so, Great King! Why is this?"

The Prajñāpāramitā is profoundly deep and subtle; the wisdom derived from hearing is coarse and shallow and cannot perceive it. Because it is the ultimate truth (paramārtha), it cannot be measured by reflection; because it is a supramundane dharma, it cannot be practiced through cultivation.
“Great King!
The Prajñāpāramitā is thus profoundly deep, such that it cannot be seen by ordinary beings or those of the two vehicles. Why is this?
"Great King! It is like one born blind who cannot see various forms, or a seven-day-old infant who cannot even see the orb of the sun; if they cannot see even this, how much less can they practice?"
For example, during the heat of summer, there was a man traveling westward through a vast wilderness. Another man, coming from the west toward the east, asked him:
"I am now parched with thirst; where is water, and where is the cool shade of trees?"
That person replied: "Good man!
From here, traveling eastward, there are two roads—one to the left and one to the right. You should take the road to the right; there is a spring of clear water and the cool shade of trees."
"Great King! What do you think?
Although one hears this name and contemplates going there, can one thereby eliminate heat and thirst or obtain the taste of water?"
"No, World-Honored One!

Only when this person has reached that place, entered the pool to bathe, drunk the water, rested under the tree, and only then been freed from his heat and thirst, will he perceive the flavor of the water."
The Buddha said, “So it is, so it is!
Great King!”
One cannot penetrate the true *prajñāpāramitā* by means of the three types of wisdom.
"Great King! What is called 'the wilderness' is precisely *saṃsāra*."
"Person" refers to sentient beings;
"heat" is a name for afflictions (*kleśa*); "thirst" is craving (*tṛṣṇā*);
and the person coming from the east is none other than a bodhisattva.
The right path is the path to *sarvajñā*—the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*, who skillfully knows the paths of birth-and-death and the supramundane;
the clear, cool water is the so-called *prajñāpāramitā*;
and the shade of the tree is great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice two dharmas, they remain far removed from the paths of ordinary beings and the two vehicles.
"Great King!
This profound Prajñāpāramitā is formless and signless; through various skillful explanations, it enables all sentient beings to enter into it."
“Great King!

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, he knows, in accordance with reality, that the powers are empty, the fearlessnesses are empty, the unique qualities are empty, the aggregate of ethical discipline is empty, and the aggregates of concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation are empty; he knows that emptiness itself is empty, and the emptiness of the ultimate truth is empty, yet even the characteristic of emptiness cannot be apprehended.”
One does not grasp at the mark of emptiness, does not give rise to views of emptiness, does not cling to the mark of emptiness, and does not rely upon emptiness.
Because one does not thus grasp or adhere, one does not fall into [the extreme of] emptiness.
"Great King!

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, he remains far removed from all marks (*nimitta*). He does not perceive internal or external marks; he is free from the mark of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), free from the mark of discrimination, free from the mark of seeking, free from the mark of greedy attachment, free from the mark of objective spheres, free from the mark of cognitive objects, and free from the marks of the knower and the known."
The Victorious Heavenly King addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates thus as signless;”
"How do the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, further contemplate?
The Buddha told King Śūra: "Great King!"
The realm of all Buddhas is inconceivable. Why is this?
Because it is free from any objective realm.
When all sentient beings attempt to deliberate upon the realm of the Buddha, their minds become deranged and confused, unable to distinguish this from that. Why is this?
Because it shares the nature of empty space; it is inconceivable, unattainable through seeking, and transcends the sphere of discursive thought and observation.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not even perceive that the realm of ordinary beings can be apprehended or conceptualized, much less the realm of the Buddhas.

Nor does he rely upon any vows; though he practices giving, he does not cling to the reward of giving, and it is likewise with his observance of precepts, patience, diligence, concentration, and wisdom. He does not rely upon or cling to any merit, even up to nirvāṇa itself.
Why is this? Because it is free from "I" and "mine," being non-dual and without distinction, for its intrinsic nature is detached.

When this Dharma-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā was being taught, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways; Sumeru, the king of mountains, Mount Mucilinda, the Cakravāḍa Mountains, the Mahācakravāḍa Mountains, the Jewel Mountains, the Black Mountains, and the Great Black Mountains—all were utterly shaken.
Countless hundreds of thousands of billions of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas removed their upper robes and spread them as a seat for the Buddha, as high as Mount Sumeru.

Countless hundreds of thousands of Śakras, Brahmās, Lokapālas, and other celestial kings joined their palms in reverence and scattered various exquisite flowers—Māndārava, Mahāmāndārava, Mañjūṣaka, Mahāmañjūṣaka, white lotuses, red lotuses, pink lotuses, and blue lotuses. On Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, which was forty yojanas in length and breadth, the accumulated flowers completely filled the area up to the knees of the Buddha.
Immeasurable sons of the gods played various celestial music, which resounded spontaneously without being struck; sighing in the air, they exclaimed:
"Once more we behold the Buddha appearing in the world; once more we see him turning the wheel of Dharma."
Excellent!

All sentient beings in Jambudvīpa who diligently cultivate merit and plant many roots of goodness are fortunate to hear such profound Prajñāpāramitā; how much more so those in future ages who are able to have faith! Such sentient beings all practice within the realm of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of great nāga kings who, by means of their supernatural power, universally raised a great cloud and sent down a rain of fragrance that sprinkled Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and the trichiliocosm; yet those who listened to the Dharma perceived only the fragrant moisture and did not see the falling drops.
Immeasurable nāga maidens all joined their palms before the Buddha and offered praise.
Immeasurable gandharvas made offerings to the Buddha with exquisite music, while the hosts of yakṣas scattered various wonderful flowers.

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, in the immeasurable and boundless lands of the ten directions, all emitted white light from between their eyebrows, illuminating Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in this Sahā world; even those dark places within the trichiliocosm where the sun and moon do not shine were entirely bathed in that radiance.
Having illuminated the world, he returned to the place where the Buddha was, circumambulated him three times to the right, and entered through the crown of the Buddha’s head.
Immeasurable hundreds of thousands of brahmins, kṣatriyas, householders, and elders made offerings to the Buddha with ointments, powdered incense, banners, flowers, standards, and parasols.

At that time, among the assembly, seventy-two billion bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti); immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings attained the pure Dharma-eye, free from dust and stain; and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, King Śūra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā is devoid of words and beyond speech; how then does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the Prajñāpāramitā, preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings?”
The Buddha said to King Śūraṅgama: "Great King!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they teach the Dharma in this way:
For the sake of practicing the Buddha-dharma, it is taught that the Buddha-dharma is ultimately unattainable;
for the sake of maturing the pāramitās, the pāramitās are ultimately unattainable;
for the sake of purifying bodhi, bodhi is ultimately unattainable.
For the sake of nirvāṇa, dispassion, and cessation, yet nirvāṇa, dispassion, and cessation are ultimately unattainable;
for the sake of the fruits of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, and arhat, yet from srotāpanna up to arhat are ultimately unattainable;
for the sake of pratyekabuddhas, yet pratyekabuddhas are ultimately unattainable.
In order to sever the grasping at a self, yet both the self and grasping are ultimately unattainable.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices this profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this manner, the mind does not discriminate among any marks (*lakṣaṇa*). Neither the one who discriminates nor that which is discriminated can be found. Thus, they accord with *prajñāpāramitā* and do not oppose the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*); though remaining within *saṃsāra*, they do not contradict *prajñāpāramitā* and accord with the nature of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
The Victorious Heavenly King addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva accord with the characteristics of dharmas while not contradicting worldly truth?”
The Buddha said to King Śūraṅgama: “Great King!

A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who accords with the profound Prajñāpāramitā does not distance himself from form, sensation, perception, formations, or consciousness; he does not distance himself from the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; he does not distance himself from phenomena, yet he does not cling to the Prajñāpāramitā, nor does he distance himself from the Path.”
"Why is this? Because they are endowed with skillful means.
Thus did King Śūra address the Buddha.
“World-Honored One!
What is the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
The Buddha addressed King Śūra-deva, saying:
“Great King!

What are called the immeasurable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are endowed with loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; they do not abandon sentient beings and are always able to benefit them.”
“Great King!

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, they possess boundless loving-kindness, non-discriminative loving-kindness, Dharma-loving-kindness, unceasing loving-kindness, non-afflictive loving-kindness, beneficial loving-kindness, impartial loving-kindness, universally beneficial loving-kindness, and world-transcending loving-kindness; thus they accomplish such great loving-kindness as these.”
“World-Honored One!
What is great compassion?
The Buddha said:
“Great King!

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, seeing sentient beings suffering and without a place of refuge, he immediately resolves upon Bodhicitta to rescue and deliver them, diligently seeking the True Dharma. Having attained it himself, he explains it to sentient beings: to those who are stingy and greedy, he teaches the practice of giving;
to those who lack precepts or have broken them, he teaches the observance of the precepts.”
To those of an evil nature, teach the practice of patience;
to those who are indolent and lax, teach them to be diligent;
to those who are distracted, teach the practice of meditative concentration.
To teach the practice of Prajñā to those who are ignorant and deluded,
and though encountering suffering and affliction for the sake of delivering sentient beings, never to abandon the mind of Bodhi—
this is called Great Compassion.
“World-Honored One!
What is great joy?
The Buddha said:
"Great King!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, he reflects thus:
'The three realms are ablaze; I have already escaped from them, and therefore I give rise to joy.'"
I have severed the rope of birth and death with which I have long been bound; therefore, I give rise to joy.
I have emerged from the ocean of birth and death, amidst its various discursive thoughts and grasping at signs; therefore, I give rise to joy.
I have now toppled the banner of pride that has stood erect since beginningless time; therefore, I give rise to joy.
I give rise to joy because, by means of vajra-wisdom, I have destroyed the mountain of afflictions so that it shall never arise again;
I give rise to joy because I am myself secure and bring peace to others, having now finally awakened from this long slumber in the world bound by the darkness of ignorance and the fetters of craving;

I give rise to joy because I have now departed from all evil destinies and have pulled sentient beings out of the miserable paths, for while sentient beings have long been deluded in saṃsāra and did not know the way out, I have now rescued them and shown them the correct path, enabling them all to reach the city of sarvajñā (omniscience).
"This is called great joy. Great King!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, regarding forms seen by the eye, he gives rise to a mind of equanimity, neither attached nor detached."
It is the same for the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and tastes, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental phenomena.
"Great King!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they accomplish these four immeasurable minds."
At that time, King Śūra devaputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom manifest various signs for the sake of delivering sentient beings?”
The Buddha addressed King Śūraṅgama, saying: “Great King!

The characteristics of the Prajñāpāramitā cannot be apprehended, nor can the characteristics of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva be apprehended; yet, through the power of skillful means, he teaches and transforms sentient beings, manifesting from dwelling in the womb up to his entry into Nirvāṇa.”
Why is this? The various devas conceive of permanence, believing there is no falling away;

however, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the Prajñāpāramitā, they employ the power of skillful means to shatter this attachment. Thus, they manifest dwelling in a womb to cause those devas to give rise to the thought of impermanence: "If even one who is the most excellent, supreme, peerless, and unattached to the five desires—one whom desire cannot defile—is still subject to falling away, how much more so for other devas?"
Therefore, you should all refrain from further negligence and instead apply yourselves with diligent vigor, cultivating the Way with a single mind.
It is like seeing that even the sun has its setting; one thereby knows that the glow of a firefly cannot endure for long.
“Great King!
Furthermore, there are negligent devas who, because they are greedily attached to pleasure, do not cultivate the True Dharma.
Although they dwell in the same celestial palaces as the Bodhisattvas, they do not go to pay them homage, nor do they seek instruction or receive the Dharma; instead, they harbor such thoughts:”
"Let us play for now; we shall visit the Bodhisattva tomorrow.
They said to one another, "The Bodhisattva has always been with us here; why is his practice so late?"

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they cultivate diligence with such urgency as if their head were on fire; they shatter that heedlessness and manifest the consequences of falling away.
This manifestation is displayed for two reasons:
first, to cause the devas to abandon negligence; second, to enable all sentient beings to behold it.
"Great King!
There are furthermore inferior sentient beings in the world who are unable to behold the Buddha attaining the Unsurpassed Way and turning the Wheel of Dharma.

For the sake of these sentient beings, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva manifests as an infant or a young child playing in the inner palace. If the Bodhisattva were to manifest in any other form to preach the Dharma, the women of the inner palace would not have faith or joy; therefore, he manifests as an infant or a young child."
“Great King!

There are those of lofty conduct who are constantly able to remain detached from the secular world; for the sake of transforming them, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva manifests the act of leaving the household life.
Great King!”
Furthermore, there were devas and humans who thought:
"If one can attain the Noble Path by sitting upright and receiving the pleasures of gods and humans.
To transform them, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva manifested ascetic practices; he also manifested ascetic practices in order to subdue the various non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthikas).
“Great King!
Furthermore, there are devas and humans who have made vows for a long night, saying:
‘When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva proceeds to the site of enlightenment, we, the various devas, shall constantly present offerings.’”

“The Bodhisattva, in order to transform these sentient beings, manifested his arrival at the site of enlightenment so that the entire multitude might all obtain the causes and conditions for awakening.
Great King!
Furthermore, there were devas and humans who thought to themselves:

"Evil Māras and externalists obstruct the True Dharma; we pray that a Bodhisattva may sit at the site of enlightenment, subdue the evil Māras and all externalists, and cause all those with right faith to perceive the Dharma."
Once the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has attained the Way, throughout the trichiliocosm, various sounds in the void will praise him, saying:
"The Buddha-sun has appeared in the world; the fireflies have vanished."
All these devas and humans spoke these words:
"May we, in a future life, all attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, just as this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does now."
"For the sake of these sentient beings, I manifest sitting at the site of enlightenment.
Great King! Furthermore, there are devas and humans who speak thus:"

"I pray that you may behold this Great Master, who has attained all-encompassing wisdom, teacherless wisdom, and self-arisen wisdom; one who does not seek liberation through external means, whose faculties are fully matured, and who is a profound vessel for the Dharma."
"For the sake of these sentient beings, he manifests the turning of the Wheel of Dharma in its three revolutions and twelve aspects.
Great King! Furthermore, there are devas and humans who delight in hearing about nirvāṇa; for the purpose of transforming those beings, the Bodhisattva manifests nirvāṇa."
"Great King!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they are able to manifest such various signs as these.
Great King!"
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they are not reborn in difficult circumstances. Why is this?
Because those who lack merit do not even hear the name of the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, he is always free from all evil karma and never violates any of the precepts taught by the Buddha; his mind is devoid of envy, and having planted many roots of goodness under countless Buddhas of the past, he is fully endowed with merit, having accomplished great vows through wisdom and skillful means, and delights in tranquility while practicing with diligent perseverance.
"Great King!
Because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the ten wholesome paths of action by nature, he is not dragged into the hells by evil karma;
because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva observes the precepts without violation, he is not dragged into the realm of animals."
Because they naturally uphold the precepts;
the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is free from envy, does not fall among the hungry ghosts, is not born into families of wrong views, and always encounters spiritual friends.
Why is this? Because they have deeply planted roots of goodness in the presence of countless Buddhas in the past, their places of birth are all characterized by right view.
When Bodhisattvas take birth, their faculties are unimpaired, making them vessels for the Buddha-dharma.

Why is this? Because in past lives they made offerings to the Buddhas, heard the True Dharma, and paid reverence to the great assembly; therefore, their faculties are complete and their features are well-proportioned, making them vessels for the Buddha-dharma.
“Great King!

A Bodhisattva is not born in a borderland where people are of dull faculties and ignorant, unable to distinguish between good and evil, whose speech and meaning are not vessels for the Buddha-dharma, and who do not recognize śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas.”

Why is this? Because a bodhisattva’s birth necessarily occurs in a central land; possessing sharp faculties and wisdom, his speech is eloquent and clear, he is skilled in understanding the meaning of words, he is a fit vessel for the Buddha-dharma, and he is well-versed in the ways of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.
Why is this? It is because of the power of the wisdom of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva from previous lives.
"Great King!..."
Bodhisattvas are not born in the long-lived heavens, for there they would neither behold the Buddhas nor benefit sentient beings.
It is for this reason that Bodhisattvas take birth in the desire realm, manifesting their emergence from the world to bring benefit to sentient beings.
Why is this? Because of skillful means.
"Great King!..."
A bodhisattva is not born in a world that is empty; in such a place there is no Buddha, one does not hear the True Dharma, and one does not make offerings to the Sangha. Why is this?
Because wherever a bodhisattva is born, the Three Jewels are necessarily present, due to the power of their past vows.

If a bodhisattva hears the names of evil worlds, they immediately give rise to weary detachment and practice tranquility; with a mind free from indolence, they extinguish all unwholesome dharmas through every kind of goodness.
“Great King!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, by this causal condition, they are not born in places of difficulty.
Great King!”
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they do not forget the mind of awakening even in their dreams, let alone while awake.

Why is this? All bodhisattvas give rise to this mind, which is precisely the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. If this mind did not exist, there would be no Buddha; if there were no Buddha, there would be no Dharma; and if there were no Dharma, there would be no Saṅgha.
It is because of this mind that the Three Jewels, as well as devas and humans, come to exist.

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas always remain free from flattery and crookedness; they are upright, gentle, and harmonious, with minds that are pure and free from doubt regarding the Buddha-dharma. When others wish to hear and receive the teachings, they do not withhold profound meanings.
Free from jealousy regarding the Dharma, one distances oneself from the karma of the three miserable realms;
throughout the beginning, middle, and end, there is no sign of inconsistency between one's actions and one's words. One upholds and protects the Mahāyāna;
seeing fellow practitioners, one gives rise to reverence, encourages others to practice, and praises the Mahāyāna.
One should always conceive the thought of a Buddha toward the Dharma teacher, draw near to spiritual friends, and stay far away from evil associates.
"Great King!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, they thus accomplish the bodhicitta; by means of this mind, they attain the knowledge of past lives."

Why is this? Because they have already made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, upheld the True Dharma, cultivated pure precepts, and remained far removed from evil karma; thus, obstacles are forever absent, their minds are constantly joyful, they diligently practice with vigor, their minds are not distracted, and their mental wisdom is never lost.

Why is this? Great King! If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has already made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas in the past, he will then revere the True Dharma; because he values the Dharma, he extensively expounds it for others; to protect the True Dharma, he does not begrudge his own body or life. His three types of action—of body, speech, and mind—are pure; once these actions are purified, he becomes free from obstacles. Being free from obstacles, his mind is constantly joyful; because his mind is joyful, he exerts diligent effort. His mental nature is upright, and he is endowed with mindfulness and wisdom (*smṛti* and *jñāna*). By virtue of mindfulness and wisdom, he knows his past lives—one, ten, a hundred, a thousand, and even up to an infinite number.
“Great King!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they thus clearly know their past places of birth.

Having understood their past lives, they draw near to spiritual friends; through these spiritual friends, they do not lose the three matters regarding the Buddhas—namely, seeing, hearing, and mindfulness—and they constantly listen to the true Dharma.”

Making offerings to the Sangha Jewel never passes in vain; it is that which all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas constantly revere, prostrate to, and honor, and from which they never depart whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—namely, extensive learning.
"Great King!

One who upholds the pure precepts constantly hears the name of the *prajñāpāramitā* with their faculty of hearing; they always diligently cultivate the dharmas that assist the path and never depart from the three gates of liberation; they practice the four immeasurables and constantly hear the name of *sarvajñatā*."
“Great King!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, by this causal condition they draw near to spiritual friends.
Great King!”
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not associate with evil friends even in their dreams, let alone while awake. Why is this?

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not dwell together with those who break the precepts; they do not dwell together with those of wrong views, those lacking dignified deportment, those who live by wrong livelihood, those who speak meaningless words, those who are indolent, those who delight in dwelling within birth and death, those who turn their backs on bodhi, or those who take pleasure in worldly affairs.
"Great King!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices such dharmas as these, he remains far removed from evil associates.
Great King!"

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they are able to attain the pure body of a Tathāgata—namely, the equal body, the pure body, the inexhaustible body, the body attained through excellent cultivation, the dharma-body, the inconceivable body, the ineffable body, the tranquil body, the body equal to space, and the wisdom-body.
The Victorious Heavenly King addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
In what stage does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva abide to be able to attain the ten kinds of bodies of a Tathāgata?”
The Buddha said to King Śūraṅgama:
“A bodhisattva attains the body of equality in the first stage. Why is this?
Because they are free from all crookedness, have attained penetration into the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and perceive equality,
they obtain a pure body in the second stage (*dvitīyā bhūmiḥ*). Why is this?
Because of pure precepts,
one dwells in the third stage and attains an inexhaustible body. Why is this?
Because they have abandoned ill-will,
in the fourth stage they attain the well-cultivated body. Why is this?
Because they constantly and diligently cultivate the Buddha-dharma,
upon dwelling in the fifth stage, they then attain the Dharma-body. Why is this?
Because one perceives the principles of the various truths,
upon dwelling in the sixth stage, one attains a body free from applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*). Why is this?
Because the principle of dependent origination is not something known through vitarka and vicāra.
Abiding in the seventh stage, one attains the inconceivable body. Why is this?
Because they are fully endowed with skillful means,
they attain the body of tranquility in the eighth stage. Why is this?
Because they are free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and devoid of afflictions (*kleśa*).
Abiding in the ninth stage, they attain a body equal to space. Why is this?
The physical marks are immeasurable because they pervade all places.
By abiding in the tenth stage, one then attains the wisdom-body. Why is this?
"It is for the sake of accomplishing all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).
King Jayadeva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Is there no distinction between the body of a Tathāgata and the body of a bodhisattva?"
The Buddha told King Śūra-deva:
"There is no difference in their bodies; it is only that their merits differ.
King Śūra-deva said:
"What is the meaning of this?
"Great King! There is no distinction between the bodies of a Buddha and a Bodhisattva."
"Why is this? Because all dharmas are of one and the same nature and characteristic, yet differ in their qualities.
"World-Honored One!"
"How is it that there are distinctions among their merits?
The Buddha said,
"Great King!"
I shall now provide an analogy for the King to clarify this point.
For example, consider a precious gem: whether it is adorned or unadorned, how does the gem itself differ?
Likewise, while there is a distinction between the merits of a Buddha and those of a Bodhisattva, there is no difference in their Dharmakāya.

Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s merits are entirely perfected, extending throughout the ten directions and pervading the realm of sentient beings; they are pure and free from defilement, with obstacles forever absent.
The body of a Bodhisattva, however, has not yet perfected its merits, as there remain residual obstructions.
For example, as with the moon on the first day of the month or on the fifteenth day, although there are differences in its waning and waxing, the nature of the moon remains unchanged.
Likewise, all these bodies are entirely firm and solid, like vajra, and cannot be destroyed.

Why is this? Because the three poisons cannot break them, worldly dharmas cannot defile them, and the sufferings of the evil realms or the human world cannot oppress them. They have completely distanced themselves from birth, old age, sickness, and death; they are able to subdue non-Buddhists and transcend the realm of Māra; they do not turn toward the vehicles of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas. For these reasons, they are indestructible.
“Great King!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, he is well able to skillfully guide all the worlds of devas, humans, and asuras.”
For example, if there is a person who is skilled at being a guide, kings, elders, householders, and others will all employ him;
so it is with the Bodhisattva—Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, and all Buddhas alike employ them as guides.
Furthermore, just as a skilled guide is respected by kings, brahmins, elders, and householders throughout the world,
so too is the Bodhisattva honored and sustained by devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and those in training and those beyond training.
Furthermore, just as travelers who are weary from the dangers and terrors of a vast wilderness encounter a skilled guide who can lead them to safety, so too is the Bodhisattva:
through the power of skillful means, he guides sentient beings out of the perils of the bandits of affliction within birth and death, leading them to secure deliverance.
Furthermore, just as a poor person relies on a wealthy elder to escape from perilous difficulties,

so too do the brahmins, the Nirgranthas, and other non-Buddhist practitioners rely upon bodhisattvas who practice the perfection of wisdom within the midst of birth and death in order to achieve liberation.
Furthermore, just as a wealthy elder with immeasurable wealth and resources is enjoyed by all people,
so too is the bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) enjoyed by the sentient beings within the six realms of saṃsāra.

Furthermore, just as a wealthy elder who wishes to cross through dangerous and difficult terrain must have many companions and be fully provided with food, drink, and provisions before he can pass through;

so too it is with the Bodhisattva: wishing to transcend the world, they gather all sentient beings through merit and wisdom, delivering them from the perils of birth and death until they reach *sarvajñā* (omniscience).
Furthermore, just as a person traveling a great distance carries many precious treasures for the sake of gaining profit, so too is the Bodhisattva:
from the ocean of birth and death until reaching *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), they extensively cultivate merit and wisdom for the sake of attaining omniscience.
Furthermore, just as worldly people seek wealth without satiety, the Bodhisattva’s delight in the Dharma is likewise free from any sense of weariness.
Moreover, just as a leader excels others in four matters—namely, wealth, preeminence, high status, and authoritative speech; so too does the Bodhisattva excel others in these four respects.
The Bodhisattva is also like this: rich in the station of merit, possessing the most supreme dharmas, sovereign, and free from discordant speech.
Furthermore, just as a person who is a skilled guide leads others to a great city;
so too is the Bodhisattva, for they are well able to lead others to the city of sarvajñā (all-knowledge).
“Great King!

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, he thoroughly understands the paths that may be traveled and those that may not, what is deviant and what is correct, what is secure and wholesome, where there is water and where there is none, the characteristics of curves and straightness, and the way of transcendence; he has complete mastery over all these.
"Great King!
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows the unerring path; whatever path he demonstrates does not contradict the faculties of sentient beings.
For those of the Great Vehicle, he demonstrates the unsurpassed path and does not speak of the paths of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas."
For those of the Hīnayāna disposition, he shows the path of the śrāvaka and does not speak of the Mahāyāna;
for those with the faculties of a pratyekabuddha, he shows the way of the pratyekabuddha and does not speak of the path of sarvajñatā;
and for those attached to the view of self, he teaches the path of non-self.
For sentient beings attached to phenomena, he teaches the path of emptiness;
for those attached to the two extremes, he teaches the Middle Way;
for those who are distracted, he teaches *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, rather than speaking of distraction itself.
For sentient beings who engage in conceptual proliferation, he demonstrates the path of suchness without uttering words;
for those attached to birth and death, he demonstrates the path of nirvana without speaking of the mundane world;
and for those lost on the road, he expounds the true path.
"Great King!
This is called the Bodhisattva’s knowledge of the wrong and right paths.

**Chapter Four: The Foundations of Mindfulness** *The Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra Spoken by the Victorious Heavenly King* At that time, the Victorious Heavenly King rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, addressing him thus:
“World-Honored One!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom is able to know in this way what is the path and what is not the path, upon what does their mind dwell?”
The Buddha addressed King Śūraṅgama, saying: "Great King!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, their mind is upright and undistracted."
Why is this? Because they maintain mindfulness of the body, mindfulness of feelings, mindfulness of the mind, and mindfulness of phenomena.

Whenever a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva travels through cities, towns, or villages and hears reports of gain or fame, they should properly recollect them as being fetters of affliction, just as taught in the Buddha’s precepts.
“Great King!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom practice mindfulness of the body?
With regard to those unwholesome and non-virtuous dharmas associated with the body, he completely abandons them through knowledge as it truly is.”

Contemplate the faults of the body, from the soles of the feet up to the crown of the head: this body is without self, impermanent, and subject to decay; it is merely held together by tendons and sinews, foul-smelling and putrid, repulsive in color and loathsome, such that one does not delight in seeing it.
Observing in this way, no desire whatsoever arises within the body, and the notion of a "self" in the body does not occur.
By these causes and conditions, all corresponding wholesome dharmas are fully brought into accord.
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom attend to sensation?
He reflects thus:
"All sensations are suffering."

Inverted sentient beings falsely give rise to the perception of pleasure; ordinary people, in their ignorance, take suffering to be pleasure, whereas the noble ones teach that everything is suffering.
One should diligently practice with vigor for the sake of its cessation, and likewise instruct others to study this Dharma.

Having performed this contemplation, he constantly reflects upon feeling (*vedanā*) but does not act in accordance with feeling; he practices to sever feeling and causes others to train in this as well.
What is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) regarding the mindfulness of the mind (*citta*)?
He reflects thus: "This mind is impermanent, yet it is called permanent;

it perceives suffering as pleasure, non-self as self, and impurity as purity. It is restless and unstable, shifting and changing with great speed. It is the root of the fetters and the gateway to all evil realms; through the causes and conditions of affliction, it destroys the path of virtue. It is the master of greed, hatred, and delusion, and is therefore untrustworthy."
Among all phenomena, the mind is the foremost; if one understands the mind well, one will fully comprehend all phenomena.
The various worlds are all created by the mind, yet the mind does not see itself.
Whether good or evil, all arise from the mind.
The nature of the mind revolves like a whirling firebrand; it is as easily turned as a horse, as capable of burning as fire, and as prone to sudden surges as water.

"Contemplating in this manner, remain unmoved within mindfulness and do not follow the movements of the mind; cause the mind to follow yourself. If you can subdue the mind, then you will subdue all phenomena."
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom attend to the Dharma?

They know evil and unwholesome dharmas as they truly are—namely, desire, hatred, delusion, and other afflictions—and they cultivate their antidotes: the antidote to desire, the antidote to hatred, and the antidote to delusion.
Having understood this, one immediately turns away from giving rise to thoughts regarding those phenomena and causes others to do so as well.
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the *prajñāpāramitā* give rise to thoughts regarding objects?
If one perceives forms, sounds, odors, tastes, or tangibles, one should reflect thus:
"How can I give rise to craving and attachment toward those dharmas that are not real?"
This is that which ordinary, ignorant people cling to, and it is unwholesome.

As the World-Honored One has said: "From craving arises attachment; from attachment arises delusion; because of delusion, one does not know wholesome dharmas or unwholesome dharmas; by these causes and conditions, one is born into the evil realms."
“The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not himself let [the Dharma] leak away or be lost, nor does he cling to sense objects; he causes others to do likewise.
Great King!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the mindfulness of the araṇya while practicing the Prajñāpāramitā, he reflects in this way:”

"An araṇya is the dwelling place of those who are free from contention and a place of tranquil abiding. Within this place, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and those with the knowledge of others' minds can all perceive my mind and its mental factors; therefore, one should not give rise to wrong thoughts here."
He immediately attains relinquishment, maintains right mindfulness toward the Dharma, and diligently practices it.
"Great King!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, he reflects in this way:"

"Urban centers and villages are not places where those who have left the household life should frequent; one should not go to such places as taverns, brothels, royal cities, or venues for gambling, singing, dancing, and music."
"Thus, one should remain entirely detached from them. Great King!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā and hears of gain and fame, they give rise to right mindfulness and reflect thus:"

"He accepts this wealth for the sake of generating the merit of giving, not out of greedy attachment; he does not give birth to children within himself, nor does he say, 'This is my wealth. He universally provides for all who are poor. One who practices in this manner is praised by others, and ultimately never conceives of an 'I' or 'mine.'"
Again, he thought:

"All people praise me for my renown as a generous donor, yet worldly existence is impermanent and perishes in an instant. How could a wise person, following that which is impermanent, unreal, non-eternal, and without a master, give rise to the notions of 'I' and 'mine'?"
"Great King! When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, regarding the mindfulness of precepts taught by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, he reflects thus:
'All Buddhas of the past studied these precepts, attained the Unsurpassed Way, and reached Nirvāṇa;'"
"The same will be true for all Buddhas of the future and those of the present.
Having understood this, one should practice with diligent vigor.
"Great King! [he said.]

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, for the sake of transforming sentient beings as well as themselves, they practice few desires and contentment, wear rag-patch robes (*pāṃśukūla*), and maintain constant mental purity. Their power of faith is firm and steadfast; they would rather lose their body and life than transgress the precepts. Their minds are free from arrogance, and though they travel through cities and towns in tattered clothing, they feel no shame. They remain far removed from indolence and constantly cultivate diligence; until what is to be done is accomplished, they never cease midway. Regarding rag-patch robes, they perceive neither faults nor defects, such as being old, worn, or ruined, and they never treat them with contempt. Rather, they take up only their virtues: "Only those who have transcended desire wear these robes; they are praised by the Tathāgata, for they extinguish stinginess, greed, and attachment."
Nor does he praise himself, saying, "I am able to master this," nor does he ever speak disparagingly of others who cannot master it.
A practitioner such as this is honored by the devas, praised by the Buddhas, protected by the bodhisattvas, and revered by both brahmins and kṣatriyas.
“Great King!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, they cultivate pure conduct in this manner.
At that time, King Śūra devaputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Since a Bodhisattva of lofty conduct is able to practice the Prajñāpāramitā, why would he wear robes made of discarded rags?
The Buddha addressed King Śūra-deva, saying:
“The great bodhisattvas will protect the people of the world.
Why is this? Because the inclinations of sentient beings in the world toward what they wish to see differ.”
"Great King!
What do you think?
How does the noble conduct of a bodhisattva compare to that of the World-Honored One?"
The Victorious Heavenly King said:
"Even with a hundred thousand myriads of koṭis of Ganges-sands, calculation and analogy cannot reach even one part of it. Why is this?
“The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is the Great Dharma King; possessing all-encompassing wisdom, there is not a single dharma that he does not clearly perceive.
“Great King, what do you think?”

When the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, manifest ascetic practices among the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, and non-humans throughout the four continents, and praise the merits of the dhūta austerities, for what purpose is this done?
The King said:
“World-Honored One!

For the sake of teaching and transforming those sentient beings who are ready to be saved, as well as those bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds, you have preached antidotes for those who have not yet severed their afflictions.”
The Buddha said, “So it is, so it is!
Great King!”
It is the same for a Bodhisattva of noble conduct who wears rag-robes.
For this reason, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, he possesses many skillful means to benefit sentient beings.
“Great King!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, he manifests in the world as one who possesses only three robes. Why is this?

Because the mind is content, one does not seek further; this is precisely "fewness of desires. Because one does not seek or solicit, there is no accumulation. Since there is no accumulation, there is no loss. Because there is no loss, suffering does not arise. Because suffering does not arise, one is free from all afflictions. Because one is free from all afflictions, there is no attachment. Because there is no attachment, this constitutes the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*).
“Great King!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, he enters cities, towns, and villages to carry his alms bowl and beg for food for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.”

Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s mind is permeated by great compassion; he observes impoverished and suffering sentient beings as they truly are, enabling them to attain wealth and joy, and thus accepts their offerings.

If entering a town or village, one maintains dignified deportment, with a mind upright and undisturbed, properly restraining the sense faculties, and looking ahead only six feet. Plowing the earth with two oxen as it were, one begs for food according to the Dharma, proceeding in sequence without bypassing poor households. One accepts food in moderation and never takes more than needed; from what has been obtained, one further sets aside a portion intended for giving and making offerings.
Why is this? Because offerings made out of faith are difficult to digest; they are for the sake of generating merit.
"Great King!..."
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they eat while remaining seated in one place without moving.
Why is this? Because once seated at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), even if Māra comes to harass and disturb them, they do not move.

Regarding supramundane meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and gnosis (*jñāna*), the emptiness of all phenomena, the path of reality as it is (*yathābhūta-āryamārga*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), suchness (*tathatā*), and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*)—in all these dharmas, he remains entirely unmoving.
Why is this? Because the dharma of sarvajñā (all-knowledge) is attained in a single sitting; for this reason, one practices eating in a single sitting.
"Great King!..."
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, they manifest such acts of begging for alms through the power of skillful means.
"Great King!

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, they train in the conduct of an araṇya-dweller. This means they constantly cultivate the pure life (brahmacarya), do not give rise to transgressions among the sense faculties, deeply delight in extensive learning, possess the strength to endure spiritual practice, remain free from the fear of self, do not harbor attachment to the body, and always abide in tranquility."

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has left the household life within the True Dharma and maintains the pure precepts of the three wheels; he thoroughly understands the characteristics of dharmas as taught by the Tathāgata, and is fully capable of comprehending the precepts for the three types of people—young, middle-aged, and old.
Not following external conditions, one reflects with one's own mind, censuring and rejecting worldly dharmas while praising those that transcend the world.

One subdues the sense faculties and does not dwell upon unwholesome objects. Residing in an araṇya at a place free from hardships, one goes for alms in a village neither too far nor too near; there is clear spring water for easy washing, and the forest abounds in flowers and fruit. It is free of predatory birds and beasts, and the mountain caves are silent, secluded, and rarely visited by people—such places one should make one’s dwelling.

Regarding the Dharma one has previously heard, one should diligently recite it three times each day and night; the voice should be neither too loud nor too low, the mind should not dwell on external objects, and with single-minded focus, one should maintain the recitation within one's breast at all times.
If a brāhmaṇa or a kṣatriya comes to the aranya, one should invite them to sit.
If they are unwilling, one should urge them with earnestness.
Observing these sentient beings, one should preach the Dharma according to their faculties and dispositions, causing them to attain joy, faith, and acceptance, and to practice accordingly.

Thus, being fully endowed with skillful means, one is immediately free from the notion of self; because there is no self, one does not give rise to fear regarding the araṇya, and being free from fear, one delights in practicing tranquility.
"In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva manifests the practice of an araṇya through the power of skillful means. Great King!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they are well able to contemplate their conduct and reflect as follows:"
"Within this world, all food and drink are pure and fragrant; yet once touched by the fire of the body, they immediately become impure, putrid, and foul-smelling.
All ordinary people, being foolish and lacking wisdom, are attached to this body and to such food and drink."
"If one observes according to reality by means of noble wisdom, they will give rise to revulsion and find no pleasure in attachment.
"Great King! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), he reflects in this way:"
"If I frequently practice anger, I will give rise to evil karma; I must now abandon it.
I shall proceed toward the Path with a straightforward mind and engage in true contemplation, rather than merely speaking with my mouth."
“Great King! When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, he reflects thus:

‘If any phenomenon has arising, it is by way of causes and conditions; the causes and conditions of phenomena, moreover, arise from conditions. How could a wise person commit an offense or fall into error regarding these phenomena produced from false causes and conditions?’”

Within the body of a bodhisattva, any obstructive factors to wholesome dharmas are spontaneously severed and eliminated; if they are unable to sever the obstructive factors to wholesome dharmas in others, their minds give rise to equanimity and do not produce ignorance.
What is meant by "obstructing wholesome dharmas"?
It is to lack reverence for the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, and pure precepts;
and to lack respect for one's fellow students.
Whether old or young, high-ranking or lowly, they look down upon others;
they incline toward the five desires and turn their backs on Nirvana, giving rise to the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-force, and the view of a person;
clinging to emptiness, they give rise to the view of annihilationism, while clinging to existence, they give rise to the view of eternalism.
They distance themselves from the noble and holy ones and draw near to ordinary worldlings;
they abandon those who uphold the precepts and rely on those who violate them;
they attach themselves to evil friends and stay far away from virtuous spiritual teachers.
Upon hearing the profound Dharma, they immediately give rise to slander;
their deportment is disordered, their speech lacks eloquence, and their minds are shrouded by afflictions as they become fully possessed of deceit and crookedness;
clinging greedily to gain and offerings, they give rise to five kinds of pride:
First, noble lineage; second, noble ancestry; third, superior views; fourth, a noble land; fifth, a large following;
they assist those with evil views and abandon those who encounter the good.
They praise women, children, and non-Buddhists;
they take no delight in practicing in forest hermitages (āraṇya), do not understand the practice of moderation in eating, and do not draw near to their teachers.
Although they may engage in recitation and study, they do not know the proper timing, and even when they encounter wholesome dharmas, they fail to give rise to even a slight sense of respect.
Seeing evil, they feel no fear; like an elephant without a goad or a horse without a bridle, they are unrestrained by their own indulgence.
They delight in giving rise to anger and resentment, failing to cultivate a heart of loving-kindness.
Seeing suffering, they do not feel compassion; encountering illness, they do not provide care; facing death, they feel no dread.
Amidst a mass of fire, they do not seek to escape; they do what should not be done and fail to do what should be done; they cannot weigh or deliberate;
they examine what is inconceivable and seek what they do not expect;
they call non-emergence emergence, call what is not a path a path, and claim to have attained what they have not attained, remaining far removed from the great and sublime Dharma.
They disparage the Mahāyāna and praise the Lesser Vehicle;
they revile those who follow the Mahāyāna and laud those of inferior learning;
they take great pleasure in inciting strife and engage in foul speech and coarse words.
Their minds lack compassion and cause others to feel fear;
their speech is coarse and vulgar, devoid of even a single word of truth;
they delight in and cling to frivolous proliferation, never relinquishing it.
"Great King!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, such matters as these are called 'obstructions to wholesome dharmas.
Great King!"
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they extinguish all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and cultivate the practice of emptiness, reflecting as follows:

"The objects of observation are entirely empty and non-existent; the observing mind is likewise so. There is no distinction between the two—the subject that observes and the object observed. All phenomena have a single characteristic, which is the characteristic of signlessness (*animitta*)."

Reflecting in this way, one eliminates internal and external signs; one does not perceive the body, does not perceive the mind, and does not perceive phenomena. One cultivates śamatha and vipaśyanā in successive continuity: through vipaśyanā, one sees phenomena as they truly are, and through śamatha, the mind is single-pointed and undistracted.
When a bodhisattva has thus cultivated the practice of contemplation, they immediately attain pure precepts; because the precepts are pure, their conduct is likewise so.
This is called the pure practice of contemplation of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā.

“Great King! When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, he upholds the treasury of the Tathāgata’s true Dharma and listens to and receives the true Dharma. He does so not for the sake of gain or offerings, but for the sake of protection; not for the sake of honor, but so that the lineage of the Triple Gem shall not be severed; not for the sake of fame, but to protect and sustain the practice of the Mahāyāna. He brings deliverance and peace to sentient beings who have no refuge, grants the eye of wisdom to those who lack it, reveals the path of the Śrāvaka to those who cultivate the Hīnayāna, and manifests the Great Way to those who wish to practice the Mahāyāna.”
Listening to the Dharma in this way is for the sake of unsurpassed wisdom; it is never for the sake of attaining an inferior vehicle. "Great King!

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, he skillfully knows the Vinaya—namely, the Vinaya and the practice of the Vinaya; the profundity of the Vinaya and the subtlety of the Vinaya; purity and impurity; the Prātimokṣa with faults and without faults; and the Vinaya of the Śrāvakas and the Vinaya of the Bodhisattvas."
"Great King!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they thoroughly understand all such disciplinary codes (vinaya).
Great King!"

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they skillfully know all modes of conduct and precepts; they skillfully train in the precepts of the śrāvakas, the precepts of the pratyekabuddhas, and the precepts of the bodhisattvas, having thus cultivated their conduct of morality.
If one observes that another's deportment does not accord with the assembly, one should immediately distance oneself and refrain from associating with them;
however, if there is a śramaṇa whose ethical conduct and deportment are exemplary, one should draw near to them.

If a Brahmin or follower of another school practices and encourages the cultivation of the Vinaya, and thus cultivates these precepts with sincerity, his mind will be free from artifice and deceit, and jealousy will be extinguished. He practices giving himself and encourages others to do so, praises giving, and feels sympathetic joy upon seeing others give, never thinking:
"One should give only to me; do not give to others."
One should simply reflect:
"All sentient beings lack much; they suffer from hunger, cold, and hardship. May they obtain wealth and enjoy peace and happiness in this present life."
"Because of hearing the Dharma, there will be peace and happiness in future lives.
I should now diligently cultivate the Way so that, together with all sentient beings, we may equally attain transcendence.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s mind free from envy, attaining equanimity toward all sentient beings, and practicing giving universally for the sake of all beings.
One cultivates morality, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), with a non-dual mind. Why is this?

The dharmas thus cultivated are shared with all sentient beings; taking them as one's objective field, one brings about the swift accomplishment of the Path, so that from the fires of birth and death, one both effects one’s own liberation and causes others to be liberated as well.
It is, for example, like a householder who has six sons, all of whom are young and whom he loves with impartial affection.
While the householder is abroad, a fire breaks out in his home.
Great King!
"What do you think?
Does the elder have the thought:
'Among these six children, shall I save them one after another, or all at once?'"
"No, World-Honored One! Why is this?
Because the father’s mind is impartial toward his son."
“Great King! It is the same for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Ordinary beings are greedily attached; dwelling within the burning house of birth and death in the six realms, they do not know how to escape.”

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the Prajñāpāramitā, they use a mind of equanimity and various skillful means to guide and transform sentient beings so that they emerge [from suffering], establishing them all within the realm of tranquility.
“Great King! When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, they are equal toward all dharmas.

That is to say: making offerings to the Tathāgata through the Dharma; making offerings to the Tathāgata with various ritual implements; making offerings to the Tathāgata through practicing according to reality; benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings; protecting the wholesome dharmas of all sentient beings; skillfully teaching and transforming sentient beings in accordance with their needs; practicing the Bodhisattva path without contradicting one’s words; and seeking Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi with a mind free from weariness. If one can act in this way, it is called making offerings to all Buddhas, rather than making offerings with material requisites.”
For what reason?
Great King!
The Dharma is the body of the Buddha; if one makes offerings to the Dharma, one is making offerings to the Buddha.
"Great King!

All Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have come from the practice of suchness; they act solely for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings, protecting their wholesome dharmas and conforming to them. Were it otherwise, they would violate their original vows."
One who is indolent and lazy cannot achieve the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*). Why is this?
Because for a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is shared with all sentient beings; if there were no sentient beings, how could a Bodhisattva attain enlightenment?
“Great King!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, making an offering of the Dharma to the Tathāgata is what constitutes a true offering.

Through such an offering, he eradicates the conceit of ‘I’ and detaches himself from worldly affairs. Having shaved off his hair and beard, he no longer maintains ties with his parents, brothers, or relatives, as if they were already dead. His appearance, clothing, and demeanor become extraordinary; carrying his alms bowl, he enters cities and towns, and even goes to the homes of his own kin or to the houses of outcasts (*caṇḍāla*) to beg for food with a humble mind, reflecting thus:”
"My life belongs to others; it is sustained by their food. For this reason, I am able to eliminate my pride.
He further reflects:
"I should now act in accordance with the intentions of my preceptors, elders, and fellow students so as to bring them joy, so that they may hear the Dharma they have not heard before."
"If one sees others being angry, quarreling, or disputing, one should immediately practice patience, humble oneself, and avoid them.
Great King!
This is how a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva [acts]."
Practicing the *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, one eradicates the conceit of "I" (*asmimāna*).
"Great King,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, they give rise to firm and correct faith."

Why is this? Because they have planted many merits in past lives; the power of their roots of goodness is strong and they are fully endowed with virtuous causes. Having accomplished right view, they do not believe in external paths; their inner minds are pure and they do not rely on other teachers. Their mental conduct is harmonious and upright, remaining far removed from flattery and crookedness. Their faculties are sharp and intelligent, and they are endowed with *prajñā*. Free from all hindrances and obstructions, their minds are pure; they distance themselves from evil associates and draw near to virtuous friends. They seek out wholesome words and do not give rise to indolence; regarding the Dharma they hear being preached, they understand the merits of the Buddha.
The Victorious Heavenly King addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We pray that, out of great compassion and pity, you will explain for us the Tathāgata’s merits and his great majestic spiritual power.”
The Buddha said to King Śūra: “Great King!
Listen attentively, listen attentively!”
"Reflect upon this well; I shall proclaim for the sake of the King a small portion of the Tathāgata’s divine virtues.
"Excellent, World-Honored One!
Indeed, we wish to hear it."
The Buddha said, “Great King!

The Tathāgata is endowed with boundless great compassion, which universally illumines all sentient beings and those comprised within the category of sentient beings; it even pervades the entirety of the ten directions throughout the realm of empty space, being utterly immeasurable.”
The great compassion of the Tathāgata is that which is not shared by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas.
Why is this? Because it is an unshared dharma (āveṇika-dharma).
In the worlds of the ten directions, there is not a single sentient being who is not illuminated by his great compassion.

Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma is inexhaustible; for the sake of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions, he preaches the Dharma through various causes and conditions without end, whether for one kalpa, a hundred kalpas, a thousand kalpas, or even immeasurable kalpas.

If all sentient beings were to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding various expressions, phrases, and meanings within the realm of sentient beings, he would distinguish and explain each one for every single being in the mere twinkling of an eye, such that no one could refute him.

Furthermore, the Tathāgata is the realm of unimpeded meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Even if all sentient beings in every world-system were to abide in the tenth stage (*bhūmi*) and enter various samādhis for hundreds of thousands of billions of eons to contemplate the Tathāgata’s concentration, they would be unable to fathom it.
Furthermore, the body of the Tathāgata is immeasurable.
Why is this? Because according to what beings wish to see, he can manifest various forms in a single thought-moment.

Furthermore, the Tathāgata possesses the pure divine eye; throughout all worlds and among infinite sentient beings—be it one sentient being or one world—he perceives all such matters within these worlds as clearly as if looking at an āmalaka fruit in the palm of his hand, which cannot be seen by the eyes of gods or humans.

The Tathāgata further possesses the pure divine ear; regarding all sentient beings, according to their respective species and the differences in their voices, the Tathāgata hears them all and understands their meanings.

Furthermore, the Tathāgata possesses the pure knowledge of others' minds; regarding all sentient beings in all worlds—their actions, their thoughts, and the retributions they receive—the World-Honored Tathāgata fully understands them all within a single moment of thought, whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is always in a state of meditative concentration, being free from distraction.
"Great King!..."
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, possess no loss of mindfulness, their minds are not distracted, and their faculties have no other objects.
Why is this? Because they are free from the habitual tendencies of afflictions, being supremely pure, tranquil, and stainless.
Those who possess afflictions have minds that are distracted and thus grasp at various objects.
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is free from outflows and untainted; having attained sovereign mastery and equanimity regarding all dharmas, he constantly abides in samādhi and samāpatti.
"Great King!

When the Tathāgata, by means of a single majestic demeanor and samādhi, proceeds through his life until his parinirvāṇa, there is not a single deva or human who can know it; how much less so when the Tathāgata has cultivated immeasurable, boundless, and myriad billions of samādhis over the course of immeasurable kalpas?"
"Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is immeasurable, inconceivable, and unobservable.
At that time, King Śūra spoke to the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I have heard that the Tathāgata attained Buddhahood after practicing for three asaṃkhyeya kalpas; why then do you say he practiced for immeasurable kalpas?
The Buddha said:
"No, Great King! Why is this?

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* through immeasurable effort and power; it is not by merely passing such a number of kalpas that one first attains entry into the principle of the equality of dharmas and is called a Buddha."
The Deva-rāja Vijaya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Excellent, excellent!”
All sentient beings constantly practice various virtues, remain far removed from obstructive karma, rejoice in the fruit of Buddhahood, and cultivate the practices of a Bodhisattva.
World-Honored One!

If there are sentient beings who, upon hearing of the Tathāgata’s great supernormal powers, give rise to joy in their hearts, accept them with faith, and praise them, you should know that such persons will before long become vessels for these supernormal powers; how much more so for those who receive, uphold, read, recite, transcribe, and proclaim them—such people as these are beyond measure.

The Buddha said, "It is so, Great King. These sentient beings are protected by the Tathāgata; having already planted roots of goodness and having made offerings to countless Buddhas in the past, they are now able to hear of the great supernormal powers of the World-Honored Tathāgata."

If these good men and women have no doubt in their hearts, bathe themselves for seven days to become pure, put on fresh and clean garments, make offerings of incense and flowers, and maintain right mindfulness with a single mind, then the Tathāgata will immediately manifest his body before them, and they shall behold the Buddha.
"Even if their requisites for making offerings are incomplete or deficient, as long as they maintain single-minded mindfulness, they will see the Buddha before them when their lives are about to end.
King Jayadeva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Are there any sentient beings who, upon hearing of the Tathāgata’s supernatural powers and merits, fail to give rise to faith and instead slander them?
The Buddha said, "There are such beings.

If they hear the Dharma-gate of the Tathāgata’s supernatural powers, they immediately give rise to poisonous, unwholesome thoughts of anger, perceiving the Dharma-preacher as an evil friend (*pāpa-mitra*). When such a person’s life comes to an end, they will be reborn in the hells."

If, upon hearing of the Tathāgata’s great supernormal powers, one can give rise to faith and acceptance, regarding the Dharma teacher as a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), one will immediately attain the state of humans and devas, and ultimately achieve Buddhahood.

At that time, the World-Honored One extended his broad and long tongue, first covering his own face, then reaching to the crown of his head, then covering his entire body, then covering the lion throne, then covering the assembly of bodhisattvas, then covering the assembly of śrāvakas, and finally covering the entire great assembly including Śakra, Brahmā, and the world-protectors. He then withdrew his tongue and addressed the great assembly, saying:
"The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, possesses such a tongue-mark; how could he ever speak falsely?"
"You all, the great assembly, should believe and accept this; you shall enjoy peace and happiness for a long night.

When this Dharma was spoken, eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas among the assembly attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings attained the pure Dharma-eye, free from dust and defilement; and immeasurable, boundless sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Śrīdevīprajñāpāramitāsūtra, Scroll Two;
The Śrīdevīprajñāpāramitāsūtra, Scroll Three.
Translated by Prince Yueposhouna of the Kingdom of Ujjayinī during the Chen Dynasty.
Chapter Five: On the Nature of Phenomena (Dharmatā-parivarta).

At that time, King Śūraṃgama rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!”
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has eloquently expounded this subtle and wondrous power of great supernormal faculties.
By what causes and conditions do the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, attain this?
We only pray that the World-Honored One will analyze and explain it for us.
The Buddha addressed King Jayasena, saying: "Great King!
The conduct of all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, is profoundly deep and inconceivable; the attainment of their fruit is likewise so."
The Victorious Heavenly King addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What dharmas do the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, practice that are called ‘profound and inconceivable’?”
The Buddha said to King Śūra: “Great King!
The dharma-nature, causes, and effects of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas are inconceivable; their merit, their teachings, and their benefit to sentient beings are likewise so.”
The Deva-rāja Vijaya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
why is the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) inconceivable?”
The Buddha said:
"Great King!
It has continued in succession within the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases of all sentient beings since beginningless time, yet it cannot be defiled."

The essence of the dharma-nature is pure; it cannot be taken as an object of arising by any mental consciousness, nor can it be discriminated by any other thoughts or reflections, nor can it be taken as an object by erroneous recollection or deliberation.

The Dharma is free from false thoughts, and ignorance does not arise; therefore, it is not produced through the twelve links of dependent origination. It is called "signless" (animitta), and thus it is not a conditioned phenomenon. It is without birth and without cessation, boundless and inexhaustible, with its own characteristic eternally abiding.
“Great King!

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, they are able to know that the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is pure. Thus, it is unstained and unattached, far removed from defilement; transcending all afflictions, one attains liberation. This very nature is the root of all Buddha-dharmas; merit and wisdom arise because of it, and its essence is luminously pure and inconceivable.”
"Great King!
I shall now speak by way of a parable; listen well and attentively.
The king said:
“World-Honored One!
We would indeed be honored to hear it.
The Buddha addressed King Śūra-deva, saying:

"It is, for example, like a priceless wish-fulfilling jewel, polished and refined until it is bright, pure, and lovely; its form is perfectly round and utterly clean, free from any stain or turbidity."
Having fallen into the mire for a long time, someone picks it up and protects it so that it does not fall further.
The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is likewise: although it remains amidst afflictions, it is not defiled by them, and later it manifests once again.
"Great King!
All Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, fully know that the intrinsic nature of sentient beings is pure, though it is obscured by adventitious afflictions, which do not enter into that intrinsic nature."
Therefore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should form this thought:
"I shall courageously and diligently cultivate vigor, and for the sake of all sentient beings, I shall expound this profound perfection of wisdom to eliminate their afflictions."
All sentient beings possess the purity of nature; therefore, do not conceive thoughts of inferiority toward them, but should instead revere them.
They are my teachers; honor them in accordance with the Dharma.
"When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva forms such a mind, he immediately gives rise to prajñā-jñāna and great compassion.
Great King!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā in this way, he is able to enter the stage of Avaivartika."
"Great King!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, he further reflects:
'These afflictions are powerless and incapable; their very nature is false and illusory, and they are contrary to purity.'"
Why is this? Because they turn their backs on omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
The pure nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is the foundation of all dharmas; its own nature has no foundation. False afflictions (*kleśa*) arise entirely from erroneous thoughts and inversions.
"Great King!
It is like the four great elements, which stand in dependence upon space, yet space itself has no further support.
So it is with afflictions: they depend upon this *dharmatā*, yet *dharmatā* has no support."
“Great King!
