When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, he contemplates and knows things as they truly are; thus, he does not give rise to opposition, and because of this conformity, afflictions do not arise.”
"Great King!
A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates afflictions and does not give rise to stained attachment.
If he were himself stained and attached, how could he preach the Dharma to enable others to transcend them?"
Therefore, the bodhisattva eliminates the mind of attachment and teaches the Dharma according to reality to untie the bonds of sentient beings.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), he further reflects:
"If, within the cycle of birth and death (saṃsāra), there is even a single affliction that benefits sentient beings, I shall embrace it."
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he further reflects:
"Just as the Buddhas of the past practiced the perfection of wisdom, so should I practice."
Why is this? Because when the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, were formerly on the stage of the causal ground, they also studied in this way and thereby attained Bodhi.
For these two reasons, the Bodhisattva employs various skillful means to know this Dharma-nature.
“Great King!

Such is the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), immeasurable and boundless, yet it is obscured and covered by various afflictions (kleśa). Following the flow of birth and death, it sinks into the six realms and revolves through the long night; because it accords with sentient beings, it is called the ‘nature of sentient beings’ (sattvadhātu).”

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, gives rise to a mind of weary detachment, eliminates the desires of the five sensory objects, and cultivates the unsurpassed path, this nature at that time is called "renunciation. Because it transcends all suffering, it is named "quiescence" and is the ultimate dharma.

That which all the world seeks and desires, the eternally abiding and subtle *sarvākārajñatā* (all-knowledge), can be attained with mastery through this *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena), whereby one receives the rank of Dharma King.
“Great King!

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, they contemplate the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) in its initial, middle, and final stages as entirely equal, primordially quiescent, and completely unimpeded—just as various forms cannot fill empty space.”
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know all the various practices taught by the Buddhas as they truly are, and they cultivate them according to their measure.

The qualities of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) cannot be fully described; they are devoid of dual characteristics, transcending the realms of identity and difference, being a single mark of equality where discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*) do not operate.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) in this manner, they are able to eliminate two marks:
the mark of a person (*pudgala-nimitta*) and the mark of phenomena (*dharma-nimitta*).
All ordinary beings are bound by attachments; they do not recognize, see, or attain the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

When Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they are able to penetrate this very nature of phenomena, which, whether residing in sentient beings or elsewhere, is non-dual and without distinction.
Why is this? Because suchness is not different [from itself].
"Great King!..."

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the Prajñāpāramitā, they cultivate all roots of goodness based on this dharma-nature; they enter the three realms of existence to benefit sentient beings, and although they manifest impermanence, it is not ultimate reality.
Why is this? Because when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the Prajñāpāramitā, they perceive the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) as it truly is.
Being fully endowed with skillful means, great compassion, and the power of their vows, they do not abandon sentient beings.
The practitioners of the Two Vehicles and ordinary worldlings do not possess such a great compassionate fundamental vow; therefore, they do not perceive the perfectly pure *dharmatā*. "Great King!

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, he contemplates the *dharmatā* in this way: there is no holy person who can cultivate it, nor is there any dharma to be cultivated; there is no one who can practice it, nor is there any dharma to be practiced; there is no mind and no mental factors; there is no karma and no retribution; there is neither suffering nor pleasure. One who contemplates in this manner is said to have attained equanimity."
It is non-different from detachment, conforms to the vast, is without self or what belongs to self, is without high or low, is truly inexhaustible, and is eternally abiding, luminous, and pure.
Why is this? Because all noble dharmas are accomplished by means of this; it is due to this nature that the noble ones are manifested.
"Great King!..."
The boundless merits and unique qualities of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas arise from this nature and emerge from this nature.
Great King!
All the categories of morality, concentration, and wisdom of all noble ones arise from this nature.
The *prajñāpāramitā* of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas emerges from this nature.

This nature is quiescent and transcends all names and marks; as this nature is reality, it is free from inversion. Because this nature is immutable, it is called "Suchness" (*tathatā*). The sphere of noble wisdom is termed the "Ultimate Truth" (*paramārtha*).

It is neither existent nor non-existent, neither eternal nor annihilated; it is neither birth-and-death nor nirvana, neither defiled nor pure; it is free from unity and difference, nameless and signless.
"Great King!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, he further reflects:
'The nature of phenomena is devoid of marks; all phenomena are devoid of marks, being neither two nor distinct.'"
Why is this? All phenomena are devoid of characteristics; that is, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is devoid of characteristics.
Since the nature of phenomena is devoid of characteristics, all sentient beings are devoid of characteristics, being identical with the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) in its lack of characteristics.
The dharma-realm is free from marks, and all dharmas are free from marks.
Such freedom from marks cannot be apprehended through seeking.
The nature of phenomena is suchness, and the suchness of sentient beings is identical and non-dual.
The suchness of sentient beings and the suchness of the dharma-nature are one and the same, without duality;
the suchness of the dharma-nature and the suchness of all phenomena are without duality or distinction;
the suchness of all phenomena and the suchness of all Buddhas are without duality or distinction.
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is suchness; the suchness of the past, future, and present does not conflict with one another;
the suchness of the past and the suchness of the future likewise do not conflict.
The suchness of the past, future, and present is itself the suchness of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases;
the suchness of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases is itself the suchness of defilement and purity;
the suchness of defilement and purity is itself the suchness of birth-and-death and nirvana.
“Samsara and Nirvana are suchness (tathatā), which is the suchness of all dharmas.
“Great King! That which is called ‘such’ is termed non-differentiation, unchanging, unborn, non-contentious, and true. Because it is non-contentious, it is designated as suchness.”

To know and see all phenomena as they truly are—unborn; though phenomena arise, they are unmoving within suchness (*tathatā*); and though suchness arises, all phenomena are unborn within suchness—this is called the purity and immutability of the Dharmakāya. It is like space, peerless and equal to nothing; among all things in the triple world, there is not a single dharma that can equal it, nor is there anything throughout the bodies of sentient beings that resembles it.
Pure and free from defilement, originally unstained, its self-nature is luminous and clear; its self-nature is unborn and its self-nature is unarisen.

It exists within mind, intellect, and consciousness, yet is not of the nature of mind, intellect, or consciousness. It is emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, pervading all places where sentient beings dwell throughout the realm of empty space. It is entirely equal, boundless and immeasurable, neither different nor distinct.
It is not form, yet it is not separate from form;
it is not feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, yet it is not separate from feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
it is not the earth element, the water element, the fire element, or the wind element, yet it is not separate from the earth element, the water element, the fire element, or the wind element.

Non-arising transcends birth; though it runs counter to saṃsāra and does not conform to nirvāṇa, the eye cannot see it, the ear cannot hear it, the nose cannot smell it, the tongue cannot taste it, the body cannot feel it, and the mind cannot know it. It does not reside within the mind, intellect, or consciousness, yet it is not separate from the mind, intellect, or consciousness.
"Great King!
This is called the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they penetrate this dharma and cultivate purity."
Throughout the trichiliocosm, and within the cities, towns, and villages of Jambudvīpa, the Bodhisattva is able to manifest a physical body.

This manifested body is neither form nor characteristic, yet it appears as form and characteristic; it is not an object of the six sense faculties, yet it transforms sentient beings without ever ceasing. For their sake, he teaches that this body is impermanent, selfless, suffering, and impure. Fully realizing that sentient beings possess a nature of tranquility, he is able to manifest immeasurable kinds of bodies, employing skillful means to bring them to transformation.
"Knowing that all bodies have no agent and no experiencer, being like wood or stone, he preaches pure conduct for the sake of sentient beings.
'Great King!'"

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā in this way, they penetrate the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and immediately attain mastery. Without any movement, they initiate the work of wisdom and sport with supernormal powers (abhijñā), manifesting various displays while abiding in sovereignty. They are able to manifest various modes of conduct with ease, proceed toward all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā), and fully penetrate all dharmas.
"Great King!
The *prajñāpāramitā* is thus sovereign; it is the mark of inexhaustibility, pervading all places, manifesting form where there is no form.
It sovereignly and universally observes the minds of all sentient beings, seeing the nature of the mind as it truly is."
He possesses mastery over recollection, maintaining an uninterrupted continuity through boundless kalpas;
he possesses mastery over transformation, abiding in the marks of liberation;
and he possesses mastery over the exhaustion of outflows, yet for the sake of sentient beings, he does not realize the exhaustion of outflows.
Mastery over transcending the world is the realm of noble wisdom;
mastery over profound depth is that which cannot be fathomed by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Possessing sovereign stability that cannot be destroyed by Māras, they are able to reach the site of enlightenment and achieve the Buddha-dharma as the most supreme;
they possess sovereignty in following the turning of the Great Dharma Wheel;
and they possess sovereignty in taming and transforming all sentient beings.
He attains mastery over his station and gains sovereignty over the Dharma.
"Great King!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, he penetrates the profound nature of phenomena (dharmatā) as it truly is, thereby attaining this sovereignty."

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas cultivate this mastery, they immediately attain the various dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, and samāpattis, remaining unbound by the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm.
Why is this? Because they are far removed from all false conceptualization, the fetters of affliction, and inverted attachments to signs.
If they take birth, they possess mastery over birth and are without bondage; if they wish to manifest cessation, they likewise possess mastery.

In whatever place they are born, they constantly embrace the Mahāyāna and accomplish the Buddha-dharma; yet, when seeking the Buddha-dharma throughout the ten directions, it is ultimately unattainable.
All phenomena are identical with the single Buddha-dharma, being neither eternal nor subject to annihilation.
Why is this? Because when one investigates this dharma, it cannot be apprehended.

Since it cannot be apprehended through investigation according to the principle of suchness, this dharma cannot be said to exist or not to exist; even its verbal description lacks names and characteristics, for it transcends such realms.
If one is free from names and signs, that is equality; if dharmas are equal, there is no attachment. That which cannot be attached to is the reality of dharmas.
To be attached to reality is itself delusion; because of non-attachment, it is not delusion.

When the mind is free from attachment and obstruction, it is unimpeded; being unimpeded, it is without hindrance; being without hindrance, it is without contention; and being without contention, it is identical to empty space.

This Dharma is not bound to the realm of desire, not bound to the realm of form, and not bound to the formless realm. If it is nowhere bound or attached, this Dharma is without color, without marks, and without form. If a Dharma is without color, without marks, and without form, that Dharma should be known in this way: following those objects, one is detached from the knower and detached from the known.
Why is this? Because within this there is not the slightest dharma that can be awakened to, nor the slightest dharma that can awaken.
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom and penetrating equality.
"Great King!

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, they contemplate great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity; yet they do not perceive a self, do not perceive sentient beings, do not perceive a life-force, and do not perceive a person. Although they practice giving, they discipline the mind;
they maintain the precepts purely while remaining detached from the conceptual signs of the precepts."
One practices patience with an inexhaustible mind;
one exerts diligence free from mental attachment;
and one cultivates meditative concentration with a tranquil mind that has no object of focus.
One practices the four foundations of mindfulness while cultivating the perfection of wisdom;
one cultivates the right efforts with a mind of equanimity;
and one cultivates the bases of supernormal power with a mind free from conceptual proliferation.
Discriminating among sentient beings, one observes their faculties; free from a mind of transgression, one cultivates the faculties and powers;
with a discriminating mind, one observes the factors of enlightenment;
and with a mind of effortless application, one practices the Noble Path.

With a mind free from attachment, one possesses pure faith; with natural wisdom, one recollects all dharmas; with a mind of equanimous wisdom, one cultivates various samādhis; with a non-discriminating mind, one contemplates the Prajñāpāramitā; with a mind of cessation, one cultivates śamatha; with a mind that sees nothing, one cultivates vipaśyanā; with a mind free from mental objects, one cultivates the recollection of the Buddha; by penetrating the mind of the equality of the dharma-realm, one cultivates the recollection of the Dharma; and with a mind that dwells nowhere, one cultivates the recollection of the Saṃgha.

With the fundamental mind pure, one teaches and transforms sentient beings; with the mind that does not give rise to discrimination regarding the dharma-realm, one encompasses all phenomena. With a mind like space, one purifies buddha-lands; with a mind of non-attainment, one attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). With a mind free from advancing or retreating, one attains the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*); with a mind far removed from signs, one does not perceive the existence of signs. With a mind of equality toward the three realms, one adorns the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). The mind is able to awaken to and know all dharmas; it turns the wheel of the Dharma without perceiving hearing, speaking, or showing, yet manifests nirvana while knowing that the fundamental nature of birth and death is equal.
“Great King!

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, they contemplate all phenomena in this way: they do not perceive a subject that contemplates, nor do they perceive an object that is contemplated; at that very moment, they are able to attain mastery in playful sport.”
Why is this? Because when one's own mind is pure, one is able to see all sentient beings as pure.
"Great King!
"Just as space pervades all things, so too is the mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*.

When this Dharma was being taught, eighty-four thousand people and devas among the assembly resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas attained the endurance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); eighty-four thousand sentient beings attained the pure Dharma-eye, free from dust and defilement; and twelve thousand bhikṣus all attained the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*).
The Buddha addressed King Śūraṅgama, saying: "Great King!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, their mind attains purity; it is as deep and vast as the ocean, and its merit and wisdom are immeasurable."
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to manifest the jewels of supramundane merits; when sentient beings utilize them, they remain inexhaustible until the attainment of bodhi.
The merits of the Bodhisattvas likewise do not perish, just as the great ocean produces many varieties of jewels.
The wisdom of the Bodhisattva is profoundly deep and difficult to enter; neither Śrāvakas nor Pratyekabuddhas are able to traverse it, just as small animals cannot enter the great ocean.
The wisdom of the Bodhisattva is vast and boundless.
Why is this? Because it is without attachment and without dwelling, without form and without marks.

The wisdom of a bodhisattva becomes progressively deeper from beginning to end: from the initial thought of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) to ultimate omniscience (*sarvajñā*). It is the natural law for a bodhisattva not to dwell together with afflictions or evil associates.

If worldly wisdom enters into the wisdom of a bodhisattva, it becomes of a single characteristic and a single flavor—namely, the flavor of signless omniscience (*sarvajñā*) which is free from conceptual discrimination.
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates all phenomena and perceives neither the increase nor the decrease of any phenomenon.
Why is this? Because they have thoroughly realized the profound nature of the equality of all phenomena.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, through the power of great compassion, does not violate his original vow; he is the locus upon which all sages rely, preaching the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings throughout eternal kalpas without end.
"Great King!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, they penetrate such a profound nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
Great King!"

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is skillfully able to penetrate the various dharmas of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Although he speaks of form (*rūpa*), it is not truly existent; when he investigates this form, he ultimately does not grasp at it. It is the same for feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Although he speaks of the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*), it is not real; when he investigates the earth element, he ultimately does not grasp at it. It is the same for the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness. Although he speaks of the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*), it is not real;
when he investigates the eye-base, he ultimately does not grasp at it. It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

Although one speaks of a "self," it is not real; yet when investigating and seeking the self, one ultimately does not grasp at it. It is the same for "sentient beings," "life-force," "nourisher," "person," "agent," "life-span," "knower," and "seer.
Although one speaks of the "world," it is not real; yet when investigating the world, one ultimately does not grasp at it.
Although one speaks of "worldly phenomena," they are not real; yet when investigating worldly phenomena, one ultimately does not grasp at them.
Although one speaks of the Buddha-dharma, it is not real; yet, when investigating the Buddha-dharma, one ultimately does not grasp at it.
Although one speaks of bodhi, it is not real; yet, when investigating bodhi, one ultimately does not grasp at it.
"Great King!
All that is spoken is called conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), which is not ultimate reality;
yet, without conventional truth, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) cannot be expressed."
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they penetrate conventional truth without contradicting ultimate truth; thus they penetrate it.

They know that phenomena are without arising, without cessation, and without destruction; they are neither "this" nor "that," being entirely free from the conceptual proliferation of speech, words, and letters.
"Great King!

The ultimate truth (paramārtha) is beyond words and quiescent; it is the domain of noble wisdom, a dharma that is unchanging and indestructible. Whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, its intrinsic nature and characteristics abide eternally."
"This is called the bodhisattva’s thorough penetration of the ultimate truth.
At that time, King Śūra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If all dharmas are neither born nor extinguished, being empty and detached by their very nature, how can there be the appearance of a Buddha in the world and the turning of the wheel of Dharma?
How can a bodhisattva perceive birth within dharmas that are unborn?
The Buddha said to King Śūra: "Great King!
Because phenomena do not cease, they do not arise."
Why is this? Because their nature does not undergo change.
It is only through the causes and conditions of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) that one perceives arising and ceasing; these are all illusory and do not exist in reality.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, through skillful means they perceive the dharma of dependent origination; they immediately know that all conventional truths are entirely empty and non-existent, seeing no solidity or substance, appearing as if present yet like a shadow, a mirage, an echo, or a magical illusion—unstable and shifting, born from causes and conditions.
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva, observing all phenomena as empty through the perfection of wisdom, and even seeing that they arise from causes and conditions, reflects thus:
"These various phenomena are now seen to have arising, abiding, and ceasing; by what causes and conditions do they arise?"

"By what causes and conditions does cessation occur? He then realized this: "With ignorance as a cause and condition, volitional formations arise; dependent on volitional formations, consciousness arises; from consciousness, name-and-form arises; from name-and-form, the six sense bases arise; from the six sense bases, contact arises; from contact, feeling arises; because of feeling, the ordinary person gives rise to craving; from craving, grasping arises; because of grasping as a cause, existence continues; from existence comes birth; with birth there is old age; and because of old age, there is death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair."
Therefore, one practices cultivation in order to sever ignorance; if ignorance is severed, the remaining eleven factors likewise perish.
It is like a human body: if the life-faculty is severed, the other faculties become useless.
“Great King!
Those heterodox practitioners with wrong views, seeking liberation, merely wish to sever death, yet do not know how to sever birth.
If a phenomenon is not born, it cannot cease.”
For example, it is like a person throwing a clod of earth at a lion; the lion pursues the person, while the clod comes to rest on its own.
So too is it with the Bodhisattva: he merely cuts off rebirth, and death ceases of its own accord.
A dog merely chases after a clod of earth and does not know to chase the person who threw it; thus, the chasing of the clod never ceases.
It is the same with those of external paths: they do not know how to sever the cycle of birth, and so they will never escape death.
Great King!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this way, they skillfully understand the arising and ceasing of all phenomena through causes and conditions.
"Great King!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know that dependently arisen phenomena are empty and lack substantial existence, and thus they do not give rise to the conceit of 'I'."
If one is born into the families of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, householders, or elders, one does not give rise to the two kinds of pride—pride of nobility or pride of wealth;

if one is born into poverty and low status, one recognizes for oneself that one's past karma was not particularly pure and that one has received an inferior retribution, thereby giving rise to a mind of weary detachment and immediately seeking to leave the household life.
He reflects thus:
"Just as this body of mine was obtained through mixed karma, I shall further cultivate pure karma to make myself pure, and cause others to do likewise.
Having already sought my own deliverance, I shall also deliver others; having already sought my own liberation, I shall also untie the bonds of others."

For these reasons, one immediately gives rise to diligence and does not fall into indolence; all unwholesome dharmas that obstruct the Path are severed and eliminated, while all wholesome dharmas that assist the Path should be increased, as one diligently cultivates vigor.
He reflects thus:
"I bear a heavy burden; I must personally extinguish all afflictions and deliver sentient beings without falling into indolence.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, he regards his teachers and preceptors—whether they are learned or of little learning, knowledgeable or ignorant, observant of the precepts or violators of them—with the same thought as toward the Buddha.
He reverently attended his fellow students and reflected:

"I now rely upon my teacher to study; may all that is good which I have not yet perfected be brought to fulfillment, and may all afflictions which I have not yet exhausted be severed until they are gone. I shall uphold wholesome dharmas and abandon the unwholesome. The All-Knowing One, who has compassion for the world, whose great compassion is a field of merit, and who is tranquil among devas and humans—this teacher is my Great Teacher, who has attained auspiciousness and prosperity; all devas and humans serve the Dharma King as their Great Teacher."
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they reflect thus:
"The Buddha has taught the pure precepts; even for the sake of my body or life, I shall not violate them."
"As the World-Honored One has said, to accord with the Buddha’s teachings is to make offerings to the Buddha.

If brahmins, kṣatriyas, householders, or elders faithfully bestow various foods and drinks, and one receives and uses them in accordance with the Dharma, it ensures that those people do not lose the fruit of their reward in vain; both the eater and the giver shall obtain benefit.
When brahmins, kṣatriyas, householders,

or elders address a bodhisattva by the name of "śramaṇa" and regard him as a field of merit, the bodhisattva should practice the true Dharma according to principle and measure, thereby manifesting the virtues of a śramaṇa and the virtues of a field of merit.
In this way, the bodhisattva practices for themselves and transforms others without ever ceasing or abandoning these efforts.
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā and cultivates in this manner, they are able to accord with all worlds.

Seeing those who are prone to anger, they give rise to a humble mind; seeing those who are arrogant, they give rise to the perception of non-self; seeing those who are crooked and perverse, they give rise to the perception of uprightness; seeing those who speak falsehoods, they give rise to truthful speech; toward those who use harsh words, they always speak with loving words; seeing those who are stubborn and rigid, they manifest gentleness; seeing those who are cruel and venomous, they practice compassion and patience; seeing those who follow false teachings, they give rise to great kindness; seeing suffering sentient beings, they give rise to great compassion; and seeing those who are stingy and envious, they practice generosity.
“Great King!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, he accords with worldly knowledge in this way and is born in a pure Buddha-field. Why is this?

Maintaining the precepts without flaw, remaining free from all impurities, and cultivating a mind of equanimity; possessing great roots of goodness toward all sentient beings while not clinging to fame or profit; maintaining pure faith without expectation of reward; practicing diligence with tireless vigor; cultivating various meditative concentrations to remain free from the dharma of distraction; and training in extensive learning through subtle wisdom.
"With faculties unimpaired, endowed with sharp wisdom, constantly cultivating great loving-kindness, and remaining far removed from anger and affliction—
for these causes and conditions, one is born in a pure Buddha-land. At that time,
King Śūra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, by practicing the dharmas such as the precepts one is born in the Buddha-lands; is it also the case that by practicing a single practice one is likewise born there?
The Buddha addressed King Śūraṅgama, saying:
"Great King!

If there is a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who, among the various dharmas previously described, purely cultivates a single practice—that is, cultivating all dharmas through that one practice—then by means of this single practice, they will attain birth in a pure land."
Why is this? Because within each and every practice, all practices are fully contained.
"Great King!"
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, practicing in this way, they are born in a pure land and are not defiled by a womb. Why is this?

Because the bodhisattva mahāsattva fashions images of the Buddha, repairs monasteries, applies fragrant mud to the ground before the stūpas of the Tathāgata and makes offerings of incense, or bathes the Buddha images with fragrant water, and sweeps and cleans the monasteries and applies plaster.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva makes offerings to and attends upon the bodies of their parents, preceptors, teachers, fellow students, and all śramaṇas, making these offerings with a mind of equanimity toward them all. He dedicates these roots of goodness for the sake of all sentient beings, dedicating them toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi so that they may attain purity.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, they immediately attain detachment from the mundane.

Why is this? Because their mind is free from grasping and attachment; they do not become stained by factions; they turn their backs on all objective spheres (*viṣaya*); they remain far removed from the conditions of craving; and they are undefiled by objective spheres.

The World-Honored One has taught the precepts for practice in accordance with reality: having few desires and being content with the four requisites as appropriate; seeking sufficiency and passing time with a mind constantly filled with awe; and delighting in tranquility and seclusion.
“Great King!

In this way, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not cling to worldly dharmas and thereby attain pure livelihood, free from hypocrisy in their deportment and without deceit in speech or thought.”

In the presence of a donor, one never feigns a display of dignified demeanor, walking slowly and calmly while looking six feet ahead; yet, once turned away from the donor, one immediately becomes unrestrained.

In the presence of a donor, one does not lower one's voice to speak in soft, sweet, and pleasing words for the sake of gain or profit to flatter their inclinations; yet, once turned away from the donor, one then gives rein to oneself.

When seeing others practicing giving, one says with the mouth that it is not needed while the mind actually desires it; this is called inner mental affliction, manifesting few desires with the mouth while the mind covets gain and offerings.
"Great King!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, they are entirely free from such deceptions and the signs of seeking gain.
If they see a donor, they must not speak thus:"
"If my three robes are worn out, my bowl is missing,
or I require medicinal decoctions," one must not say before a donor:
"A certain donor gave me this item because that person thought I was observant of the precepts, learned, possessed of great compassion, and pure in heart."
"Although they praise me in this way, I possess no such virtues; I should only practice cultivation to repay the kindness of my donors.
A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should not thus praise themselves and disparage others, nor should they seek gain and offerings by conforming to the ways of laypeople."

If one gives to others, one should not give rise to anger or vexation; one should not take wealth through flattery or deceit; one should not harm others under the guise of feigned friendship to seize their property; and one should not take wealth by means of playing tricks upon others.

If a donor intends to give a gift, whether to a person who has been praised, a Dharma teacher, the assembly as a whole, or has not yet designated a recipient, or if the gift has not yet been finalized, a Bodhisattva must not enter among them to take a share.

If one receives gifts of wealth, one should not be attached to them, thinking, "This is mine" or "This is my property. Instead, one should immediately redirect them for the sake of śramaṇas, teachers, the monastic community, parents, and other indigent persons, so that they may be used with equanimity.
If one's wealth and possessions are exhausted, one does not give rise to sorrow; even if for a short time one does not obtain [them], the mind remains free from suffering and affliction.
"Great King!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva receives a gift and dedicates it to others, both are pure."
Because their conduct is pure, their minds do not grow weary. Why is this?

When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the *prajñāpāramitā*, they remain for a long time within saṃsāra for the sake of benefiting sentient beings without ever feeling weariness or distress. Even when confronted by demonic activities or the pressure of manifold sufferings, their minds never regress. If there are those who wish to follow the path of the two vehicles, they immediately preach the Dharma for them without shrinking from fatigue; thus, as the Bodhisattvas themselves cultivate the factors that assist enlightenment, they never experience weariness or exhaustion.
"Great King,
when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā with such diligence, they are able to act in accordance with the true teaching of the Buddha."

Why is this? Because when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they remain free from all negligence, their mind is always cautious, and they skillfully restrain themselves; they do not commit any evil or unwholesome dharmas, and the same applies to their speech and mind.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, although they dwell in the present, they are constantly apprehensive of the future; they sever all evil and unwholesome dharmas so that they do not arise.

One's speech must always accord with principle, constantly expounding the teachings of the Dharma, and one must not speak what is not the Dharma. Completely abandoning defiled karma and purely cultivating pure conduct, one does not disparage the Buddha’s teachings and remains far removed from the impure dharmas of affliction; this is called protecting the Tathāgata’s true teaching, severing and distancing oneself from all evil and unwholesome dharmas.
“Great King!

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, he accords with the pure teaching of the Buddha in this way: he regards all sentient beings with a face that first smiles, never once frowning.”
Why is this so? Because their minds are free from defilement; their faculties are pure, unstained and devoid of impurity; their minds are without anger and inwardly free from the knots of resentment.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā* in this manner, they immediately attain great learning (*bahuśruta*), and they are able to observe birth and death as they truly are: how the fire of desire blazes, the fire of hatred burns, and the fire of ignorance constantly causes delusion and confusion.

He also knows things as they truly are: that conditioned phenomena are impermanent, all formations are suffering, and all dharmas are without self; that worldly beings are addicted to conceptual proliferation, and that among all dharmas, only nirvāṇa is tranquility.
If one hears others speak, one immediately contemplates the meaning and transmits it to others, giving rise to great compassion and a firm resolve;
if one does not hear the Dharma, there will be no contemplation or cultivation.
Therefore, the wisdom derived from hearing is like the primary alphabet; all other forms of wisdom arise because of it.
Once one has attained extensive learning, one then protects the True Dharma.
"Great King!

In the future, at the end of the age when the True Dharma is extinguished, there will be sentient beings who delight in diligent practice, yet they will not encounter the torch of the Dharma, and no one will preach the profound Dharma for them.

At that time, the Bodhisattva immediately expounded for them the profound and wondrous Dharma, namely the Prajñāpāramitā, causing all sentient beings to attain precepts, meditative concentration, and wisdom; he further praised them, saying:
"Good sons!..."
Thus, at the time when the True Dharma is extinguished in the final age, you are able to give rise to the bodhicitta, seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi for the benefit of sentient beings.
This Prajñāpāramitā is that which has been practiced by all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
If you cultivate it with diligence, you will not be far from Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Why is this? Because the Prajñāpāramitā is not separate from bodhi.
It is like a person who has sown grain and seen it sprout; one should know that the harvest will surely be before long.
The Bodhisattva is likewise; when seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and hearing the Prajñāpāramitā, one should know that they are certainly not far from Buddhahood.
“Great King!
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to abandon the *prajñāpāramitā* and seek *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by relying on other dharmas instead, such a thing is impossible.”
It is just as if a prince were to abandon his father the king and seek to become a crown prince under another person; this could never be achieved.
So it is with the Bodhisattva: one must necessarily rely on the *prajñāpāramitā* to attain *sarvajñatā*.
It is like a calf that, if it desires milk, must rely upon its mother; if it approaches another cow, it cannot obtain it.
"Great King!

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who draws near to the Prajñāpāramitā always has his body adorned with the marks of a Dharma Prince; he adorns his physical form with excellent flowers, and his faculties are unimpaired."

They constantly traverse the sphere of activity of the Tathāgata; they awaken to the path traversed by the Buddha-Tathāgata according to his awakening; they rescue and protect sentient beings who suffer in the world; they are well able to penetrate the teachings spoken by the Buddha; they constantly cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya); and they guard the city of the Tathāgata’s omniscience (sarvajñatā).
“Great King!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, he becomes a prince of the Dharma, revered by Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors.”

Why is this? Because an irreversible bodhisattva practicing the bodhisattva path cannot be moved by any māras; they dwell securely in the Buddha-dharma, penetrate the principle of the equality of all emptiness, and do not rely on external conditions.

Thus abiding in the wisdom of the Buddha-dharma, which is not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, they transcend the world and dwell in the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
“Great King!

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, they are able to know the minds of all sentient beings as they truly are—whether their greed, hatred, and delusion are of superior, middling, or inferior grade—and they likewise know their wholesome minds and steadfast minds as they truly are.”
Having known them as they truly are, he preaches the various remedial dharmas to each of them accordingly; in this way, he is able to skillfully transform sentient beings.

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, if there are sentient beings who should be transformed and delivered by seeing the body of a Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva immediately manifests the body of a Buddha and preaches the Dharma for them;
if they should be transformed and delivered by means of the body of a Bodhisattva, he manifests the body of a Bodhisattva.
To those who should be transformed by the body of a pratyekabuddha, he manifests the body of a pratyekabuddha;
to those who should be taught and transformed by the body of a śrāvaka, he manifests the body of a śrāvaka;
and to those who should be taught and transformed by the bodies of Śakra, Brahmā, a brāhmaṇa, a kṣatriya, a householder, or a lay devotee, he manifests all these forms to deliver them.
"Great King!
Thus does the bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the prajñāpāramitā to transform sentient beings.

When the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, his mental nature is compassionate and harmonious, upright, gentle, and kind; he is free from all flattery, crookedness, jealousy, and defilement, and his mind is ever pure."
Their speech is not coarse; they distance themselves from harsh words and frequently practice patience while associating intimately with sentient beings.
"Great King!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā in this way, they dwell in peace and happiness wherever they may be."

Why is this so? Because they are fully endowed with right view and pure vision, as well as pure conduct; the spheres of their activity correspond to their minds, and regarding those mental states that are contrary—namely, evil and unwholesome dharmas—they do not engage in such spheres or defiled places.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they see the minds of their fellow practitioners with joy and share with others both material wealth and the Dharma.
One should practice only the single path, which is the Buddha-way.
One should take only the Buddha as teacher and not honor anyone else.
Great King.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they abide in peace and happiness in this manner, employing the methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) to gather in sentient beings. They gather in sentient beings through the gift of benefit, the gift of peace and happiness, and the inexhaustible gift; they gather in sentient beings through beneficial speech, meaningful speech, speech in accordance with the Dharma, and non-contradictory speech. They gather in sentient beings through equality in the benefit of material wealth, equality in the benefit of the body, equality in the benefit of life, and equality in the benefit of requisites.

"Great King! Beneficial giving is the gift of the Dharma; giving for the sake of peace and happiness is the gift of material requisites; inexhaustible giving is the manifestation of the Path. Beneficial speech causes others to produce wholesome roots; meaningful speech causes others to perceive the principle; speech in accordance with the Dharma conforms to the Buddha’s teaching; and non-contradictory speech explains the Dharma as it truly is."
Equality regarding material benefit refers to things that may be eaten, chewed, drunk, sipped, or licked, as well as clothing and the like.
Equality regarding physical benefit refers to protecting and benefiting one's own body in such a way that one causes others to do the same.
Regarding the equality of benefit for life: pearls, lapis lazuli, coral, and agate are termed external life.
Regarding the equality of benefit for requisites: elephants, horses, chariots, and all pure wealth [constitute these].
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they share this practice both with themselves and with others.

"Great King! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they are born with a handsome and upright appearance. They are always able to cultivate a tranquil deportment, a sincere deportment, and a pure deportment; they are a joy for all to behold. They are warm and kind both inwardly and outwardly, such that those who gaze upon them never grow weary and their hearts are gladdened. They are beloved and respected by all sentient beings; whoever sees them gives rise to a virtuous mind, and even those who harbor anger find their hearts immediately liberated upon seeing them."
“Great King!

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, such upright majesty makes him worthy of being relied upon; he protects sentient beings so that their afflictions are extinguished, and can lead them out from the boundless wilderness of birth and death. He can ferry sentient beings across the perils and difficulties of the world, acting as a kinsman for those without kin, a skilled physician for the disease of afflictions, a protector for those without protection, a refuge for those without refuge, and a Dharma-torch for sentient beings shrouded in ignorance.”
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the Prajñāpāramitā, they serve as a refuge for all sentient beings, curing all diseases like the king of medicinal trees.

"Great King, it is like the great tree Sudarśana, whose roots, trunk, branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, colors, fragrances, tastes, and textures all serve to cure the various illnesses of sentient beings."
It is likewise for the bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom.

From the first production of the thought of enlightenment, they treat the various ailments and the diseases of the afflictions for the sake of all sentient beings; through the merit and wisdom of the bodhisattva mahāsattva, those who see or hear them are all cured of their illnesses.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they are constantly in accord with merit; according to their capacity, they make offerings to the Triple Gem. If there is illness, they provide medicinal decoctions; if they see those who are hungry or thirsty, they provide food and drink; if they see those who are cold and frozen, they provide clothing.
The preceptors and upādhyāyas shall serve him with all their heart, while his fellow students and dharma-brothers shall join their palms in reverent respect.
They shall construct monasteries for him and donate fields and gardens;
from time to time, they shall provide whatever is available to the community of monks, and their subordinates and servants shall manage these affairs in accordance with the Dharma.
When he hears of śramaṇas, brahmins, or practitioners of the path who possess renown and virtue, he goes to visit them from time to time.
Great King!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he is able to give rise to all kinds of goodness and employs skillful means to teach and transform sentient beings.
Without moving the body from this buddha-field, they travel to immeasurable worlds of various buddhas to inquire about the True Dharma;
without moving the body from this buddha-field, they travel to immeasurable worlds of various buddhas to listen to and receive the True Dharma;
without moving the body from this buddha-land, they manifest in immeasurable buddha-fields to make offerings to the Tathāgatas.
Without moving his body from this buddha-field,
he travels to immeasurable worlds of the Buddhas to perfect the provisions for unsurpassed bodhi;
without moving his body from this buddha-field, he travels to immeasurable worlds of the Buddhas to make offerings and pay respect to those bodhisattvas who are realizing the path to Buddhahood.
Without moving his body from this buddha-field,
he manifests the attainment of enlightenment in immeasurable worlds;
without moving his body from this buddha-field, he manifests the turning of the wheel of Dharma in immeasurable buddha-lands.
Without moving his body from this buddha-field, he manifests parinirvāṇa in immeasurable buddha-fields;

without shifting his body from this buddha-field, he manifests emanation bodies for those who are to be delivered in immeasurable buddha-fields, causing them all to see him, yet without any conceptualization or volitional intent regarding what he does.
At that time, King Śūra devaputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva perform various transformations with a mind free from discrimination?"
The Buddha said to King Śūraṅgama: “Great King!

For example, the sun and moon illuminate the four continents without discrimination, yet they provide light for the world; it is through the karmic retribution of sentient beings that they themselves experience the illumination of the sun and moon over the world. It is just so with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practicing the Prajñāpāramitā: although he manifests transformation bodies, he remains without discrimination.”
Why is this? Because sentient beings each possess their own wholesome karma from past lives.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, while practicing on the causal ground in former times, made vows to deliver sentient beings, by the power of these vows, they manifest in accordance with whatever is thought of, all without a mind of discrimination.
"Great King!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they teach and transform others through such skillful means, swiftly proceeding toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving and maintains the purity of precepts—unpierced, unimpaired, and untainted—with a pure aggregate of morality that transcends the realms of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; he is fully endowed with patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, vows, power, and knowledge, possessing all the unique qualities of a Tathāgata, World-Honored One, and has already transcended the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
“Great King!
From the first stage through the tenth stage, the bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom; by cultivating such conduct, they attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
When this Dharma-gate was being taught, twenty thousand devaputras within the assembly attained the pure Dharma-eye, free from dust and defilement;
thirty thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attained the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti);
and eighty-four thousand devas and humans resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Countless hundreds of thousands of billions of gandharvas and kiṃnaras all joined their palms, praising the Tathāgata as they circled around Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain;
countless hundreds of thousands of billions of yakṣas rained down various lotus flowers as they circled around Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain.
Bodhisattvas from immeasurable worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions gathered together and praised the Tathāgata, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is wonderful that you have so skillfully expounded the profound Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of all bodhisattvas.”
World-Honored One!

By means of this Prajñāpāramitā, there come to be humans and devas; the stage of entering the stream and the fruit of the stream-enterer, up to the stage of entering arhatship and the fruit of arhatship; the path of the pratyekabuddha; the ten stages and ten pāramitās of the bodhisattva; and the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, eighteen unique dharmas, and all-knowledge—all of these emerge from within the Prajñāpāramitā.
“World-Honored One!
Just as all sentient beings in the world rely upon space, yet space itself has no basis, so too is it with the *prajñāpāramitā*:
it is the source of all phenomena, yet it is itself without basis.”
"May we, in future ages, preach the Prajñāpāramitā for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, just as the Buddha now preaches it.
They then scattered various kinds of incense and flowers upon the Tathāgata.
At that time, the deva of Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain and the others who had gathered praised from mid-air, saying:
"We recall that in past ages, immeasurable Buddhas preached this Dharma of the Prajñāpāramitā on this Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain, just as they do today."
At that time, King Śūra devaputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
How do the devas in the sky come to know the realm of the Tathāgata—that the Buddhas of the distant past have taught this matter of the Prajñāpāramitā?"
The Buddha said, "Great King!
These devas all abide in inconceivable liberation; therefore, they are able to know distant events of the past."
"Great King!

In the past, when I was a bodhisattva, I also took birth in the realm of those celestial deities. There I beheld immeasurable Buddhas attaining enlightenment, preaching the Dharma, and even entering parinirvāṇa; I constantly praised them, joined my palms in reverence, and prostrated before them."
"Why is this? Because the lifespan in that celestial realm of the gods is long.

At that time, there was a son of heaven among the assembly named Prabhāśrī. He immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas should roam in pure lands; this Sahā world is impure. Why has the World-Honored One appeared in this land?”
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Devaputra Prabhāśrī:
"In the abodes of all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, there are no defiled lands.

Thereupon, by means of his supernatural power, the World-Honored One manifested this trichiliocosm such that the ground was as level as the palm of a hand, composed of lapis lazuli, and devoid of mountains, hills, mounds, or thorns. Everywhere there were heaps of jewels, fragrant flowers, soft grasses, flowing springs, bathing pools with water of eight virtues, and stairways made of the seven treasures; the trees, flowers, and fruits all proclaimed the irreversible Dharma-wheel of the Bodhisattvas.
There were no ordinary beings; one saw only the great bodhisattvas of the ten directions.
No other sounds were heard, only the sound of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Everywhere there were lotuses as large as chariot wheels—blue, red, and white—and within each flower sat a bodhisattva in the full lotus posture.

He then saw the Tathāgata in the midst of the great assembly, expounding the profound Dharma for the sake of the bodhisattvas, surrounded before and behind by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Śakras, Brahmās, and Lokapālas, who were making offerings, paying homage, showing respect, and offering praise, saying:
"How rare, World-Honored One!"
"How extraordinary, World-Honored One!
What you have spoken is without falsehood; it is true and non-dual.
As the World-Honored One has said, the dwelling places of all Buddhas are truly free from defiled lands; it is only because sentient beings possess meager merit that they perceive them as impure."
"Blessed One!

If there are good sons or good daughters who hear even the name of the Prajñāpāramitā, it is already most rare; how much more so for those who copy it, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, and explain it to others."
The Buddha said:

"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to give wealth and goods to others with an unimpeded mind for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kalpas, yet another person were to write down this sutra with pure faith and transmit it to others, the latter’s merit would be greater than that."
Why is this? Because material giving has its exhaustion, while the giving of Dharma is inexhaustible. Why is this?
The gift of material wealth can only yield worldly fruits—whether as humans or devas—which one has obtained before, fallen from, and now regains.
However, through the gift of the Dharma, one attains for the first time what was never attained before: namely, Nirvana.

If someone were to teach and transform all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm so that they all dwell securely in the ten paths of wholesome action, yet another son or daughter of good family, with pure faith, were to receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain the Prajñāpāramitā to others, their merit would surpass that of the former.
Why is this? Because all wholesome dharmas arise from the Prajñāpāramitā.

If someone were to teach and transform all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm so that they all attain the fruits of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, or the path of a pratyekabuddha, yet another person were to, with faith, receive, uphold, read, recite, and transcribe the Prajñāpāramitā, the merit of the latter would surpass that of the former.

Why is this? Because the dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are all born from the perfection of wisdom; all the dharmas of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are born from the perfection of wisdom; and it is because of this perfection of wisdom that Buddhas appear in the world.
Wherever the Prajñāpāramitā resides, one should know that this very place is the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and the place where the wheel of Dharma is turned;
one should reflect: "In this very place dwells my Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
Why is this? Because all Buddhas are born from the Prajñāpāramitā.
If a person makes offerings to the physical image of a Tathāgata, it is not as good as making offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā.
Why is this? Because all Buddhas of the three periods of time are born from the Prajñāpāramitā.
— *The Sutra of the Prajñāpāramitā Spoken by King Śūra* (Śūradatta-rāja-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra), Scroll Three.
The Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra on the Perfection of Wisdom, Scroll Four, translated by Prince Yueposhouna of the Kingdom of Ujjayinī during the Chen Dynasty.
Chapter Six: On Equanimity.

At that time, King Śūraṃgama rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is equal. What is this equality?
By being equal to what phenomena is it called "equality"?
The Buddha said to King Jayasena: “Great King!
To contemplate all phenomena as neither arising nor ceasing, their self-nature being quiescent—this is called equality.”
All afflictions are false conceptualizations; being neither arising nor ceasing, their intrinsic nature is quiescent, and this is called equality.
Names, signs, and delusive thoughts are neither arising nor ceasing; their intrinsic nature is quiescent, and this is called equality.
To extinguish all inversions and not give rise to objective grasping is called equanimity (*samatā*).

When the perceiving mind is extinguished, ignorance and craving for existence are both stilled; because delusion and craving are extinguished, the notions of "I" and "mine" do not arise—this is called equanimity.
The cessation of "I" and "mine," and the stilling of name-and-form (nāmarūpa), is called equanimity.
Because name-and-form has ceased, extreme views do not arise; this is called equanimity.
Because it extinguishes and severs [the views of] annihilation and permanence, the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is stilled; this is called equanimity.
"Great King!

All afflictions that grasp at subject and object and obstruct wholesome dharmas arise based on the view of a self-body. When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is able to extinguish the view of a self-body, all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are entirely stilled, and even their active aspirations cease."
For example, when a great tree has its roots and stumps uprooted, its branches and twigs wither and die; or as a person without a head finds their life-force immediately severed.
All afflictions (*kleśa*) are likewise: if the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is severed, the remaining latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) perish of their own accord.
"Great King!
If a person can contemplate that all phenomena are without self, then both the grasper and the grasped are entirely stilled.
Thus did the Deva-rāja Vijaya address the Buddha.
“World-Honored One!
How does the arising of the view of self obstruct the true principle?
The Buddha addressed King Śūraṅgama, saying:
“Great King!
To falsely cling to a self within the body of the five aggregates gives rise to the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
The true Dharma is equal by its very nature (*svabhāva*), devoid of subject and object; since the view of self is contrary to this, it constitutes an obstruction.”
"Great King!
This view of mine does not exist internally, nor externally, nor both internally and externally. To have no abiding place is called tranquility; this is precisely equanimity."
To remain far removed from the view of self and to penetrate into equality is called the contemplation of true emptiness (*bhūta-śūnyatā*).
Emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness are by nature quiescent; they are neither arising nor ceasing, neither grasped nor attached to. To be far removed from the view of self is termed "equality."
“Great King!
That which is called ‘self’ neither comes nor goes; it possesses no reality and is a false conceptualization.
Phenomena arise from delusion and are likewise false.”
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they contemplate these dharmas as being far removed from falsehood; therefore, this is called "quiescent equality."
Great King, that which can grasp and that which is grasped is called "blazing";
freedom from these is called "quiescence. Delusive hindrances constitute blazing; freedom from them is quiescence.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā with skillful means, they are able to know things as they truly are: that the extinction of all afflictions serves to increase wholesome dharmas. By severing and eliminating afflictions, they perceive neither that which arises nor that which ceases; this is called "equanimity."
To cultivate the pāramitās while remaining far removed from demonic obstacles, neither perceiving anything to be cultivated nor perceiving anything to be abandoned, is called equanimity.

When a bodhisattva constantly takes the factors conducive to enlightenment as their object, without giving rise to the mind of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, and does not perceive any mark of difference between those factors conducive to enlightenment and the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, it is called equanimity.

"Taking omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) as the object of focus, the mind never ceases to constantly cultivate the practice of emptiness; yet, by the power of great compassion, one does not abandon sentient beings—this is called 'equanimity.
Great King!"

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is fully endowed with skillful means and practices the perfection of wisdom, they immediately attain mastery over the objects of the mind. They cultivate awakening with a mind focused on the signless, yet they do not perceive any difference between the signless and awakening; this is called equality.
The mind takes non-aspiration as its object yet does not abandon the triple world; seeing no difference between non-aspiration and the triple world is called equanimity.
One contemplates the impurity of the body while the mind dwells in purity;
one contemplates the impermanence of conditioned phenomena while the mind dwells within birth and death without weariness or seeking escape.
Observing the suffering of sentient beings, they abide in the bliss of nirvana;
observing the selflessness of phenomena, they give rise to great compassion for all sentient beings— constantly preaching the medicine of impurity without perceiving the disease of greed,
and constantly preaching great loving-kindness without perceiving anger or resentment.
He constantly teaches dependent origination, yet does not perceive the accumulation of diseases such as ignorance;
he teaches impermanence and lack of bliss, yet does not perceive the distinction between these diseases and impermanence.

In this way, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom through the power of skillful means, attaining mastery over the mental objects of all phenomena, and taking as his object the dharma of detachment in order to transform the śrāvakas.
Conditioned by the dharma of being free from hatred, one transforms pratyekabuddhas;
conditioned by the dharma of being free from delusion, one acts for the sake of transforming bodhisattvas;
conditioned by all forms, one vows to attain the form of a Buddha through non-apprehension.
When the mind takes various sounds as its object, may it aspire to obtain the subtle and wondrous voice of the Tathāgata;
when the mind takes various fragrances as its object, may it aspire to obtain the pure fragrance of the Tathāgata’s precepts;
when the mind takes various flavors as its object, may it aspire to obtain the Tathāgata’s mark of being the foremost among great men regarding taste.
With the mind taking all contacts as its object, may I attain the Tathāgata’s soft palms;
with the mind taking all phenomena as its object, may I attain the Tathāgata’s tranquil mind;
with the mind taking generosity as its object, may I achieve a body endowed with the primary and secondary marks.
The mind takes ethical discipline as its object, for the sake of attaining a pure Buddha-land;
the mind takes patience as its object, vowing to attain the Tathāgata’s great Brahma-voice and body of pure radiance;
the mind takes diligence as its object, for the sake of delivering sentient beings.
The mind takes meditative concentration as its object in order to achieve the great supernormal powers;
the mind takes Prajñā as its object in order to sever all views and afflictions;
the mind takes great compassion as its object, impartial and unimpeded, so that all sentient beings may attain peace and happiness.
The mind takes great compassion as its object in order to protect the True Dharma;
the mind takes great joy as its object in order to attain the delight of preaching the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings;
the mind takes great equanimity as its object, seeing neither the afflictions nor the fetters of sentient beings.
"Great King!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom through the power of skillful means, they do not perceive two things; this is called 'equal practice.'"
The mind takes the four means of attraction as its object for the purpose of teaching and transforming sentient beings;
it takes the fault of envy as its object for the purpose of relinquishing material wealth;
and it takes the loss resulting from breaking the precepts as its object for the purpose of abiding in pure morality.
To remedy the loss caused by anger, one practices patience;
to remedy the loss caused by laziness, one attains the power of a Buddha;
to remedy the loss caused by distraction, one attains the Tathāgata’s tranquil meditative concentration.
The mind takes coarse objects as its focus in order to perfect the Tathāgata’s unimpeded wisdom;
it takes śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas as its focus out of a desire to accomplish the unsurpassed Mahāyāna;
and it takes the evil realms as its focus out of a desire to rescue and deliver all sentient beings.
When the mind takes the various devas as its object, it knows that all phenomena are subject to decay;
when it takes sentient beings as its object, it knows they lack solidity or substance;
when the mind takes mindfulness of the Buddha as its object, it is for the sake of attaining the realization of meditative concentration that aids the Path.
One contemplates the Dharma with the mind in order to attain penetration into all secret treasuries;
one contemplates the Sangha with the mind in order to achieve non-retrogression;
one contemplates renunciation with the mind in order to be free from attachment.
The mind contemplates the precepts in order to attain pure precepts;
the mind contemplates the heavens in order to achieve the Buddha-way and be praised by all the devas;
the mind contemplates one's own body in order to attain the Buddha-body.
When the mind takes its own speech as an object, it is for the sake of attaining the Buddha’s speech;
when the mind takes its own mind as an object, it is for the sake of attaining the Tathāgata’s impartial mind;
when the mind takes conditioned phenomena as an object, it is for the sake of attaining the Buddha’s wisdom.
When the mind takes the unconditioned as its object, it attains tranquility.
"Great King!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, there is not a single thought or a single action that passes in vain without being directed toward sarvajñatā (all-knowledge)."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they universally take all phenomena as objects of focus yet remain unattached; this is called *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means). Observing all phenomena, they see that there is nothing that does not tend toward enlightenment.
"Great King!
It is like the great earth of the trichiliocosm, from which all things arise, and there is nothing that people do not make use of.

So it is with the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom: whatever objects they take as their focus, there is none that does not benefit them as they advance toward enlightenment."
Just as among all forms there is none that is not composed of the four great elements, so too,
among the objective spheres perceived by a bodhisattva, there is not a single phenomenon that does not tend toward enlightenment.
Why is this? The various practices cultivated by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are all established through external conditions.
For example, it is through persons characterized by stinginess and envy that the bodhisattva’s perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā) is brought to fulfillment.
Through those who do not recognize kindness, one accomplishes the Bodhisattva’s perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā);
through sentient beings of evil nature and malice, one accomplishes the Bodhisattva’s perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā);
and through those who are indolent, one accomplishes the Bodhisattva’s perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā).
Because of distracted people, they accomplish the Bodhisattva’s dhyāna-pāramitā;
because of those who are ignorant and dull-witted, they accomplish the Bodhisattva’s prajñā-pāramitā.
If there are sentient beings who harm or afflict a Bodhisattva, the Bodhisattva does not give rise to a mind of anger on account of this.
If a bodhisattva sees one practicing wholesome dharmas directed toward enlightenment, they conceive of that person as their own self and regard them with the heart of a parent toward a child.
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva feels no joy when others praise them, nor does they feel anger when others disparage them;
seeing suffering sentient beings, they give rise to great compassion, and seeing those experiencing happiness, they give rise to great joy.
If, because sentient beings are difficult to transform and are stubborn and perverse, the bodhisattva then gives rise to the mind of *śamatha*;
because of those who practice through faith, the bodhisattva immediately attains the wisdom of recognizing kindness;
and if he sees that sentient beings have strong external adverse conditions and weak wholesome causes, the bodhisattva then gives rise to a mind of protection.
If a bodhisattva perceives that the power of causes is strong in someone, they employ various skillful means to cause that person to receive the teaching;
if a bodhisattva perceives sentient beings whose wisdom is awakened and who understand the meaning, they then expound the profound Dharma for them;
if there are wise people, the bodhisattva then teaches the Dharma to them in successive stages.
For those attached to words, he explains the meaning of phrases;
for those who have already previously studied śamatha, the bodhisattva explains vipaśyanā;
and for those who have previously studied vipaśyanā, he should explain various samādhis to them.
If one is attached to the observance of precepts, he speaks of hell for them; if they observe precepts without attachment, he does not speak of it.
If one is attached to learning, he speaks of reflection and cultivation;
if one is attached to samādhi, he speaks of entering into prajñā.
To those who delight in the *āraṇya*, one should teach the Dharma of mental seclusion;
to those who wish to hear of the Buddha’s virtues, one should teach noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*);
and for those who are greedy, one should teach the Dharma of impurity (*aśubha*).
For those who are prone to anger, he teaches the Dharma of loving-kindness and compassion;
for those who are deluded, he teaches the Dharma of dependent origination;
for those who are characterized by equanimity...
He expounds various dharmas—sometimes teaching on impurity, sometimes on loving-kindness and compassion, and sometimes on causes and conditions;
he transforms and guides sentient beings by teaching them pure precepts, meditative concentration, and wisdom;
and for those who should enter the Buddha Vehicle and receive transformation, he teaches the various *pāramitās* in successive order.
For those who should be transformed through suppression and defeat, one should first refute their arguments and then preach the Dharma;
for those who should be transformed through various modes of speech, one should immediately explain causes and conditions and parables so that they may attain understanding;

for those who should be transformed through the profound Dharma, one should immediately explain the Prajñāpāramitā and the power of skillful means, wherein there is no person, no self, and no characteristics of dharmas.
For sentient beings who cling to views, he preaches the dharma of emptiness;
for those with excessive discursive thought and observation, he preaches signlessness;
and for those who delight in clinging to the conditioned, he preaches wishlessness.
For sentient beings attached to the aggregates, he teaches that they are like illusions;
for sentient beings attached to the elements, he teaches that they are non-existent;
for sentient beings attached to the sense bases, he teaches that they are like dreams.
For those attached to the desire realm, he teaches the burning;
for those attached to the form realm, he teaches the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*);
for those attached to the formless realm, he teaches the impermanence of conditioned existence.
For sentient beings who are difficult to transform, he praises the noble lineages;
for those who are easy to transform, he speaks of the various meditative concentrations and the immeasurable states of mind;
and for those who are transformed upon hearing of rebirth in heaven, he speaks of bliss.
For those who are transformed by means of the Śrāvaka-dharma, he teaches the various truths (satya);
for those who are transformed by means of the Pratyekabuddha-dharma, he teaches dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda);
and for those who are transformed by means of the Bodhisattva-dharma, he teaches the pure mind and the dharma of great compassion (mahākaruṇā).
For bodhisattvas who are practicing the path, one should speak of their merits and wisdom;
for those bodhisattvas who are non-retrogressive (avaivartika), one should speak of the purification of buddha-fields;
and for those in their final birth before enlightenment (ekajātipratibaddha), one should speak of the adornment of the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
For those who are to be transformed by the Buddha’s teaching, he speaks in a continuous succession.
“Great King!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the pure Prajñāpāramitā, he attains all forms of mastery through the power of skillful means, and his preaching of the Dharma benefits others without fail.”

When this Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva’s Sovereignty was being expounded, thirty thousand devas and humans among the assembly conceived the aspiration for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and five thousand bodhisattvas attained the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

At that time, the World-Honored One smiled with joy. It is the natural law of all Buddhas that when they smile, great rays of light are emitted from their faces—blue, yellow, red, white, purple, and crystal-colored—which illuminate immeasurable and boundless worlds, reaching upward as far as the Akaniṣṭha Heaven. They then return to the Buddha’s presence, circumambulate him three times to the right, and enter through the crown of his head.

At that time, the Greatly Wise Śāriputra rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, do not manifest such rare and auspicious signs without a great cause and condition.
