For what reason and by what cause does the World-Honored One now emit this radiance that shines everywhere throughout the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions?
"I pray that the World-Honored One will explain this.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"O son of good family!

This King of Celestial Devas, in the past, throughout immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, practiced the various *pāramitās* in the presence of all Buddhas. To protect and uphold this *prajñāpāramitā* for the sake of all bodhisattvas, he will, in a future age after immeasurable hundreds of thousands of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, complete the provisions for unsurpassed *bodhi*. Thereafter, he shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, becoming a Buddha named Guṇavyūha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. His land shall be named Vyūha-viśuddhā, and his kalpa shall be named Viśuddhā.
That land is abundant and prosperous, its people live in peace and happiness, and it consists entirely of a multitude of bodhisattvas.

That country is adorned throughout with the seven treasures—namely gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, agate, musaragalva, and pearl—with these seven treasures interspersed to form its ground. It is as level as the palm of a hand, beautified by fragrant flowers and soft grasses, and free from mountains, hills, mounds, or thorns.
Adorned with various banners, flowers, pennants, and canopies, the city was named Durdharṣa. A network of seven precious jewels covered it from above, and golden bells hung from its corners.
Six times throughout the day and night, the devas in the sky spontaneously played celestial music, scattering various divine incenses and exquisite celestial flowers.
The people of that land experience joy and delight surpassing even those of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations.
Humans and devas come and go without obstruction, and the three evil realms do not exist there.
The sentient beings of that land seek only the wisdom of the Buddha; even the name of the two vehicles does not exist.

That Buddha, the World-Honored One, expounds the Dharma of purity for the sake of the high-practicing Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. His immeasurable and boundless assembly of Bodhisattva followers is free from those who break the precepts, those of wrong livelihood, those attached to views, the blind, the deaf, the mute, the hunchbacked, the naked, or those with deficient faculties; they are all fully endowed with the twenty-eight marks that adorn their bodies.
The Buddha’s lifespan will be eight minor kalpas;
among the multitudes of devas and humans, none shall suffer premature death. Good son!

That Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses such immeasurable merits that whenever he wishes to preach the Dharma, he first emits a radiance that illuminates the land. When those bodhisattvas encounter this light, they immediately know that the World-Honored One is about to preach the Dharma and think, "We should now go to listen."
At that time, the devas prepared for the World-Honored One a lion throne one hundred yojanas high, adorned with various ornaments and provided with immeasurable offerings.

Seated upon it, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma for the assembly. Those bodhisattvas were intelligent and of sharp faculties; upon hearing it once, they realized and understood the absence of self and what belongs to self.
"Food and drink as provisions shall be obtained the moment one thinks of them.

When this Dharma-gate of the Prophecy of King Śūra was being spoken, fifty thousand devas and humans among the assembly gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, all vowing to be born in that land in the future.

At that time, when King Śūra heard the Buddha, the World-Honored One, bestow upon him this prediction of enlightenment, his heart was filled with great joy at having attained what he had never experienced before; he leaped into the air to a height of seven tala trees.

At that time, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways; the musical instruments of the devas resounded spontaneously without being struck, and they scattered various celestial flowers as an offering to the Buddha and to King Śūraṅgama.
Then, King Śūra descended from mid-air, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
Chapter Seven: Manifesting Signs *The Sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom Spoken by King Śūra*, Chapter Seven: Manifesting Signs At that time, the Greatly Wise Śāriputra addressed King Śūra, saying:

“When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom and penetrates the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), he should immediately sit upon the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and turn the wheel of Dharma. For what cause and condition does he first practice austerities to subdue Māra?”
At that time, King Śūra replied to Śāriputra, saying:
"Good son! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, there is truly no ascetic practice."

He manifested this in order to subdue the non-Buddhists; yet that celestial Māra was truly unable to destroy him. Because he is the lord of the desire realm, he manifested his subjugation of him to transform all sentient beings.
“Śāriputra! Non-Buddhists claim that their own ascetic practices are supreme; therefore, the Bodhisattva manifests ascetic practices in order to be able to surpass them. Śāriputra!”

There are some sentient beings who see the Bodhisattva standing with one knee bent; or see him standing with both hands raised; or see him standing while gazing at the sun; or see him performing the "five heats" asceticism; or see him standing on his head;

or see him lying on a bed of thorns, or lying on cow dung, or sitting on a square stone, or again lying on the bare ground, or lying on a wooden plank, or lying on a pestle, or lying in dust and dirt;
or see him wearing a garment of boards, or a garment of *mālu* grass, or a garment of grass, or a garment of tree bark, or again being naked, or wearing a garment of reeds.
Some face the sun and turn along with it;
some eat millet, or are seen eating wheat; some eat grass roots mixed with various tree leaves, or eat fruits and flowers; some eat yams, or are seen eating taro, or are seen eating lotus roots;
some eat once every six days, or are seen eating beans, or eating large beans, or eating parched grain; some are seen eating sesame, or are seen eating rice.
Some see them passing their days by drinking water;
some see Bodhisattvas passing their days by eating a single measure of ghee, or a single measure of honey, or a single measure of milk;
some see them eating nothing at all, or see them sleeping soundly.
“Śāriputra! The bodhisattva-mahāsattva manifests such various ascetic practices for six years, without failing in even a single matter.

In reality, the bodhisattva has no such ascetic practices; it is because sentient beings perceive them as existing that he displays them, so that those sentient beings who should be liberated through asceticism may do so. For their sake, the bodhisattva manifests these, and sixty nayutas of people thereby abide in the Three Vehicles.”

“Śāriputra! Furthermore, there are devas and humans whose roots of goodness from past lives have deeply delighted in the Mahāyāna; they see the Bodhisattva seated upon a terrace of the seven treasures, his body and mind unmoving, his face smiling with joy as he enters samādhi.”
In this manner, he did not arise from his meditative concentration for six years. Śāriputra!
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who deeply delight in the Mahāyāna and wish to hear it; to them, they see the Bodhisattva sitting upright and preaching the Dharma.

Śāriputra! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom through the power of skillful means, transforming and delivering all sentient beings with great compassion, and being able to subdue the celestial Māras and overcome all non-Buddhist paths.

After the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva had completed six years, he arose from meditative concentration and, conforming to worldly custom, went to the Nairañjanā River. Having bathed and emerged, he stood by the riverbank; there was a cowherd girl who milked a hundred cows to feed a single cow, and she took the milk from that cow to prepare a gruel which she offered to the Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, there were six hundred million devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas, each bringing food and drink to offer as a tribute, saying these words:
"O Great Being!..."
Accept my offerings,
O Noble One!
Accept my offerings!
The Bodhisattva accepted them all; yet those cowherd women, devas, nāgas, and yakṣas did not see one another, for each deva and so forth saw the Bodhisattva receiving their food alone.

Śāriputra! These sentient beings attain awakening because they see [the Bodhisattva] receiving offerings; therefore, the Bodhisattva manifests this for their sake, yet this Bodhisattva does not actually bathe or receive such offerings.
“Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, through the power of skillful means, he manifests the act of proceeding to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).

At that time, there was a terrestrial devaputra named Wondrous Ground (Miaodi), who, together with various celestial deities, swept this great earth, scattered many exquisite flowers, and sprinkled it with various kinds of fragrant water.”

The hosts of devas beneath Mount Sumeru throughout the trichiliocosm rained down celestial flowers; the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings and those of the Trāyastriṃśa and Yāma heavens offered praise from mid-air while performing various musical performances. Śakra, King of the Tuṣita Heaven, covered the world with nets of the seven treasures, from which bells of Jāmbūnada gold hung at each of the four corners, as they all rained down a multitude of jewels to make offerings to the Bodhisattva.

The King of Skillful Transformation among the gods of the Nirmāṇarati heaven covered the world with nets of Jambūnada gold, performed various musical performances, and rained down all kinds of flowers as an offering to the Bodhisattva.

The devaputras of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, together with the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others, each prepared various kinds of offerings.
When the Devaputra Īśvara and Mahābrahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, saw that the Bodhisattva had proceeded to the site of enlightenment, they immediately addressed all the Brahmās, saying:
"O noble sons!..."

You should know that such bodhisattva-mahāsattvas adorn themselves with a firm and great body; they do not violate their original vows and their minds are free from weariness or indolence. They have fully perfected all bodhisattva practices, attained mastery in teaching and transforming immeasurable sentient beings, and gained sovereign power over all the bodhisattva stages.
Toward all sentient beings, their minds are pure, and they skillfully understand their faculties and natures.

They have thoroughly penetrated the profound and secret treasury of the Tathāgata; they have transcended all demonic activities; their roots of goodness do not follow external conditions; they are protected by immeasurable Buddhas; they are able to open the gate of liberation for sentient beings; as great generals and guides, they subdue all Māras; they alone are courageous within the great trichiliocosm; they skillfully bestow the medicine of the Dharma as great kings of physicians; having received the empowerment of liberation, they occupy the throne of the Dharma King and radiate the light of wisdom; they cannot be stained by the eight worldly dharmas, like a great lotus flower; they have mastered all *dhāraṇīs*, which are as deep as the ocean; they abide immovably like Mount Sumeru; their wisdom is pure and free from defilement, like a *maṇi* jewel; and they have attained mastery over all phenomena and maintain pure Brahma-conduct.
"Good son!

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates the prajñāpāramitā, he proceeds to the site of enlightenment through the practice of skillful means, desiring to subdue evil Māras. Seated beneath the Bodhi tree, he seeks to accomplish the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities; he turns the great wheel of Dharma and lets out the lion’s roar, bestowing the gift of the Dharma so that all sentient beings may be fully satisfied.
He does this in order to purify the Dharma-eye of sentient beings and to use the unsurpassed true Dharma to subdue those of external paths."
To demonstrate that the original vows of all Buddhas have been fulfilled and that they have attained mastery over all dharmas,
noble sons, you should go to make offerings to this Bodhisattva.

“Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, through the power of skillful means, he manifests the act of proceeding to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), and beneath his feet there immediately appears the subtle and wondrous light of the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel.
All those in the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts who encountered this radiance were entirely freed from suffering and attained peace and happiness.
When it shone upon the dragon palaces, the Dragon King Kālika encountered this radiance and immediately addressed the dragons:
"This golden light comes to illuminate our dragon palaces, causing all of you to attain peace and happiness in body and mind."
"In the past, I have seen this sign when a Buddha appeared in the world;
since this radiance today is no different from before, one should know that a Buddha will surely appear in the world."

One should prepare various kinds of incense for burning, unguents, and powdered incense; gold, silver, pearls, musaragalva, agate, coral, and white jade; as well as banners, flowers, pennants, and canopies, and perform various musical performances. Then, proceeding to the Bodhisattva’s palace, one should bring all these excellent things as offerings.

Then the Naga King Kālika, together with his retinue, raised a vast cloud and caused a rain of fragrant water to fall. He approached the Bodhisattva, performed various musical offerings, circumambulated the Bodhisattva to the right, and praised him, saying:
"This golden radiance brings joy to all; it is certain that you are the most supreme, and there is no doubt that a Buddha has appeared."

The great earth was adorned with various kinds of miscellaneous jewels, and all the grasses and trees growing from the ground were transformed into precious gems; the rivers and streams were all stilled, devoid of the sound of wind or waves. Inferring from such auspicious omens, there is no doubt that a Buddha has appeared in the world.
The radiance of Śakra, Brahmā, the sun, and the moon does not appear; the evil realms become purified; there is no doubt that a Buddha has appeared.
It is like a person who lost his parents in youth and, having grown to maturity, suddenly regains them—his heart is filled with immense joy;
so it is for all the world when they behold the arising of a Buddha.
"We have already made offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past; now that we have encountered the Dharma King, the Lion among Men, our births have not been in vain."

"Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, by the power of skillful means he takes grass and spreads it for a seat; he circumambulates the Bodhi tree seven times to the right and sits upright with right mindfulness."
Inferior sentient beings see such a sign. Śāriputra, furthermore,

there are great bodhisattvas of sublime conduct who see eighty-four thousand sons of heaven having spread out eighty-four thousand great lion thrones— composed of various jewels, with nets of the seven treasures covering them, golden bells at every corner, and banners, flowers, pennants, canopies, and silken streamers arranged in rows.

At that time, the Bodhisattva sat upon each and every one of these eighty-four thousand seats throughout their entirety; yet the sons of the gods did not see one another, each thinking, "The Bodhisattva is sitting alone on my seat and has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
For these reasons, their hearts were filled with joy; having attained what they had never experienced before, they all realized the state of *avaivartika*. "Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, by the power of skillful means, he immediately emits light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows, which illuminates the palaces of all Māras; the palaces of all Māras throughout the trichiliocosm lose their radiance."
At that time, each of the Māras had this thought:
"By what cause and condition has the radiance of our respective palaces failed to appear?
Could it not be that the Bodhisattva is sitting at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) to realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
They immediately looked together and saw the Bodhisattva sitting upright at the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree.

At that time, the various evil Māras gathered an army of immeasurable thousands of billions from their own palaces; they possessed all manner of colors, all manner of forms, all manner of appearances, and all manner of heads and faces. They carried various weapons, various banners and pennants, and made various sounds such that anyone who heard them would have blood flow from their ears, noses, and mouths.
At that time, by the power of great compassion, the Bodhisattva causes the hosts of Māra’s army to be unable to utter a sound. Śāriputra,
this is called the power of the skillful means of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the Prajñāpāramitā.

“Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, through the power of skillful means, they practice for immeasurable billions of kalpas: giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of awakening, the path, *śamatha*, *vipaśyanā*, the three knowledges, and liberation. With their golden-colored body and right arm, they stroke from the crown of their head down to their entire body, saying these words:
‘The sentient beings are afflicted by suffering; I wish to rescue and deliver them, and thus I give rise to great compassion.’”
At that time, when Māra and his retinue heard the Bodhisattva’s words, they all fell prostrate.
Through the power of great compassion, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva caused a voice to resound from the air, saying to the hosts of Māras:
"You should take refuge in the Seer who possesses the power of upholding the precepts; he is able to bestow fearlessness and rescue and protect all sentient beings."
When Māra and his retinue heard these words, they remained prostrate on the ground and spoke thus:
"We pray only that the Righteous One, the Great Being, will save our lives!"
"Śāriputra! At that time, when the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, he emits a great radiance through the power of skillful means; all who encounter it are freed from fear."
When Māra and his retinue saw this supernatural power, they were filled with both terror and joy. "Śāriputra!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, some sentient beings may see this subduing of Māra, while others do not see this event."

There are some sentient beings who see the Bodhisattva sitting upon spread grass; some see him sitting upon a great lion-jewel terrace; some see him sitting on the ground; and some see him sitting peacefully upon a lion-throne that has appeared spontaneously in mid-air.
There are some sentient beings who see the Aśvattha tree as the Bodhi tree; some see the Pārijātaka tree; and some see the Bodhi tree composed of various jewels.

There are some sentient beings who see the Bodhi tree to be seven *tāla* trees in height; and there are some sentient beings who see the Bodhi tree to be eighty-four thousand *yojanas* in height, with the lion-throne being forty-two thousand *yojanas* in height.
There may be sentient beings who see from afar the Bodhisattva sporting in mid-air, or they may see the Bodhisattva seated at the Bodhi tree.
Śāriputra, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, through the power of skillful means, he manifests such various supernatural transformations to deliver sentient beings.
“Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, through the power of skillful means, he manifests sitting at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).

Bodhisattva mahāsattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the worlds of the ten directions—all immeasurable and boundless—gather together and abide in the midst of space, uttering these words to comfort, settle, and gladden the bodhisattva:”
“Excellent! You possess swift and courageous diligence and great auspiciousness; do not give rise to fear.
With a mind like a vajra, sport in supernatural powers to benefit sentient beings.”
"In a single thought-moment, all-knowledge manifests. Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva sits at the site of enlightenment, even if Māra comes to cause disturbance, he does not give rise to anger; in a single kṣaṇa of mind, he accords with the Prajñāpāramitā, and there is nothing among what is known, seen, or realized that he does not penetrate."
"Śāriputra!
At that time, the Tathāgatas of the worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions praised him with one voice, saying:
'Excellent, O Great Being!'"
"They have attained spontaneous wisdom, unimpeded wisdom, impartial wisdom, and teacherless wisdom, adorned by great compassion. "Śāriputra!
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they are able to manifest such various displays through the power of skillful means."
There may be sentient beings who see this Bodhisattva attaining enlightenment for the first time now, or who see him having attained enlightenment long ago;

or they may see the Four Heavenly Kings of a single world offering him the alms bowl, or they may see the Four Heavenly Kings of worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions offering him the alms bowl.
Śāriputra! At that time, for the sake of delivering sentient beings, the Bodhisattva accepted the various bowls and, stacking them within his palms, merged them into one.
The various heavenly kings could not see one another, and each thought, "The World-Honored One is using my bowl alone."
"Śāriputra!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they manifest this matter through the power of skillful means.
When this Dharma-gate was being taught, thirty thousand bodhisattva mahāsattvas among the assembly attained the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
Thirty-six thousand bodhisattvas all attained non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
eighty thousand humans and devas attained the pure Dharma-eye, free from dust and defilement;
and immeasurable, boundless sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Śāriputra! Furthermore, sixty thousand devaputras had previously come to present offerings due to their past vows, saying:
'If a bodhisattva attains the Way, we vow that he shall first accept our offerings.'"
At that time, by the power of skillful means in the *prajñāpāramitā*, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva manifested the intent to turn the wheel of Dharma.

Śikhin, the Brahmā King and lord of the Sahā world, together with six million eight hundred thousand Brahmās, came to the World-Honored One’s presence, prostrated with their heads at his feet, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and spoke these words:
“We pray only that, out of great compassion, you will turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma!”
"May you, out of great compassion, turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma!
At that moment, there appeared a great lion throne forty-two thousand yojanas high, adorned with various ornaments, firm and secure.
In the same manner, the immeasurable Śakradevānām-Indras of the ten directions all prepared lion thrones for the Tathāgata.
At that time, by means of his supernormal powers, each of those devas perceived the Bodhisattva sitting upon their respective thrones and turning the wheel of Dharma.

Once the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has sat upon this seat, the immeasurable and boundless worlds of the ten directions all tremble and emit great radiance, and he immediately enters the Samādhi of the Boundless Realm.

All sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions shall immediately attain peace and happiness, be entirely freed from the three poisons, and regard one another like a mother and her child, no longer harboring any malicious intent.
At that time, this trichiliocosm was without any empty space, as if it were a single pore.
Gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others all filled its entirety.
If there are sentient beings who should be transformed by the teaching of suffering, they hear the Buddha speak of suffering;
those who should be transformed by non-self, emptiness, tranquility, detachment, or impermanence—all are likewise treated in this way.

Those who should be transformed by the teaching that things are like illusions hear the discourse on being like an illusion; those who should be transformed by [the teachings that things are] like dreams, like the moon in water, like shadows, or like echoes—all are likewise treated in this way.
Those who should be transformed through emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness immediately hear the Buddha preach the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
or they hear the Tathāgata say that all dharmas arise from causes and conditions;
or they hear the teaching on the aggregates (skandhas), or the teaching on the elements (dhātus), or the teaching on the sense bases (āyatanas).
They may hear the sound of the teaching on suffering, or the sound of the teaching on its origin, or the sound of the teaching on the path;

they may hear the teaching on the foundations of mindfulness, or the teachings on the right efforts, or the teachings on the bases of psychic power, or the teachings on the faculties, or the teachings on the powers, or the teachings on the factors of enlightenment, or the teachings on the path; they may hear the teachings on śamatha, or the teachings on vipaśyanā, or the teachings on the Dharma of the pratyekabuddhas, or the teachings on the Mahāyāna.

Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, through the power of skillful means, they manifest various turnings of the wheel of Dharma, causing immeasurable sentient beings to rejoice and benefit according to their respective faculties and natures.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed King Jayoṣadha, saying:
"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, through the power of skillful means, their profound realm is difficult to know, difficult to conceive, and difficult to enter."
At that time, King Śūra answered Śāriputra, saying:

“Regarding the superior merits of the bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, what I have now described does not equal even one hundredth part; it does not equal even one part in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions, nor even by calculation or analogy. Only a Tathāgata is able to describe them in their entirety.”
That which I have now spoken is but a small portion, all of it received through the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata. Why is this?
Even Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who are in their last birth before Buddhahood cannot exhaustively fathom the realm of the Buddhas, much less other bodhisattvas.
Śāriputra! The realm of all Buddhas is quiescent and beyond description; it can be realized only by the non-conceptual wisdom that follows. Śāriputra!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to enter the realm of all buddhas should study the *prajñāpāramitā*,
the *śūraṅgama-samādhi*, the *māyopama-samādhi*, the *vajropama-samādhi*, the *vajra-samādhi*,
the *akṣobhyamati-samādhi*, the *sarvatragaprativedha-samādhi*, and the *anālambana-viṣaya-samādhi*.
the Lion Sovereignty Samādhi, the King of Samādhis Samādhi, the Merit-Adorned Samādhi, the Tranquil Mind Samādhi,
the Transcendence Samādhi, the Unattached Samādhi, the Mind-Adornment King Samādhi,
the Peerless Samādhi, the Equal Awakening Samādhi, and the Perfect Awakening Samādhi.
The Samādhi of Delightful Intent, the Samādhi of Joy, the Samādhi of Purity, the Samādhi of the Flame, the Samādhi of Radiance,
the Samādhi Difficult to Conquer, the Samādhi of Constant Manifestation, the Samādhi of Non-proximity, the Samādhi of Non-arising,
the Samādhi of Thorough Penetration, the Samādhi of Supreme Excellence, and the Transcendence of the Realm of Māra.
The samādhi of equanimity, the samādhi of the mind of omniscience, the samādhi of the banner-sign, the samādhi of great compassion, the samādhi of joy,
the samādhi of affectionate mindfulness, and the samādhi of not seeing phenomena.

“Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, by means of the power of skillful means, having mastered such immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of billions of *gaṅgā*-sands of samādhis, they are then able to enter the realm of all Buddhas.”
His mind is peaceful and secure, and all fear has vanished, just as the lion king does not stand in awe of birds or beasts. Why is this?
Because once a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has cultivated such samādhis as these, wherever he travels, he is entirely without fear and perceives no enemy before him.
Why is this? Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, by means of the power of skillful means, the mind has no object of focus and no place of abiding.

For example, it is as if there were a person born in the formless realm who, for eighty-four thousand kalpas, possesses only a single consciousness that has neither a place of abiding nor an object of perception;
so too it is with the bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom—the mind has neither a place of abiding nor an object of perception.
Why is this? Because the mind does not function, there is no place for its functioning;
because the mind is without conceptualization, there is no place for conceptualization.
The mind does not take objects as its conditions, so there is no place of conditioning;
the mind does not cling, so there is no place of clinging;
the mind is not distracted, so there is no place of distraction.
The mind is without high or low; it neither conforms nor opposes, neither rejoices nor grieves;
it is without discrimination and free from discrimination;
it is free from śamatha and vipaśyanā, and the mind does not follow after wisdom.
The mind does not abide in itself, nor does it abide in another; it does not abide depending on the eye, nor does it abide depending on the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind;
it does not abide depending on forms, nor does it abide depending on sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena.
The mind is neither within nor without; the mind does not take dharmas as its object, nor does it take wisdom as its object; it does not abide in the past, the future, or the present.
“Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not grasp at a single dharma.

Because their mental activity is pure, they possess unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding all dharmas; they see all dharmas as entirely stainless. They do not grasp at the signs of seeing, they do not differentiate what they see, and they remain free from all conceptual proliferation.”

Śāriputra! The prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is not associated with the fleshly eye, nor is it associated with the divine eye; it is entirely dissociated from the wisdom-eye, the dharma-eye, and the buddha-eye.

It is not associated with the divine ear, nor with the knowledge of others' minds, nor with the knowledge of past lives, nor with the knowledge of supernormal powers, nor with the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows.
Śāriputra! This *prajñāpāramitā* is neither associated with all phenomena nor dissociated from them.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, through the power of skillful means, they attain the wisdom of equality regarding all phenomena; they are able to observe the mental activities of all sentient beings and know all that is defiled or pure exactly as it is, never losing mindfulness of the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities, and the Buddha’s omniscience.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, through the mind of non-effort, they penetrate all dharmas; being without mind, thought, or consciousness, they constantly abide within the samādhi of stillness. Without abandoning this samādhi, they transform and teach sentient beings, performing Buddha-works without rest. They attain unimpeded wisdom regarding all Buddha-dharmas, and their minds are free from defilement or attachment.

“Śāriputra! It is like a manifested Buddha who further manifests another Buddha; that which is manifested has no mind, thought, or consciousness, no body or bodily karma, no speech or vocal karma, and no mind or mental karma, yet it is able to perform all the works of a Buddha to benefit sentient beings.”
Why is this? It is because of the Buddha’s spiritual power, Śāriputra!

The transformation of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas through the Prajñāpāramitā is likewise thus: they possess no body and no bodily karma, no speech and no verbal karma, and no mind and no mental karma; yet, by means of effortlessness, they constantly perform the work of a Buddha to benefit sentient beings.
Why is this? Because when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they penetrate all phenomena as being like illusory appearances, and their mind is free from discrimination;
yet sentient beings constantly hear them preaching the Dharma.

Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva’s wisdom such as this does not abide in the conditioned, nor does it abide in the unconditioned; it does not abide in the aggregates, nor does it abide in the elements or the sense bases; it does not abide in the internal or the external, nor does it abide in wholesome or unwholesome dharmas; it does not abide in the mundane or the supramundane; it is neither defiled nor pure; it does not abide in the outflows, nor does it abide in the absence of outflows; it does not abide in the past, the future, or the present; it does not abide in cessation through deliberation, nor does it abide in cessation not through deliberation.
Śāriputra!

When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the prajñāpāramitā in this way, their minds abide nowhere yet they are able to penetrate all dharmas; with unimpeded wisdom and effortless power, they preach for the sake of sentient beings, remaining ever in tranquility while their work of teaching and transforming never ceases.
"Śāriputra! Because the power of their past vows is strong, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas preach the Dharma for others with effortlessness. Śāriputra!"
Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas possess the power of skillful means through the Prajñāpāramitā, they are free from all fears.
Why is this? It is because the Vajradhara deity constantly protects them; whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, he never remains far from them.

Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing the teaching of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, is not startled, not terrified, does not doubt, and does not regret, you should know that this person has already received the prediction of enlightenment.
Why is this? Because by believing in and accepting the *prajñāpāramitā*, one draws near to the realm of the Buddhas.

Through this single-mindedness, one is able to penetrate all Buddha-dharmas; having penetrated the Buddha-dharmas, one benefits sentient beings, perceiving no difference between sentient beings and the Buddha-dharmas.
Why is this? Because principle is non-dual.
*Śrī-māyā-devī-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, Scroll Four.
The Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra (Śūraṅgama-rāja-prajñāpāramitā Sūtra), Scroll Five, translated by Prince Yueposhouna of the Kingdom of Ujjayinī during the Chen Dynasty.
Chapter Eight: On Non-Apprehension. Chapter Eight: On Non-Apprehension.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva in the assembly named Susīma, who addressed King Śūra, saying:
"Has the Tathāgata bestowed a prophecy of enlightenment upon the Great King?"
The Victorious Heavenly King replied to the Bodhisattva Good Contemplation, saying:
"Good son, I grant a prediction of enlightenment that has the characteristic of being like a dream."
He asked again:
"Great King! By receiving such a prophecy, what dharma will you attain?"
He replied,
"Good son! The Buddha has bestowed upon me a prediction of enlightenment, yet ultimately there is nothing to be attained."
He asked again:
"What dharma is this 'non-attainment'?
He replied:
"One does not apprehend sentient beings, life-span, persons, or nourishers; one finds nothing at all in the aggregates, elements, or sense-bases.

Whether wholesome or unwholesome, defiled or pure, with outflows or without outflows, mundane or supramundane, conditioned or unconditioned, or whether it be birth-and-death or nirvāṇa—one finds nothing at all."
He asked again:
"If there is nothing to be attained, what is the use of receiving a prediction of enlightenment?
He replied:
“Good son! Because there is nothing to be attained, one receives the prediction of enlightenment.
He asked again:
"If it is as the Great King has explained the meaning, then there would be two kinds of knowledge:
first, non-attainment; second, the attainment of the prediction of enlightenment.
He replied:
“If there were duality, there would be no prophecy.
Why? Because the Buddha’s wisdom is non-dual.”
"The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, bestow the prediction of enlightenment upon bodhisattvas by means of non-dual wisdom.
He asked again:
"If wisdom is non-dual, how can there be the conferring of a prediction and the receiving of one?"
He replied:
"The attainment of the prediction and the conferral of the prediction are non-dual at their limit.
He asked again:
"If the limit of non-duality is such, how can there be a prediction [of enlightenment]? He replied,
"To penetrate the limit of non-duality is itself the prediction."
He asked again:
"Great King, abiding in what limit have you received this prediction?
He replied:

"One receives the prediction of enlightenment by abiding in the limit of the self; one receives the prediction by abiding in the limit of sentient beings, the limit of life-span, and the limit of the person.
He asked again:
"Where should one seek the limit of the self?"
He replied:
"One should seek it at the limit of the Tathāgata’s liberation.
He asked again:
"Where, then, should one seek the limit of the Tathāgata’s liberation?
He replied:
"One should seek it at the limit of ignorance and craving for existence."
He asked again:
"Where should ignorance and craving be sought?
He replied:
"One should seek it within the limit of ultimate non-arising.
He asked again:
"Within what should one seek the limit of ultimate non-arising?"
He replied,
"One should seek it at the limit of non-knowing.
He asked again:
"If one is without knowledge, there is nothing to be known; how, then, can one seek within this limit?
He replied:
"If there were something to be known, seeking would be impossible to achieve; it is because there is no knowledge that one seeks within this limit."
He asked again:
"At this juncture there are no words; how can it be sought?
He replied:
"Because it is brought to an end through speech, it can be sought.
He asked again:
"In what way is it brought to an end through speech?"
He replied,
"All dharmas rely on the meaning, not on the words.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'relying on the meaning'?
He replied: "It is not perceiving the characteristics of the meaning."
He asked again:
"In what way is it not seen?
He replied:

"The non-arising of conceptualization regarding objects is that which is to be relied upon; I am that which relies [upon it]. Because these two things do not exist, it is called 'thorough penetration' (*prativedha*).
He asked again:
"If one does not perceive objects, what is there to be sought?"
He replied,
"Because one does not see and does not grasp, it is called 'seeking.
He asked again:
"If a dharma can be sought, then there is seeking.
He replied, "Not so!"
Now, one who seeks the Dharma has nothing to seek.
Why is this? If there were something to be sought, it would not be the Dharma.
He asked again:
"What is this Dharma?
He replied:
“The Dharma has no letters and is also beyond speech.
He asked again:
“Within that which is free from words and letters, what is the Dharma?”
He replied:
"The nature of words and letters is detached; the sphere of mental activity has ceased—this is called the Dharma.
All dharmas are ineffable, and even that ineffability cannot be expressed."
"Good son!
Whatever is spoken is itself false; within it there is no real dharma.
He asked again:
"Are all the words spoken by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas invariably false?
He replied:
"The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have not uttered a single word from beginning to end; how, then, could they be false?"
He asked again:
"If there is something spoken, what would be the fault?
He replied:
"It refers to the fault of speech.
He asked again,
"What is the fault in speech?"
He replied, "It is said to be the fault of deliberation.
He asked again:
“What dharma is without fault?
He replied:
“To have no discourse regarding what is spoken, and not to perceive dualistic characteristics—this is to be without fault.”
He asked again:
"What is the root of transgression?
He replied:
"Grasping is the root.
He asked again,
"What is the root of grasping?"
He replied,
“Attachment is the root.
He asked again:
"What is the root of attachment?
He replied:
"It is false conceptualization."
He asked again:
"What is the root of false discrimination?
He replied:
"Grasping at objects is the root.
He asked again:
"What is it that grasps at objects?"
He replied,
"Conditioned by visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'not having an object'? He replied:
"If one is free from craving and grasping, then there is no object."
"For this reason, the Tathāgata constantly teaches that all dharmas are equal.

When this Dharma-gate was being taught, five thousand bhikṣus within the assembly attained the pure Dharma-eye, free from dust and defilement; twelve thousand bodhisattvas attained the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti); and immeasurable, boundless sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

At that time, King Śūraṃgama rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Good sons and good daughters, having heard this Prajñāpāramitā, how is it that those who have not yet resolved to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi are able to immediately resolve their minds upon it, all fully achieving non-retrogression, and constantly practicing with superior progress without falling away?
The Buddha said to King Jayasena:
"Great King! Listen attentively and reflect well upon it; I shall speak for your sake."
“Good sons and good daughters, upon hearing the Prajñāpāramitā, they will attain superior progress in their practice and shall never fall back.
King Śūra said,
“Excellent, World-Honored One!”
"Indeed, we wish to hear it.
The Buddha addressed King Śūraṇa, saying:
"Great King!"

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, upon hearing the *prajñāpāramitā*, gives rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* with a pure intention, being endowed with right faith, associating with the worthy and the noble, delighting in hearing the true Dharma, remaining far removed from envy, being free from stinginess, constantly practicing tranquility, taking pleasure in practicing giving, having a mind free of obstruction and always detached from defilement, possessing right faith in the causality of karma, and being without doubt as they know the retribution of black and white deeds—then even for the sake of their own body or life, they would never do that which ought not to be done.
"Great King!

When a son or daughter of good family practices the *prajñāpāramitā* in this manner, they remain far removed from killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous speech, covetousness, malice, and wrong views; their minds are constantly focused upon these ten wholesome dharmas."
“Great King!

When a son or daughter of good family practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, through the power of skillful means, if they see a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who practices with right effort, whose moral precepts are pure, who is learned and understands the meaning [of the teachings], and who constantly gives rise to right mindfulness; whose mind-nature is tamed, tranquil, and undistracted; who always speaks kindly and remains far removed from all evil and unwholesome dharmas; who cultivates various virtues, neither being self-conceited toward others nor disparaging them; who refrains from harsh speech and meaningless talk; who does not abandon the foundations of mindfulness and whose mind is straight and upright; who is able to sever the flow of existence (*bhava-srotas*), skillfully extract the poisoned arrow, cast off the heavy burden, transcend the perils of existence, and has already crossed over to the further shore.”
"Great King!

When a son or daughter of good family practices the Prajñāpāramitā, if they see such a bodhisattva mahāsattva, they should draw near to and rely upon that person as a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra)."
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, through the power of skillful means, preaches the Dharma for them, saying:
"Good sons! Through giving one attains great wealth; through upholding the precepts one is reborn in heaven; and through listening to the Dharma one gains great wisdom."
Again, he further said:
"This is giving; this is the retribution for giving.
This is jealousy; this is the retribution for jealousy."
This is patience, and this is the retribution for patience;
this is diligence, and this is the retribution for diligence;
this is meditative concentration, and this is the retribution for meditative concentration.
This is wisdom, and this is the retribution for wisdom;
this is ignorance, and this is the retribution for ignorance;
this is wholesome bodily karma, and this is the retribution for wholesome bodily karma.
This is bodily unwholesome karma and the retribution for bodily unwholesome karma;
this is verbal wholesome karma and the retribution for verbal wholesome karma; this is verbal unwholesome karma and the retribution for verbal unwholesome karma;
this is mental wholesome karma and the retribution for mental wholesome karma.
This is mental unwholesome karma; this is the retribution for mental unwholesome karma.

Sons and daughters of good family, regarding these dharmas—this should be done and this should not be done—if one practices in this way, it will lead to happiness for a long night; if one acts otherwise, one will undergo suffering for a long night.
"Great King!
A son or daughter of good family, through the power of skillful means, approaches virtuous friends and hears such sequential teachings on the Dharma."

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows that a person is a vessel for the Dharma, they should then expound the profound *prajñāpāramitā*—namely, emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), and non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*)—as well as non-arising and non-ceasing, and the absence of self, sentient beings, life-force, or person. They should further explain the profound law of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*): "Because of this dharma, that dharma arises; because of the cessation of this dharma, that dharma ceases"—namely, ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions grasping; grasping conditions existence; existence conditions birth; and birth conditions old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair.

With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; and with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair cease.
“Great King!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, he speaks thus through the power of skillful means; yet within ultimate reality, there is not a single dharma that can arise or cease.”

Why is this? All phenomena in the world arise from causes and conditions; they are without self or agent. Through the conjunction of causes and conditions, there is not a single real dharma that undergoes birth and extinction.
They are merely false conceptualizations; within the three realms, there exist only provisional names, which receive retribution according to karma and afflictions.

If one observes all phenomena as they truly are by means of the perfection of wisdom—seeing them as neither arising nor ceasing, and having no agent or recipient—and if one sees that since phenomena have no agent there is likewise no activity, then the mind will have no attachment to any phenomena; that is to say, it does not attach to form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness; it does not attach to eye, forms, or eye-consciousness; it does not attach to mind, mental objects, or mind-consciousness.
"Great King! When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva speaks thus— that all dharmas are empty and detached by their very nature, and are neither grasped nor clung to—
then that son or daughter of good family will, because of such speech, never suffer any falling away."

“Great King! When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, he delights in seeing all Buddhas and delights in hearing the True Dharma. He does not fall into lowly or base states; wherever he is born, he never parts from seeing the Buddhas, hearing and receiving the True Dharma, and making offerings to the Saṅgha. He beholds the Buddhas face-to-face, seeking the True Dharma with courageous diligence, and does not cling to conditioned phenomena. He has no greedy attachment to wife, children, servants, or the necessities of life, nor is he defiled by any desires.”

Constantly relying on the true teachings, they maintain mindfulness of all Buddhas; having left the secular world to become renunciants, they practice according to what they have heard and explain it to others without seeking anything for themselves. Seeing the assembly listening to the Dharma, they constantly give rise to great loving-kindness and arouse great compassion toward all sentient beings. Having heard much and studied extensively, they do not spare their own bodies or lives; possessing few desires and being content, they always delight in seclusion. They grasp only the essential principles and do not cling to mere words; their preaching of the Dharma and their practice are not for their own sake, but solely to transform sentient beings so that they may attain unsurpassed bliss—namely, the wisdom of the Buddha.
“Great King!

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, he cultivates in this manner: remaining far removed from negligence, he guards his sense faculties. If the eye sees a form, he does not cling to the characteristics of that form, but observes the faults of that form as they truly are. It is the same for sounds heard by the ear, odors smelled by the nose, flavors tasted by the tongue, tangibles felt by the body, and mental phenomena cognized by the mind.”
If one allows the sense faculties to run wild, it is called negligence; if one is able to restrain and protect them, it is called non-negligence.
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, taming their own mind and guarding the intentions of others is called non-negligence.

To remain far removed from greed and desire, to align the mind with wholesome dharmas, and to distance oneself from all unwholesome states—namely, the unwholesome roots of discursive thought, hatred, and delusion, as well as physical misconduct, verbal misconduct, and wrong mindfulness—is called non-negligence.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, their mind is always in right mindfulness; this is called non-negligence.

"Great King, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, faith is the foremost of all dharmas. One who possesses right faith is not born in the evil realms, does not commit evil with the mind, and is praised by the noble ones."
"Great King!

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the Prajñāpāramitā and cultivate it according to the Dharma, they always encounter the Buddhas in whatever place they are born; they remain far removed from the two vehicles and abide securely in the Right Path, attaining great mastery and accomplishing the Great Task—the Right Wisdom of the Tathāgata."
“O Great King! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom and seeks peace and happiness, they should diligently follow the path to omniscience (sarvajñatā).”

Now that this great assembly has been able to hear the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they must have already made offerings to various Buddhas and cultivated roots of goodness throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas in the past; therefore, you should apply yourselves with diligent vigor and not allow [this merit] to decline or be lost.
"Great King!

Whether a deva or a human, one who can restrain the sense faculties and remain unattached to the five desires, who stays far removed from the mundane world and constantly cultivates that which transcends it, whose three karmas are pure, and who practices the dharmas that assist the Path—this is called non-negligence."
"Great King!

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, being fully endowed with right faith and maintaining a mind free from negligence, diligently cultivating vigor to attain the supreme Dharma—this is called 'heedfulness' (apramāda)."
"Great King!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to be endowed with right faith, whose mind is not negligent, and who is diligent and possesses right mindfulness, should study the Prajñāpāramitā."
"By means of this mindfulness and wisdom, one can swiftly accomplish the dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
'Great King!

When a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, being fully endowed with right faith and with a mind free from negligence, they diligently cultivate vigor and thereby attain right mindfulness. By means of this mindfulness and wisdom, they know what exists and what does not exist.'"
What is meant by "existence" and "non-existence"?
If one practices right conduct and attains right liberation, this is called existence;
if one practices wrong conduct and attains right liberation, this is called non-existence.
The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind exist according to worldly convention;
in ultimate reality, they do not exist.
That a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, through diligent and energetic cultivation, is able to attain bodhi—this is what is called "existence."
If a lazy bodhisattva were to attain *bodhi*, this is called "non-existence.
If one says that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) all arise from false delusions and inversions, this is called "existence.
If one claims that worldly phenomena arise spontaneously without depending on causes and conditions, this is called "non-existence."
That form is impermanent, suffering, and subject to decay is called "existence";
if one says it is permanent, blissful, and not subject to decay, this is called "non-existence."
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
When ignorance conditions volitional formations, this is called "existence";
if volitional formations were to arise apart from ignorance, this is called "non-existence."
The same applies to everything from consciousness conditioned by formations up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair being conditioned by birth.
To obtain great wealth through giving is called "existence";
to fall into poverty through giving is called "non-existence."
To be born in the good realms by maintaining pure precepts is called "existence";
to be born in the evil destinies is called "non-existence.
Even so, that the perfection of wisdom can bring about the attainment of sainthood is called "existence."
To practice the perfection of wisdom and yet remain an ordinary person is called "non-existence.
If one cultivates extensive learning and is able to attain great wisdom, this is called "existence";
to attain delusion is called "non-existence."
If the cultivation of right mindfulness can lead to liberation, this is called existence;
that it cannot is called non-existence.
If one practices wrong mindfulness and fails to attain liberation, this is called existence; [that one does not fail is called non-existence].
To have "attainment" is non-existence.
To attain liberation while there is no self or what belongs to a self is called existence;
to attain liberation while there is a self and what belongs to a self is called non-existence.
If one says that space pervades all places, this is called "existence";
that there is a self within the five aggregates is called "non-existence.
That one can attain liberation through practicing wisdom according to reality is called "existence."
If one attains liberation while clinging to false wisdom, this is called "non-existence.

If one can attain the wisdom of emptiness by being free from the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-span, and the view of a person, this is called "existence. If one clings to the views of a self, a sentient being, a life-span, and a person while claiming to attain the wisdom of emptiness, this is called "non-existence."
"Great King!

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, they thus know the existence and non-existence of the world and are able to cultivate equanimity. They clearly understand that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions; therefore, according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), they acknowledge their existence without giving rise to the view of eternalism. Knowing that the intrinsic nature of causal phenomena is itself empty, they do not give rise to the view of nihilism, and they penetrate the teachings of the Buddhas as they truly are."
“Great King, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, briefly teach these four dharmas for the sake of bodhisattvas:
the śramaṇas, brahmins, and devas of long life in the world all cling to permanence; to shatter this attachment, they teach the practice of impermanence.
There are devas and humans who are deeply attached to pleasure; to shatter this notion, I speak of universal suffering.
There are followers of external paths with false views who are attached to a self within the body; to break this clinging, I speak of non-self.
Furthermore, to refute those with overweening pride, I therefore speak of the tranquility of nirvana.
To speak of impermanence is to cause them to aspire toward the ultimate Dharma;
to speak of suffering is to cause them to abandon longing and seeking;
to speak of non-self is to manifest the gate of emptiness.
To speak of tranquility is to cause one to attain the signless.
Great King!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā and trains in this manner, they never fall back from any wholesome dharmas and will swiftly achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, King Śūra devaputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, what kind of conduct does he cultivate to protect and uphold the True Dharma?”
The Buddha addressed King Śūra-deva, saying: “Great King!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), he acts without contradicting his words; he respects and honors his elders and superiors, and accords with the true Dharma. His mental conduct is disciplined and upright, his faculties are tranquil, and he remains far removed from all evil and unwholesome dharmas while cultivating roots of goodness. This is called ‘protecting the true Dharma.’”
"Great King!

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, they cultivate compassion in their physical actions, compassion in their verbal actions, and compassion in their mental actions; they do not seek fame or profit, and by maintaining pure precepts and remaining far removed from all views, this is called 'protecting the True Dharma.'"
"Great King!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), not following the course of desire, not following the course of hatred, not following the course of delusion, and not following the course of fear, this is called 'protecting the true dharma'."
"Great King!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom and cultivates a sense of shame and remorse, this is called 'protecting the true Dharma.
Great King!"
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the Prajñāpāramitā, they preach the Dharma and cultivate its practice exactly as they have heard it; this is called "protecting the True Dharma.
Great King!

Because the Buddhas of the three periods of time protect the True Dharma, they therefore protect the Heavenly Kings and Human Kings, causing the Dharma to abide for a long time, and they speak this dhāraṇī:
Tadyathā | A-hu-lā hu-lā-paṭi ||
Hā siddhaṃ thoraṇu svāhūṭa ṭu ṭa ṭa ṭa ṭa ṭa ṇivaraṇa pūrṇa cūḍa.
...kṣata kṣayanta kṣaye svāhā (the same for all subsequent terms)...

śamane karau lou lou pade kili pade kiṃki āviṣade śade nīśare nīśe nīśe mate abhyate bhyate vada vada rūsati prauda rūsati-smiti-deve rūsati-smiti-deve. "All sentient beings—whether nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, or mahoragas—shall all attain peace and security."
"Great King!

This great divine mantra was taught by the Buddhas of the three periods of time to protect the True Dharma and to guard the celestial kings and human kings; you should recite and uphold it, for all enemies, bandits, evil calamities, and demonic obstacles to the True Dharma will be completely extinguished."
The Tathāgatas, in order to cause the True Dharma to abide long in the world, protect the kings of devas and humans, causing them to protect the Dharma.

When this Dharma-gate of the divine mantra of the Prajñāpāramitā was spoken, all the celestial palaces, the great earth, the various mountains, and the great oceans trembled; and among the assembly, eighty thousand sentient beings resolved their minds upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, King Śūra, having covered the Buddha with a net of the seven precious jewels, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, what dharmas should they cultivate so that their mind does not waver from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?”
The Buddha addressed King Śūraṅgama, saying: “Great King!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, they cultivate unimpeded great loving-kindness and insatiable great compassion, thereby accomplishing the Great Task.”

Exerting diligent effort, they study the samādhi of emptiness and cultivate equanimous wisdom; through the power of skillful means, they are able to penetrate the pure great wisdom, clearly understanding the equality of the three periods of time as they truly are without obstruction, and treading the path traversed by the Buddhas of the three periods.
"Great King!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā and cultivates such dharmas, his mind remains unshakable regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
The Victorious Heavenly King addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practice the prajñāpāramitā so that, upon hearing of the inconceivable matters of the Buddha, they do not feel fear or dread, nor are they startled or remorseful?”
The Buddha addressed King Śūraṅgama, saying: "Great King!

A bodhisattva should be fully endowed with *prajñā* and fully endowed with *jñāna*; they should draw near to spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), delight in hearing the profound Dharma, and understand that all phenomena are entirely like illusions. They should realize that the world is impermanent, their minds should not dwell in attachment—remaining like space—and they should know that all phenomena which arise must necessarily cease."
"O Great King!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā and cultivates such dharmas,
upon hearing of the inconceivable matters of the Buddha, they do not feel fear, dread, alarm, or regret."
The Victorious Heavenly King addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, attain mastery in all places?”
The Buddha addressed King Śūraṅgama, saying: "Great King!

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, cultivates the five supernormal powers, and is fully endowed with the unimpeded gates of liberation, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, and the skillful means of Prajñāpāramitā, they attain mastery in all places."
The Victorious Heavenly King addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, what gate does he attain?”
The Buddha addressed King Jayasena, saying: “Great King!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they attain the gateway of jñāna (gnosis) and are able to enter into the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of sentient beings.”
They attain the gate of prajñā, discerning the meanings of phrases;
they attain the gate of dhāraṇī, comprehending all languages and sounds in their entirety;
they attain the gate of non-obstruction, preaching the Dharma without end.
"Great King!
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practicing the Prajñāpāramitā and attaining these various gateways.
Thus did King Śūra speak to the Buddha.
“World-Honored One!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, what kind of power does he obtain?
The Buddha addressed King Śūraṅgama, saying:
"Great King!
You have attained the power of tranquility because you have accomplished great compassion;
you have attained the power of diligence because you have accomplished the state of non-retrogression (avaivartika)."
They attain the power of extensive learning, because they accomplish great wisdom;
they attain the power of faith and joy, because they accomplish liberation;
they attain the power of practice, because they accomplish renunciation.
They attain the power of patience for the sake of lovingly protecting sentient beings;
they attain the power of the bodhicitta for the sake of severing the view of self;
they attain the power of great compassion for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings.
Having attained the power of the endurance of non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti) and having accomplished the ten powers (daśabala),
O Great King,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) accomplishes such powers as these.

When this Dharma-gate was being taught, five hundred bodhisattvas among the assembly attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); eight thousand devaputras attained the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*); twelve thousand devaputras attained the pure Dharma-eye, free from dust and defilement; and forty thousand humans and devas resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Chapter Nine: Encouragement through Realization At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, King of Devas, saying:

“In a past age, incalculable and beyond measure—through *asaṃkhyeya* upon *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas—there was a Buddha named Guṇaratnarāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. His land was named Ratnavyūha, and his eon was named Sudarśana.”

At that time, the world was prosperous and joyful, free from all illness and affliction; humans and devas came and went without obstruction. The ground was as level as the palm of a hand, devoid of mountains, hills, mounds, or thorns.
Delicate grasses grew there, soft and deep blue like peacock feathers, four inches in length; when one set foot upon them, they would bend down, and as the step was lifted, they would rise again.
Various kinds of famous flowers—sumana flowers, campaka flowers, and other soft grasses—were spread everywhere.
It is neither cold nor hot; the four seasons are harmonious.
Its ground is composed entirely of pure blue lapis lazuli.
The sentient beings of this world have gentle and supple natures; they skillfully subdue the three poisons and do not follow their influence.

At that time, the Buddha Guṇaratnarāja had a community of twelve thousand nayutas of śrāvakas and a community of six billion bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. At that time, the human lifespan was thirty-six billion nayuta years, and there were no more premature deaths.

There is a land named Vimalavyūha; its city is one hundred and twenty-eight yojanas wide from south to north and eighty yojanas from east to west, adorned with ten thousand gardens and surrounded on all sides by ten thousand small kingdoms.

The name of the wheel-turning sage king was Jie-shi (Treatise on the World); he was fully endowed with the seven treasures and ruled over the four continents under heaven. Having already made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, he had deeply planted roots of goodness and never retreated from his resolve for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
There are four parks, adorned with exquisite flowers, delightful in their merit, where peacocks sport and all four seasons provide pleasure.
The city walls are sixteen yojanas thick; the gates, battlements, and watchtowers are all made of the seven precious gems.

There are four great ponds, each half a yojana in width, with banks made of the seven precious gems and stairways fashioned from Jāmbūnada gold; their bottoms are strewn with golden sand, and the water within them possesses the eight meritorious qualities. Precious lotuses grow therein, and ducks, geese, swans, cranes, mandarin ducks, and *śiṅxing* birds sport amidst them.
The banks were lined with various trees—such as white sandalwood, red sandalwood, and śīrṣa—and upon them, parrots, śāris, and kāra birds flew about and gathered to sport.
The king’s inner palace consisted of seventy thousand women of upright appearance who served the precious queen; they all resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

The king had a thousand sons, who were of great strength and valor, capable of crushing enemies; their bodies were adorned with the twenty-eight marks of a mahāpuruṣa, and they had all already resolved their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

At that time, the Tathāgata Guṇaratnarāja, surrounded before and behind by immeasurable devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, entered the great city of Vimalavyūha.

The holy king of that world, together with his seven treasures, a thousand sons, and palace attendants, went out to welcome the World-Honored One and prepared various kinds of subtle and exquisite offerings.
At that time, having accepted the offerings, the World-Honored One and the great assembly returned to their original place.
The King, accompanied by his seven treasures, a thousand sons, and his inner court ladies, went out of the city to see him off and then immediately returned to the palace.
At that time, King Śāsanādhipati suddenly sighed to himself:

"Human life is impermanent; wealth and honor are like a dream. To possess unimpaired faculties and firm right faith is exceedingly rare; to encounter a Buddha and hear the Dharma is as difficult as finding an udumbara flower."

At that time, the thousand sons, knowing that their father the king yearned for the World-Honored One and delighted in hearing the True Dharma, immediately constructed for him a wondrous pavilion made of ox-head sandalwood and adorned with the seven treasures—the fragrance of a single *liang* of which was worth the entire Jambudvīpa. This pavilion was ten *yojanas* wide from east to west and thirteen *yojanas* from south to north; its four corner pillars were magnificently adorned with various jewels.
A thousand precious wheels were brought by the sons as an offering to the Holy King.
Having accepted them, the King praised them, saying:
"Excellent, my sons!"
"I wish to go to the Buddha to listen to and receive the True Dharma.

At that time, the thousand sons constructed lion thrones within this pavilion for the noble king and his palace attendants. On all four sides of the pavilion, silk banners and canopies were suspended; it was covered with nets of the seven precious gems, with golden bells hanging from the corners. Various kinds of flowers—campaka flowers, sumana flowers, utpala flowers, kumuda flowers, puṇḍarīka flowers, and kāmala flowers—were scattered upon the pavilion.
They burned priceless incense, anointed it with fragrant clay, and scattered powdered incense upon it.

At that time, the thousand sons together supported this platform, each holding one wheel; they soared through the air like the king of swans, proceeding toward the Buddha’s dwelling with serene composure and without wavering. Upon reaching the ground, they descended slowly and arrived before the Buddha.
They prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, circumambulated the World-Honored One and the great assembly seven times to the right, and then withdrew to stand to one side.

At that time, the holy king and his court ladies descended from the jeweled terrace; the king removed his jeweled crown, and they each removed their leather sandals. Approaching the World-Honored One, they prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated the World-Honored One and the great assembly seven times to the right, and then withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the Buddha Ratnavyuha addressed him, saying:
"Noble King!
Have you come now to listen to the True Dharma?"
At that time, King Rājarṣi rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"What is this Right Dharma that you speak of?
At that time, the World-Honored One praised King Śaṃkara, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
Since you are able to ask such profound questions for the benefit of immeasurable devas and humans,
the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha shall explain them in detail for the sake of the Great King.
The Holy King who Governs the World then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Indeed, I wish to hear it.”
At that time, the Buddha addressed King Rājādhirāja, saying:
"Great King!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā and penetrates all dharmas, this is called the True Dharma."

What are called the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path—being empty, signless, and wishless, and penetrating equality—is termed the True Dharma.
The Holy King who Governs the World addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practice the prajñāpāramitā so that, within the Mahāyāna, they constantly attain superior progress and do not fall back?”
The Buddha said to King Śibi: "Great King!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they attain superior progress by virtue of right faith."
What is right faith?

It is knowing that all phenomena are neither arising nor ceasing, and that their intrinsic nature is quiescent. One should constantly draw near to those who practice correctly; regarding things that should not be done, one never performs them. With a mind free from distraction, one listens to and receives the True Dharma, seeing neither the speaker nor oneself as the listener. One diligently cultivates vigor to attain supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and with a body and mind that are light and buoyant, one teaches and transforms sentient beings, yet without perceiving that "I possess supernormal powers capable of transforming others" or that "sentient beings are being transformed by me."
Why is this? Great King!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, they perceive neither a self nor sentient beings; because these two positions are equal, they attain further progress and do not fall back.
"Great King!

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, he restrains and guards his sense faculties so as not to allow them to grasp at objects; he conceives the notion of impermanence regarding all means of livelihood, understands that all phenomena are quiescent, and recognizes that life is like a temporary loan."
Great King!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this way, they remain heedful regarding the Great Vehicle.
Great King!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom,
they do not forget the mind of awakening even within their dreams,
and they teach and transform sentient beings, causing them to cultivate the path to buddhahood!
Dedicate all roots of goodness toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*!
Seeing the Buddha’s supernormal power, one rejoices and offers praise.
Great King!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā in this way, they will swiftly accomplish anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Therefore, Great King!
"You should be diligent and energetic; do not give rise to negligence.
Great King! A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who seeks the Dharma must not be attached to the five desires."
All ordinary worldlings are insatiable regarding sensual desires, whereas those who have attained noble wisdom are able to renounce them.
Human existence is impermanent and life is brief.
Therefore, Great King!
One should renounce the mundane and seek the supramundane path.
