Great King, regarding the roots of goodness obtained from making offerings to the Tathāgata now, you should perform these four kinds of dedication:
the inexhaustible sovereignty, the inexhaustibility of the Dharma, the inexhaustibility of wisdom, and the inexhaustibility of eloquence.
These four dedications are identical to the Prajñāpāramitā; they are all entirely inexhaustible.
Great King!
A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the Prajñāpāramitā should purify the precepts of body, speech, and mind.

Why is this? It is for the sake of hearing, reflecting, and cultivating; by the power of skillful means, they teach and transform sentient beings; by the power of prajñā, they subdue all māras; and through the fulfillment of their vows, their practice does not contradict their word.
At that time, the Universal Monarch Rājācakravartin, having heard the profound Prajñāpāramitā spoken by the Buddha, felt great joy in his heart and attained what he had never experienced before.
He immediately took his jeweled crown and untied his own necklaces to offer to the Tathāgata; he relinquished the four continents to present them all to the Buddha and made this aspiration:
"May I constantly cultivate the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), study this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and with a resolute mind, advance toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."

When the women of the royal palace heard the Buddha preach the Dharma, they all gave rise to joy and resolved to attain bodhicitta; they removed their upper garments and jeweled necklaces to offer as an act of worship to the Tathāgata.
The Wheel-Turning Sage King of the World immediately relinquished the jeweled terrace to offer it to the Buddha and sought to leave the household life.
At that time, the Buddha Śrīguṇavyūharāja praised the Wheel-Turning Sage King Rājan said:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Great King!
What you have practiced today does not contradict your former vows.

Great King, you have skillfully cultivated generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom. The Buddhas of the past cultivated these dharmas and attained the Way of the Buddha; the Buddhas of the future shall likewise cultivate these dharmas and attain Buddhahood."
At that time, the Holy King who Governs the World addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving, is it different from the prajñāpāramitā?”
The Buddha said to King Śibi: "Great King!
As for the practice of giving, if it is devoid of the *prajñāpāramitā*, it is merely called *dāna* (charity), but not a *pāramitā*."
It is because of the *prajñāpāramitā* that it is named the *dānapāramitā*.
The same applies to ethical discipline (*śīla*), patience (*kṣānti*), diligence (*vīrya*), meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).
"Why is this? Because the nature of the *prajñāpāramitā* is equanimous, and because it is adorned with merit.
When the Buddha preached this Dharma, the Holy King Who Governs the World attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The Buddha told King Śūra:
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) should be like that king.
At that time, the world-ruling wheel-turning sage-king was none other than Dīpaṃkara Buddha.”
"The thousand sons of that king are the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa.
At that time, King Śuddhodana addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, train so as to swiftly accomplish the path to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
The Buddha said to King Śūra: “Great King!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they cultivate great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) and do not give rise to thoughts of affliction toward any sentient beings. They fully accomplish the diligent practice of the various perfections (*pāramitā*), as well as the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) and the four immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa*), which are dharmas that assist awakening. They train in the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) and master skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*). There is no wholesome dharma (*kuśaladharma*) that they do not cultivate to fulfillment. One who practices in this manner will swiftly attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
"Great King!

The path to enlightenment consists of what are called: a mind of faith, a pure mind, a mind free from guile and crookedness, a mind that practices equanimity, and a mind that bestows fearlessness, which causes all sentient beings to draw near with affection and to practice diligently."
The retribution of giving is inexhaustible; by firmly upholding the pure precepts, one remains free from obstacles;

by practicing patience, one is detached from all anger and affliction; through diligent application of vigor, practice becomes easy; because of meditative concentration, one does not give rise to distraction;
being endowed with wisdom, one can skillfully penetrate all things; and because of great compassion, one never regresses.
Because they possess great joy (*muditā*), they are able to gladden the minds of others; by practicing great equanimity (*upekṣā*), they do not give rise to discrimination.

Because they are free from the three poisons, they are detached from all thorns; because they do not cling to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, or tangibles, they extinguish all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Being without afflictions (*kleśa*), they remain far removed from enemies; thus they abandon the thoughts of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) and purify their minds.
Vast and expansive, it possesses all-encompassing wisdom and can produce all manner of jewels.
Great King!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā and trains in this way, they will swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, King Śūra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, what appearance and form does he manifest to transform and guide sentient beings?”
The Buddha addressed King Śūraṅgama, saying:
“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they manifest physical forms that possess no fixed characteristics.”
For what reason?

According to the inclinations of the hearts of sentient beings, they perceive the Bodhisattva’s appearance in such ways: sometimes manifesting a golden color, sometimes a silver color, sometimes the color of crystal, sometimes the color of lapis lazuli, sometimes the color of agate, sometimes the color of musaragalva, or the color of pearl; blue, yellow, red, or white; or the colors of the sun and moon, fire, or flames; the color of Śakra, the color of Brahmā, the color of frost, the color of topaz, vermilion, the color of campaka, sumana, vārṣika, padma, kuvalaya, puṇḍarīka, the color of a meritorious deity, the color of a goose, the color of a peacock, the color of coral, the color of a wish-fulfilling jewel, or the color of space.
The devas see them as devas; humans see them as humans.
"Great King!

Within the worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva manifests himself in all such ways as the physical forms, appearances, and characteristics of all sentient beings."
Why is this? Because when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not abandon a single sentient being, and are thus able to universally embrace them all. Why is this?
The minds of all sentient beings are each different; for this reason, the Bodhisattva manifests in various ways. Why is this?

Because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva possesses the power of great vows from past lives, he manifests whatever body is desired by those who would be transformed according to what their own minds delight in seeing.
"Great King!

It is like a pure, bright mirror which originally has no images; yet, according to various external forms—whether beautiful or ugly—all things appear therein. Furthermore, it does not discriminate, thinking, 'My substance is clear and pure, and I am able to manifest all these colors.'"

It is likewise for the bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom: with effortless mental application, they manifest in various ways according to the inclinations of sentient beings, causing them all to be delighted, yet without discriminating that "I am able to manifest these bodies."
"Great King! When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, within a single sitting, according to the various assemblies of listeners,
he may see a bodhisattva preaching the Dharma, or see a Buddha preaching the Dharma, or see a pratyekabuddha preaching [the Dharma]."
He may see the Dharma; or he may see a śrāvaka preaching the Dharma;
or he may see Śakra, or Brahmā, or Maheśvara, or Vaiśravaṇa, or the Four Heavenly Kings, or a universal monarch (cakravartin);
or he may see a śramaṇa, or a brāhmaṇa, or a kṣatriya.
Some see Vaiśyas or Śūdras; some see householders or elders;
some see them seated within jeweled towers, or seated upon lotus flowers; some see them walking upon the ground, or soaring through the void;
some see them preaching the Dharma, or entering into samādhi.
"Great King!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of delivering sentient beings, there is not a single form or a single deportment that he does not manifest."
"Great King!

The Prajñāpāramitā is formless and signless; it is like space, pervading all places. Just as space is free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), so too is the Prajñāpāramitā; it transcends all words and speech."
Furthermore, just as space is utilized by all beings in the world, so too is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) utilized by all ordinary beings and sages.
Moreover, just as space is devoid of discrimination, so too is the perfection of wisdom free from a discriminating mind.
Just as space accommodates all forms, so too can the perfection of wisdom accommodate all Buddha-dharmas.
Just as space can manifest all forms, so too can the perfection of wisdom manifest all Buddha-dharmas.
Just as all grasses, trees, medicinal herbs, flowers, and fruits grow in dependence upon space, so too it is with the perfection of wisdom: all roots of goodness grow in dependence upon it.

For example, just as space is neither permanent nor impermanent and is not a phenomenon that can be expressed in words, so too is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā); it is neither permanent nor impermanent and is entirely beyond verbal expression.
"Great King!
Among the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of the world, whether they be Śakras or Brahmās, none are able to fathom the Prajñāpāramitā.
Great King!"

In the Prajñāpāramitā, there is not a single dharma that can serve as a metaphor; if a son of good family or a daughter of good family has faith in and accepts the Prajñāpāramitā, the merit they obtain is inconceivable.
If these meritorious qualities possessed form and shape, the realm of space would not be able to contain them.

Why is this? Because the Prajñāpāramitā gives birth to all mundane and supramundane wholesome dharmas: whether it be humans or devas; whether it be kings of devas or kings of humans; whether it be those on the path to Srotāpanna or the fruit of Srotāpanna, up to those on the path to Arhatship or the fruit of Arhatship; the path of the Pratyekabuddha; the ten stages of the Bodhisattva, the ten pāramitās, the Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of all Buddhas, and the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā); as well as the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities—all are born from the Prajñāpāramitā.

When this Dharma-door was being expounded, fifty thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas among the assembly attained the stage of non-retrogression; fifteen thousand devaputras attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); twelve thousand gods and humans attained the pure Dharma-eye, free from dust and defilement; and beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges gave rise to the mind set on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

In the heavens, various celestial musicians performed music that resounded spontaneously without being struck; they scattered myriad heavenly flowers as an offering to the Tathāgata’s Prajñāpāramitā. Devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others scattered all kinds of flowers and precious objects as offerings to the World-Honored One’s Prajñāpāramitā, and with one voice and in unison, they praised it at once, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
“World-Honored One!
It is well that you have spoken this Prajñāpāramitā.
*Śrīdevī-bodhisattva-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, Scroll Five.
The Śrīmaladevī-siṃhanāda-prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll Six.
Translated by Prince Yueposhouna of the Kingdom of Ujjayinī during the Chen Dynasty.
Chapter Ten: On the Description of Virtues. Chapter Ten: On the Description of Virtues.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

For how many eons has the bodhisattva mahāsattva practiced the prajñāpāramitā, and how many buddhas has he made offerings to, that he is able to thus proclaim the Tathāgata and expound the profound prajñāpāramitā as the King of Victorious Devas does?
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī:
“Good son, such a matter is inconceivable.”
If one has not cultivated various practices and planted roots of goodness for countless hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas, then one will not even hear the name of this Prajñāpāramitā.
O son of good family!

While the number of Ganges-sands in the worlds of the ten directions, as many as there are Ganges-rivers, may still be known, the number of kalpas during which this bodhisattva-mahāsattva has practiced the prajñāpāramitā and the number of Buddhas he has made offerings to are unknowable.

Mañjuśrī! In the past, immeasurable, boundless, incalculable, and inconceivable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Bahudhara Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. His land was named Sūryaprabhā, and the kalpa was named Abhyudgata.
At that time, the Buddha Bahusruta expounded the Dharma-gate of Purity for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, saying:
"O sons of good family!
Diligently cultivate vigor; do not regard your own bodies or lives."

At that time, there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva in the assembly named Jinli (Vīryabala). He rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, as you have said:
‘Diligently cultivate vigor; do not regard body or life.’”
"As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should be indolent, and only then will they swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

Why is this? If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva were to apply himself with diligent vigor alone, he would be unable to remain long within birth and death (*saṃsāra*). However, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā and suppresses and eliminates the afflictions (*kleśa*), he remains long within birth and death; he never seeks his own deliverance by swiftly realizing nirvāṇa without transforming sentient beings.
World-Honored One!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas take delight in dwelling within birth and death, rather than taking delight in nirvāṇa. Why is this?
“World-Honored One!

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva takes delight in the work of benefiting sentient beings; according to what they find pleasing, he employs skillful means to preach various teachings so that they may attain peace and happiness.
If he were to realize the exhaustion of outflows, he would be unable to benefit all sentient beings.”
World-Honored One!
For this reason, a bodhisattva contemplates birth and death, gives rise to great compassion, does not abandon sentient beings, and fulfills their original vow.
World-Honored One!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, endowed with the power of skillful means, dwell for a long time within birth and death; they behold immeasurable and boundless Buddhas, hear immeasurable and boundless True Dharma, and transform immeasurable and boundless sentient beings. For this reason, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not weary of birth and death, nor do they delight in nirvāṇa.
World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates birth and death and gives rise to fear and terror, they fall into a non-path; they will be unable to benefit all sentient beings or penetrate the profound realm of the Tathāgata.
What is the non-path?
It is that which consists in delighting in the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and lacking great compassion for all sentient beings. Why is this?
The path of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha is not the path of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

Why is this? Because the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas fear birth and death and seek swift deliverance; thus, their merit and wisdom are not fully perfected. For these reasons, it is not the path of the bodhisattva.
At that time, the World-Honored One Bahusruta praised the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vīryabalasamudgata, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!
O son of good family!”
"It is as you have said.
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should cultivate their own practice and must not study non-paths.
The Bodhisattva Vīryabala addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is the path practiced by the bodhisattva-mahāsattva himself?
At that time, the World-Honored One, the One of Great Learning, addressed the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Vigour-Power, saying:

“Good son! The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva accomplishes all merits and wisdom; by the power of great compassion, he does not abandon sentient beings; he remains far removed from the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; having attained the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), he does not abandon the three realms of existence (*tri-bhava*); his mind is free from seeking or expectation as he increases his roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*); through skillful means (*upāya*) he practices the various *pāramitās*; and by the power of wisdom, he gives rise to all roots of goodness with a non-discriminating mind, thereby accomplishing the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and immeasurable merit.”

There is not a single dharma that arises through skillful means, yet there is the manifestation of arising; there is not a single sentient being who is taught and transformed through skillful means, yet one knows that all dharmas are devoid of intrinsic nature. One contemplates the Buddha-lands as being like empty space, yet through skillful means, one adorns and purifies those Buddha-fields.

Knowing that the Dharma-body of all Buddhas is formless, they manifest through skillful means the adornments of the primary and secondary marks, and are able to respond to and provide for whatever the minds of sentient beings require or desire.

The Bodhisattva’s body and mind are perpetually tranquil and detached, yet they preach the Dharma to sentient beings in various ways; through skillful means, they remain far removed from clamor and distraction, cultivating all meditative concentrations and realizing that self-nature is empty. They are fully able to penetrate profound wisdom, yet through skillful means, they preach the Dharma for others.
Without realizing the fruits of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, one seeks the liberation of a Buddha and does not abandon any of the bodhisattva’s practices.
Son of good family!
This is called the path of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

"Mañjuśrī! When the Bodhisattva Vīryabalavat heard from the World-Honored One of Many Hearings (Bahusruta) the exposition on the sphere of activity of a bodhisattva, he attained what he had never experienced before and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'How rare, World-Honored One!'"
"As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is fully endowed with skillful means; for all dharmas, there is none that is not his path.
World-Honored One!"
Just as space is able to contain all forms and colors,
so too does the bodhisattva, through the path practiced with perfected skillful means, encompass all phenomena.

Furthermore, just as trees, medicinal herbs, fruit-bearing trees, and fragrant trees grow because of space, yet these various things neither defile nor purify space, nor cause it to feel anger or joy;

so too, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva possesses skillful means and the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), taking all phenomena as the path—whether they be the phenomena of ordinary beings, the phenomena of those in training (śaikṣa), the phenomena of pratyekabuddhas, the phenomena of bodhisattvas, or the phenomena of Tathāgatas.
Why is this? Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have attained complete penetration.
Furthermore, it is like fire: if it encounters trees, bamboo, or grass, it never retreats; these very plants and trees all benefit the fire by causing its light to manifest.
All dharmas are likewise; they are all the path of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

For example, just as the nature of a diamond is firm and dense—such that a blade cannot cut it, fire cannot burn it, water cannot rot it, and poison cannot harm it—so too the skillful means and wisdom of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva cannot be destroyed by the afflictions of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or any of the various non-Buddhists.
“World-Honored One!
Just as a water-purifying jewel makes turbid water clear when placed within it,
so too does the *prajñāpāramitā* jewel of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva cause the afflictions of all sentient beings to become entirely pure.”
“World-Honored One!
It is like a wondrous medicinal jewel that does not coexist with poison, yet can eliminate all poisons;
so too, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the skillful means of the prajñāpāramitā, they do not coexist with any afflictions, but are able to completely sever and extinguish them.”
“World-Honored One!
By these causes and conditions, all dharmas are the path of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva. “Mañjuśrī!”

When the Bodhisattva Jinli (Power of Progress) preached this Dharma-gate, eight thousand bodhisattvas among the assembly resolved their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and two hundred bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
“Mañjuśrī! The Bodhisattva Jinli (Power of Advancement) under the Buddha Bahusruta of the past is none other than the present King Śūra.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*, attain the power of firmness to protect and uphold the true Dharma?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:

“Good son! A bodhisattva-mahāsattva would rather sacrifice his own body and life than abandon the True Dharma; he is humble and respectful toward others and does not give rise to arrogance; he is able to endure being insulted by those who have no power; he bestows the most excellent food and drink upon sentient beings who suffer from hunger and thirst; he grants fearlessness to those in distress; he provides medical treatment according to the Dharma for all who are ill; he causes impoverished sentient beings to abound in wealth and treasures; he whitewashes and coats the stūpas and temples of the Buddhas; he conceals evil deeds and glorifies virtuous ones; and he bestows peace and happiness upon sentient beings who are suffering.”
Mañjuśrī! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom and cultivates such conduct, they attain the power of firmness to protect and uphold the true Dharma.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, how is he able to subdue the mind?”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they do not interfere in the affairs of others, but act only after careful reflection; their mental nature is disciplined and upright, free from deceitful conduct; they do not boast of themselves, and their mind is always supple.”
“Mañjuśrī! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices in this manner is able to subdue the mind.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā and cultivates such practices as these, in which realm will they be reborn?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā* in this manner, they may be born among the gods or born among human beings.
If born among the gods, they become Śakra and encounter the appearance of a Buddha in the world;
or they become a Great Brahmā King or the Lord of the Sahā World and encounter the appearance of a Buddha in the world."
If born among humans, they become universal monarchs, elders, or householders, and encounter the appearance of a Buddha in the world.
Mañjuśrī! It is through the taming of mental conduct that Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain such births.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
from what dharma does right faith flow forth?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva:
“Right faith flows forth and one thereby obtains a spiritual friend.
“World-Honored One! [Mañjuśrī replied.]
"What dharma does giving flow forth?
The Buddha said,
"It flows forth great wealth."
“World-Honored One!
From what dharma does extensive learning flow forth?
The Buddha said:
“The Perfection of Wisdom flows forth.
“World-Honored One,
what dharma does the observance of ethical discipline flow forth?”
The Buddha said:
"It flows forth all wholesome paths.
[He asked: "World-Honored One!"
"What dharma flows forth from patience?
The Buddha said,
"It flows forth as the capacity to accept sentient beings."
“World-Honored One!
From what dharma does diligence flow forth?
The Buddha said:
“It can accomplish all Buddha-dharmas.
“World-Honored One!
What dharma flows forth from contemplation?”
The Buddha said:
“It flows forth as tranquility.
“World-Honored One!”
"What dharma does Prajñāpāramitā flow forth?
The Buddha said,
"Prajñāpāramitā flows forth the transcendence of all afflictions."
“World-Honored One!
What dharma flows forth from listening to the Dharma?
The Buddha said:
"It flows forth from being free of the net of doubt.
"World-Honored One,
what dharma does such a question flow forth from?"
The Buddha said:
“It produces definitive wisdom. [He asked:
“World-Honored One!”
"What dharmas flow forth from abiding in tranquility?
The Buddha said,
"Meditative concentration and the various supernormal powers flow forth."
“World-Honored One!
From the correct cultivation of what dharma do these flow forth?
The Buddha said:
"It flows forth as the path of disenchantment.
"World-Honored One,
what dharma does the sound of impermanence flow forth?"
The Buddha said:
"It flows out without being grasped or protected. [He asked:
"World-Honored One!"
"What dharma does the sound of suffering flow forth?
The Buddha said,
"It flows forth as non-arising."
“World-Honored One!
What dharma does the sound of ‘non-self’ issue forth?
The Buddha said:
"It issues forth the cessation of 'I' and 'mine.
World-Honored One,
what dharma does the sound of emptiness issue forth?"
The Buddha said, "It flows forth from tranquility.
"World-Honored One! [he asked.]
"What dharma flows forth from right mindfulness?
The Buddha said,
"Noble right view flows forth."
“World-Honored One,
from what dharma does the noble mind emerge, being free from outflows?
The Buddha said:
“The flow-out of samādhi and supernormal powers.
“World-Honored One,
what dharma does the noble path flow out?”
The Buddha said, “It flows forth as the fruits of sanctity.
“World-Honored One! [he asked.]
"What dharma does faith and joy flow forth?
The Buddha said:
"It flows forth as the accomplishment of all liberations."
“World-Honored One!
From what dharma does the Buddha’s birth and manifestation flow?
The Buddha said:
"It flows forth all factors that assist enlightenment.
At that time, King Śūra devaputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What is the birth of a Buddha?
The Buddha told Śūraṅgama Deva:
"It is like the arousal of the bodhicitta."
“World-Honored One!
How does one generate the bodhicitta?
The Buddha said:
“Great King! It is like the arising of great compassion.
“World-Honored One!”
"How does one give rise to great compassion?
The Buddha said:
"By not abandoning any sentient being."
“World-Honored One!
How does one not abandon all sentient beings?
The Buddha said:
“As with not abandoning the Three Jewels.
“World-Honored One!
Who does not abandon the Three Jewels?”
The Buddha said:
“They are those who have no afflictions.
At that time, King Śūra deva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Rare, World-Honored One! Rare, Sugata! The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess such secrets that are profound and subtle;

they constantly teach that all phenomena are empty, unarisen, unceasing, and quiescent, yet they do not destroy the retribution of the good and evil deeds one cultivates, remaining far removed from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism.”
"Bhagavān!
Within this world, are there any sentient beings who, upon hearing such a Dharma as this, would fail to give rise to right faith and a heart of reverent respect, but instead produce slander?"
World-Honored One!

These sentient beings, in past lives, obtained human bodies due to their wholesome karma; yet, because they associated with evil friends, they did not believe in such profound Dharma and thus betrayed their past wholesome karma.

The grace and virtue of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are so deep and heavy that even if one were to cut one's own flesh and shed one's own blood to make offerings to the Tathāgata, one could never repay it.
"By the grace of the Buddha, today our roots of goodness have increased; we have attained the great joy of the Dharma and abide in great sovereignty.
World-Honored One!
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom!"
You should recognize the Buddha's kindness!
Draw near to virtuous friends!
You should study the Buddha's conduct so as to attain the fruit of Buddhahood.

When this Dharma was being taught, twenty-five thousand bodhisattvas among the assembly attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); forty-five thousand persons and devas resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; and twelve thousand sons of gods attained the pure Dharma-eye, free from dust and defilement.

Chapter Eleven: Manifestation by Transformation The Sutra of the Perfection of Wisdom Spoken by the Victorious Heavenly King, Chapter Eleven: Manifestation by Transformation At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sucintita addressed the Victorious Heavenly King, saying:
"Can the Buddha manifested through the Tathāgata’s transformative power further manifest others?"
At that time, King Śūra answered the Bodhisattva Sucintita, saying:

"Now, with the World-Honored One as my witness, I declare that the emanated Buddha created by the Buddha can further manifest as countless emanated Buddhas, equal in number to the sands of the Ganges, possessing various physical forms and preaching the Dharma through supernormal powers to benefit sentient beings."
“Good son! Because the power of the original vows of all Buddhas was pure in past lives, they are able to act in this way.
Bodhisattva Sucintita addressed King Vijayottama, saying:
“Great King!
You have well expounded the profound Dharma; the vow-power of all Buddhas throughout past lives is pure.
We only pray, Great King!”
“I request the Buddha’s spiritual power to cause this Prajñāpāramitā to abide long in the world without ever disappearing.
King Śūra replied to the Bodhisattva Sucintita, saying: “Good son!
The Prajñāpāramitā is protected and sustained by all Buddhas. Why is this?

Because the Prajñāpāramitā as expressed through words—these very words are neither born nor extinguished, and they never disappear; likewise, the meaning revealed by these words is also neither born nor exhausted, and it never disappears.
Good son! The profound prajñāpāramitā of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, likewise does not disappear. Why is this?
Because phenomena are unarisen.
If a phenomenon is without arising, it is likewise without cessation; this is the secret teaching of the Tathāgata.

Whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, its intrinsic nature and characteristics abide eternally. This is called the Dharma-realm, also termed Suchness (tathatā), and named the Limit of Non-differentiation.
"To accord with causes and conditions without opposition is the True Dharma; its nature is eternally abiding and never disappears.
The Bodhisattva Subhāvitacitta addressed King Jayasena, saying: "Great King!"
"What kind of person is capable of protecting the true Dharma?
The Victorious Heavenly King replied to the Bodhisattva Good Contemplation:
"Good son!..."
If one does not oppose or contradict any phenomena, this is called protecting the true Dharma.
Why is this? Because being free from contentious debate and not contravening the principles of reality is what is meant by protecting the true Dharma.
He asked again:
"In what way does it not contradict reason?
He replied:
"If one follows the literal words without contradicting the underlying principle and remains free from dispute, this is called 'protecting the True Dharma. Why is this?
Ordinary people in the world are all attached to various views; those who follow the principle always speak of emptiness, and for this reason, disputes arise in the world."
Thus, while ordinary people cherish and value the phenomena of existence (*bhava*), those who follow the correct principle regard them as light;

the world speaks of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, whereas those who follow the correct principle speak of impermanence, suffering, impurity, and non-self. For this reason, worldly disputes arise.
"Good son!
All ordinary worldlings follow the worldly stream; those who accord with the principle of reality go against the worldly stream. For this reason, disputes arise in the world."

All ordinary beings are attached to the aggregates, elements, and sense bases; those who follow the correct principle explain that all dharmas are entirely without attachment, and for this reason, disputes arise in the world.
“Good son!
Those who conform to the world do not act according to principle; those who follow principle are at variance with the world.
The Bodhisattva Sucintita addressed King Jayottama, saying:
“Great King!
What dharma do you now apprehend?
King Śūraṃgama replied to the Bodhisattva Sucintita:
"I do not grasp at persons, nor do I grasp at dharmas.
He asked again:
"In what way do you not grasp?"
He replied:
"I am detached, sentient beings are detached, and phenomena are detached; this detachment is entirely unapprehendable.
Detachment in the past, future, and present is likewise unapprehendable."
The Buddhas are detached, yet the Buddhas are not detached; the Buddha-lands are detached, yet the lands are not detached; phenomena are detached, yet phenomena are not detached. Good son!
"Such practice as this is called 'conforming to principle,' characterized by neither grasping nor non-grasping.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Good Contemplation praised the Deva King Vijaya, saying:
"Excellent, Great Being!"
Excellent, O noble being!

You are able to expound such profound *prajñāpāramitā*, which is without grasping and without attachment, without name and without letter, extinguishing all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), and free from both the subject that discriminates and the object that is contemplated.

At that time, there was a son of heaven in the assembly named Bhadraśrī. He rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"As for that which is called 'non-conceptualization' by King Śūra, what dharma is this?
The Buddha addressed the Devaputra Bhadraguṇa, saying:
"The dharma of non-conceptualization is itself tranquility."
Why is this? Because grasping and the object of grasping do not exist; being free from "I" and "mine," there is neither arising nor ceasing. This is called the non-conceptual dharma. Good son!
"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates in this way, they are able to protect the true Dharma, yet they do not perceive one who protects nor that which is protected.
When this teaching was spoken, the minds of ten thousand bhikṣus within the assembly were liberated, and one thousand devaputras attained the pure Dharma-eye, free from dust and defilement.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sucintita addressed King Śubhavimokṣa, saying:
"What kind of eloquence is it that can thus expound such profound Dharma?
King Śubhavimokṣa replied to the Bodhisattva Sucintita:

"Good son! One who is free from all habitual tendencies of affliction can speak with such eloquence; this eloquence is able to express the ultimate wisdom that transcends the path of language and cannot be proclaimed by names."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sucintita asked the Devaputra Bhadraguṇa: "Noble son,
how does one speak with eloquence within the dharma of non-arising?"
At that time, the Devaputra Bhadra replied to the Bodhisattva Sucintita:
"If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not abide within the dharmas of non-arising and non-ceasing, then there is no eloquence to expound the profound Dharma."

Why is this? Because, being far removed from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), they perceive neither the object of cognition nor the subject of cognition; since the mind abides nowhere, they are thus able to teach.
Not abiding in persons or phenomena, not abiding in "this" or "that," but abiding only in the pure ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), they are thus able to teach.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sucintita addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Devaputra Bhadraśrī is truly rare, for he is able to penetrate the most profound Dharma with inexhaustible eloquence.”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Sucintita, saying: "Good son,
this Devaputra Bhadrapāla has come from the presence of the Buddha Akṣobhya in the world-system Abhirati to this Sahā world in order to hear and receive the profound Prajñāpāramitā."
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Sucintita, saying:

"The noble and virtuous Devaputra has already cultivated the gateways of dhāraṇī for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas in the past; even if he were to preach the Dharma for the duration of an entire kalpa, it would never come to an end."
The Bodhisattva Sucintita addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is this dhāraṇī?”
The Buddha said,
“Good son! It is called the dhāraṇī of the non-entry of the multitude of dharmas.”
"Good son!
This dhāraṇī transcends all written characters; words cannot enter it, and the mind cannot measure it. All internal and external phenomena are therein unattainable."
"Good son!
There is not even the slightest dharma that can enter this; therefore, it is called the 'Dhāraṇī of the Non-Entry of All Dharmas. Why is this?"

This Dharma is equal, without high or low, and without coming or going; not a single syllable enters from without, nor does a single syllable go forth from this Dharma, nor does a single syllable abide within it. Furthermore, there are no words that perceive one another, nor is there any discrimination between what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma.
These syllables do not decrease when spoken, nor do they increase when not spoken; from the very beginning, they have neither been produced by anyone nor have they been destroyed by anyone.
Good son! As it is with letters, so it is with the mind;
as it is with the mind, so it is with all phenomena.

Why is this? Because all phenomena transcend language and transcend conceptualization; since they are fundamentally without arising or ceasing, there is neither entering nor exiting. This is called the *dhāraṇī* of the non-entry into all phenomena.
If one can thoroughly penetrate this dharma-gate, one’s eloquence will be inexhaustible.
Why is this? Because one has penetrated the uninterrupted and inexhaustible Dharma.
"Good son!
One who is able to enter empty space is able to enter this dharani-gate.
Good son!"
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are able to penetrate this gateway of dhāraṇī, their minds attain purity, as do their bodies and speech;

their conduct accords with principle, their prajñā is firm and solid, and no māras whatsoever can disturb them. No heterodox practitioners dare even to look upon them, and no afflictions can destroy them. They achieve physical strength, their minds are free from cowardice, and their speech is inexhaustible;

they are able to proclaim all the profound Noble Truths. Their wisdom and learning are like the great ocean; they dwell securely in samādhi like Mount Sumeru; they remain fearless among the masses like a lion king; they are unstained by worldly dharmas like a lotus flower; they benefit sentient beings like the great earth; they wash away all defilements like the great waters; and they bring maturity to the world like the great fire.

Pure and cool in their equanimity, they gladden the minds of all sentient beings like the moon; they shatter all darkness as if by the sun. They are called "valiant" for crushing the enemies of affliction; their minds are tamed like great dragons. They can shake the thunder of the Dharma, for which the great cloud serves as a metaphor; they rain down all teachings universally, for which the great rain serves as a metaphor. They remove the disease of affliction for all sentient beings like a skilled physician; they govern the world through the Dharma like a king. They protect sentient beings and protect the True Dharma like the Four Heavenly Kings;

among humans and devas, their wealth and excellence are supreme like Śakra. Their minds have attained mastery like the Great Brahmā King who rules over the Sahā world; their bodies have attained non-obstruction like the Garuḍa bird; they instruct and guide sentient beings like a father of the world.

It is able to produce the treasure of the Dharma, similar to how King Vaiśravaṇa is able to produce all manner of jewels; it is adorned with merit and wisdom, benefiting all sentient beings who behold it, praised by all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and protected by the entire host of devas.

"Noble son! When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva attains this *dhāraṇī* gateway of the non-entry into all phenomena, they exercise various forms of mastery to benefit sentient beings. They preach the Dharma through skillful means without exhaustion, their minds free from weariness and seeking neither fame nor profit. Their giving of the Dharma is impartial and devoid of envy; their observance of the precepts is pure, such that body, speech, and mind are forever free from transgression. Their patience is pure, being free from all anger and affliction; their diligence is pure, accomplishing and establishing all that is to be done; their meditative concentration is pure, skillfully taming the mind; and their wisdom is pure, entirely free from doubt or obstruction. Possessing the four immeasurables like a Brahmā king, they practice various *samādhis* and *samāpattis*, cultivating the unsurpassed path as the most supreme in the world. Endowed with all merits and all-encompassing wisdom, they receive the position of consecration."

When this dharma-gate of dhāraṇī was being preached, sixty-four thousand bodhisattvas within the assembly attained non-retrogression; thirty thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti); twenty thousand humans and devas attained the pure Dharma-eye, free from dust and defilement; and immeasurable, boundless humans and devas resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Chapter Twelve: The Chapter on Dhāraṇīs In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Chapter Twelve: The Chapter on Dhāraṇīs. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee upon the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, addressing him thus:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!”
“The merit accomplished by a bodhisattva mahāsattva who attains this ‘Dhāraṇī of Non-Entry into All Dharmas’ as taught by the Tathāgata is immeasurable and boundless.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying: “Good son!
“Such merits as these, even if the Tathāgata were to speak of them for a hundred or a thousand years, would never be exhausted.
At that time, there was among the assembly a bodhisattva-mahāsattva named Śāntamati, who addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:

“When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains this dhāraṇī and is praised by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, such a person has truly attained great benefit; their own practice and their transformation of others are both entirely not in vain.”
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī replied to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Śāntamati:
"Good son, within the ultimate truth (paramārtha), there is no dharma to be praised; it is without form and without marks. Since it is without form and marks, what is there to be praised?"
“Since there is nothing to be praised, in what could one take delight?
The Bodhisattva Śāntamati addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
“As I have heard it stated in the Buddha’s sūtras:”
"All phenomena are without self or what belongs to a self; they can neither cause delight nor cause anger. This is the equality of phenomena, which a bodhisattva should study."

“It is, for example, like the great earth resting upon the waters: if one digs a well or a pond, one obtains water for use, whereas for those who do not dig, there is no means by which it can be brought forth.

In this same way, the realm of noble wisdom pervades all phenomena; if one diligently cultivates the skillful means of prajñā, one will immediately attain it, but how could those who do not cultivate it ever obtain it?”
Therefore, a bodhisattva who seeks awakening must not be indolent, but must diligently cultivate vigor; in this way, such dharmas will appear before them. Good son!
Just as one born blind cannot see forms, so too sentient beings blinded by afflictions cannot see the Dharma.
Just as a person with eyes cannot see forms without external light,
so it is with a practitioner who, though possessing wisdom, cannot see the Dharma without a virtuous friend.
Just as one with the divine eye can see forms by themselves without depending on external light,
so too do Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have entered the stream of the Dharma naturally advance.
It is like a being in the womb, who grows day by day yet does not perceive it for themselves.
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice with diligent vigor, they do not perceive their own various practices increasing, yet they are able to accomplish all Buddha-dharmas.
It is like the Snowy Mountains, where there is a king of medicinal trees that neither withers nor decays;
likewise, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas diligently cultivate vigor, all their various practices neither regress nor are lost.
For example, when a Wheel-Turning Sage King appears in the world, he possesses the seven treasures;

likewise, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva resolves upon the bodhicitta, they possess the seven jewels of the Dharma, namely: generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, and the power of skillful means.
Furthermore, just as a Wheel-Turning Sage King travels through the four continents with a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings,
so too is it with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who benefits sentient beings by means of the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
Furthermore, wherever a Wheel-Turning Sage King resides, there is no dispute or litigation;
likewise, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva teaches the Dharma according to reality, there is no contentious debate.
It is like when the trichiliocosm is first formed, there immediately arise Sumeru, the king of mountains, and the great ocean.
The Bodhisattva is likewise: if he gives rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, he immediately possesses both *prajñā* and great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Just as when the sun rises, its light first shines upon the high mountains;
so too, when the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva obtains the torch of *prajñā*, its light first shines upon those Bodhisattvas of lofty conduct whose roots of goodness are matured.
Just as the great earth bears all things—flowers, fruits, trees, shrubs, and medicinal herbs—with complete impartiality;
so too the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, having attained this dharani-gate, maintains a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Śāntamati,
saying: "Good son,
it is as you have said."
"Good son!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains this dharanī gateway, whatever they speak—not even a single phrase or a single word—is anything other than the Buddha’s word."
Good son! This Dharma that is being taught is free from form, sound, odor, taste, and touch. Why is this?

Because it is not a worldly dharma, it is inexhaustible and boundless, capable of entering all things; body and mind are light and agile, such that even if one were to preach before hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, one would feel no timidity.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have attained the power of the Buddha’s sustaining grace (*adhiṣṭhāna*), their minds are free from attachment—they do not attach to a self, they do not attach to sentient beings, and they do not attach to phenomena. They thereby attain the pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the pure Tathāgata, and the pure reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*);
they attain the inexhaustibility of dharmas, the inexhaustibility of syllables, and the inexhaustibility of exposition.
They immediately gave rise to joy because they had attained *prajñā*, attained *jñāna*, and were free from the net of doubt.

While this *dhāraṇī* dharma-gate was being expounded, eight thousand bodhisattvas among the assembly attained this *sarvadharmaniravaśeṣapraveśa-dhāraṇī*; twelve thousand bodhisattvas attained the stage of non-retrogression; five thousand bodhisattvas attained the realization of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); sixteen thousand devaputras attained the pure Dharma-eye, free from dust and defilement; and immeasurable, boundless sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Śāntamati, saying:

"This dhāraṇī can subdue all Māras, destroy all heterodox teachers and those who harbor malice toward the Dharma, extinguish the fire of afflictions, and kindle the lamp of Prajñā. It protects Dharma-preachers so that they reach Nirvāṇa, tames one's own mind, and skillfully transforms external assemblies. It beautifies physical deportment so that all who see it rejoice; for those who practice correctly, it expounds the Dharma with impartiality, observing the faculties and natures of sentient beings as they truly are, neither too early nor too late."

When this Dharma was being taught, all the Mount Sumerus and the great oceans of the trichiliocosm quaked violently; the devas rained down flowers—Māndārava, Mahāmāndārava, Mañjūṣaka, Mahāmañjūṣaka, utpala, kumuda, puṇḍarīka, and kāmalā flowers—and in the sky, the devas produced various kinds of music that resounded spontaneously without being struck.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Śāntamati, saying: "Good son!

In the past, immeasurable, boundless, incalculable, and beyond counting eons ago, a Buddha appeared in the world named Ratnacandra Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. His land was named Adūṣya, and the eon was named Nandana."
He had thirty-two billion śrāvaka disciples and an incalculable number of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
When this Buddha attained the Way, there were no ascetic practices nor any subduing of celestial Māras.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva among the assembly named Ratnaguṇa, who possessed skillful eloquence and expounded the Dharma in various ways.
Then, the great multitude entreated the Buddha to remain in the world and not enter parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Ratnaguṇa addressed the great assembly, saying:
"The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is neither born nor extinguished; why then is there a need to exhort him not to enter nirvana?"
If space were to enter nirvāṇa, then the Tathāgata would enter nirvāṇa;
if the limit of reality, suchness, the dharma-realm, and the inconceivable realm were to enter nirvāṇa, then the Tathāgata would enter nirvāṇa.

Why is this? Because the Dharma of the Tathāgata is without formation and without destruction, without defilement and without purity; it is neither mundane nor supramundane, neither conditioned nor unconditioned, and neither annihilated nor eternal.

Even if one possessed ten tongues in a single mouth, and each of those tongues were to produce a hundred more tongues, and each of those tongues were to produce a thousand more tongues, one still could not describe the formation and dissolution of the Tathāgata.

When the Bodhisattva Ratnaguṇa preached this Dharma, eighty-six thousand bodhisattvas attained the stage of non-retrogression; seven thousand bodhisattvas attained the dhāraṇīs of Boundless Merit, Pleasing, Unimpeded, Joyful, Great Compassion, Moon-Love, Moonlight, Sun-Love, Sunlight, Sumeru Mountain, Great Ocean, and Virtuous King; and thirty-six thousand humans and devas attained the pure Dharma-eye, free from dust and defilement.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Śāntamati, saying:
"At that time, was the Bodhisattva Ratnaguṇa anyone else?
He was none other than you yourself."
"For this reason, you are able to speak of this dharani-gate.
At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva spoke in verse:
"The dhāraṇī is like a wondrous medicine, Able to cure the diseases of manifold delusions."
"Just like the nectar of the gods, those who obtain it shall never die.
At that time, the Bodhisattva King of Merit-Flowers spoke in verse:
"Dhāraṇī is without letters; letters manifest dhāraṇī."
"By the power of Prajñā and great compassion, it is explained beyond words and letters.

At that time, the Deva-king Śakra, Lord of the Tuṣita Heaven, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, are inconceivable; the Dharma taught by the Buddhas is also inconceivable; and the conduct and teachings of the great Bodhisattvas are likewise inconceivable.
"We gods have, through the profound roots of goodness planted in our past lives, encountered the Tathāgata and heard him preach this Dharma.
Thereupon, they scattered various celestial jewel-flowers, heavenly flowers, and heavenly incense over the Buddha, the Tathāgata, as an offering.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Heavenly King Śāṇakavatsa, saying:
"Great King!
Those who wish to make offerings to the Buddha, the Tathāgata, should cultivate three dharmas."
That is to say: generating the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, upholding the true Dharma, and practicing according to what has been heard.
Great King!
If there is one who practices these three dharmas, such a person is said to be making offerings to the Tathāgata.
"Great King!
Even if the Tathāgata were to live for an eon and remain in the world to speak of the meritorious rewards of this offering, he could not exhaustively describe them.
Therefore, Great King!"
If one wishes to make offerings to the Buddha, the Tathāgata, it is only when these three dharmas are complete that it is called an offering.
Great King!

If there is anyone who protects and upholds even a single four-line verse of the Tathāgata, that person thereby protects and upholds the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas of the past, present, and future.
Why is this? All Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are born from the Dharma; thus, the offering of the Dharma is called the true offering, which no material wealth can equal.
Among all offerings, the offering of the Dharma is the foremost.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Deva King Śāntuṣita, saying:
"I recall that in the past, during immeasurable, boundless, asaṃkhyeya-asaṃkhyeya kalpas while practicing the bodhisattva path, I heard various devas in the air reciting this verse:
'The gods and humans have lost their great treasure store; It has been taken away by kings, thieves, water, and fire. "
The Dharma is difficult to hear in hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas; though one may hear it, one does not uphold or practice it.

Taking the bodhicitta as the foundation for transforming sentient beings, practicing according to reality with a tranquil mind, and possessing an impartial mind that benefits both self and others—one who practices in this way makes offerings to the Buddha.
"Great King!
In the past, when I first heard this verse, I immediately recited it for others, and eight thousand people resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Therefore, Great King,
making offerings with the Dharma is the most supreme. Why is this?
"Because all Buddhas are born from the Dharma.
*The Sūtra of the Prajñāpāramitā of the Victorious Heavenly King*, Fascicle Six;
*The Sūtra of the Prajñāpāramitā of the Victorious Heavenly King*, Fascicle Seven.
Translated by Prince Śaśivigraha of the Kingdom of Oḍḍiyāna.
Chapter Thirteen: Exhortation.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding this profound *prajñāpāramitā* spoken by the Tathāgata, will there be any sentient beings in the final age of future generations who are able to believe and accept it?”
“If good sons or good daughters, upon hearing this sūtra, give rise to faith and do not slander it, what kind of merit will such persons achieve?
The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, saying:

“In the future, at the end of the age, there will be good sons and good daughters who have cultivated pure morality, meditative concentration, and wisdom under immeasurable Buddhas. These true children of the Buddhas are able to believe in this sūtra; the merit they thereby attain is beyond calculation. This most excellent and supreme Dharma is born from wisdom.”
With a pure mind, receive this with faith; I shall now briefly explain it to you through a parable. Mañjuśrī!

The continent of Jambudvīpa is seven thousand yojanas in length and breadth, broad in the north and narrow in the south; the faces of the people therein are likewise shaped according to the topography of the land.

The entire continent was filled with stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and others, as dense as a grove of bamboo, hemp, sugarcane, or reeds, such that there was not even the slightest space or gap between them.
If there were good sons or good daughters who provided the four types of offerings to the noble ones for the duration of their lives;

or again, if they filled this continent with the seven treasures, piling them up as high as the Brahma-heaven, and gave such quantities to each noble one individually for the duration of these good sons' and good daughters' lives, continuing day and night without interruption for thirty *muhūrtas*.
Mañjuśrī, what do you think? By reason of this,
would the merit of such a person be great?
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is very much so, Bhagavān!
It is very much so, Sugata!"
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva:

"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family does not slander this sūtra, their merit will surpass that of the former; the latter does not equal even one hundredth part of it, nor one thousandth, nor one hundred-thousand-millionth part, nor can it be reached by any calculation or analogy."
Mañjuśrī! The continent of Aparagoyānī is eight thousand yojanas in length and breadth, and its shape is like a half-moon; the faces of its inhabitants are likewise.

The entire continent is filled with srotāpannas, sakṛdāgāmins, anāgāmins, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas, as dense as a forest of bamboo, hemp, sugarcane, or reeds, such that there is not even the slightest empty space or gap between them.

If there are sons or daughters of good family who provide the four types of offerings to the noble ones for the duration of their lifetimes, and after they have entered parinirvāṇa, erect stūpas for their relics;

or alternatively, if they fill this continent with the seven precious jewels, piling them up as high as the Brahma-heaven, and bestow such quantities upon each and every noble one, continuing this unceasingly day and night for thirty *muhūrta* throughout the entire lifespan of these sons or daughters of good family.
Mañjuśrī! What do you think?
By reason of this, would that person acquire much merit?
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is very much so, Bhagavān!
It is very much so, Sugata!”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī:

"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family has faith in this sūtra, their merit shall surpass that [of the former], such that the latter does not equal even one hundredth part of it; it does not equal one thousandth, nor one ten-thousandth, nor one hundred-thousand-millionth part; indeed, it is beyond the reach of calculation or analogy."
Mañjuśrī! The continent of Pūrvavideha is nine thousand yojanas in length and breadth; its shape is like the full moon, and the faces of its inhabitants are likewise.

The entire continent is filled with srotāpannas, sakṛdāgāmins, anāgāmins, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas, as dense as a grove of bamboo, hemp, sugarcane, or reeds, such that there is not even the slightest space or gap between them.
If there are good sons or good daughters who provide the four types of offerings to the noble ones for the duration of their lives;

or again, if they fill this continent with the seven treasures, piling them up as high as the Brahma Heaven, and bestow such an amount upon each noble one individually for the entire lifespan of these good sons or good daughters, continuing day and night without interruption for thirty *muhūrta* periods.
Mañjuśrī, what do you think?
By reason of this, would that person acquire much merit?
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Very many, Bhagavān! Very many, Sugata!"
“Mañjuśrī! The continent of Uttarakuru is ten thousand yojanas square, and the faces of its inhabitants are likewise square.

Within that continent, śrotāpannas, sakṛdāgāmins, anāgāmins, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas fill it completely, as densely as a grove of bamboo, hemp, sugarcane, or reeds, such that there is not even the slightest space or gap between them.”
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to provide the four types of offerings to the noble ones for the duration of their lifespans;

or again, were to fill this continent with the seven treasures piled up as high as the Brahma-heaven, and bestow such quantities upon each and every noble one for the entire lifespan of that son or daughter of good family, continuing day and night without interruption for thirty *muhūrta* periods.
Mañjuśrī! What do you think?
By reason of this, would that person obtain much merit?
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Very many, Bhagavān! Very many, Sugata!”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva:

"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, maintains, reads, and recites this sūtra, their merit shall surpass that [of the former], such that the former does not equal even one hundredth part of it; it does not equal one thousandth, nor one hundred-thousand-millionth part, nor can it even be reached by calculation or analogy."
Mañjuśrī! Suppose the Sahā world were entirely reduced to atoms, and there were as many holy ones as there are such atoms.
If a son or daughter of good family were to provide them with the four types of offerings for the duration of their lives;

If one were to fill as many trichiliocosm worlds as there are atoms in that number with the seven treasures, piling them up as high as the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, and each noble person were to bestow such an amount upon them for the entire lifespan of these good sons and good daughters; [the merit of the latter would still be greater].
Mañjuśrī! What do you think?
Is the merit great or not?
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The previous merit was already inconceivable; how much more so this merit!”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva:

“If a son of good family or a daughter of good family circulates this sūtra and expounds it for others, their merit shall surpass that [of the former], such that the latter does not equal even a hundredth part of it; it does not equal a thousandth, a hundred-thousandth, or even a ten-millionth part; indeed, it cannot be reached by any calculation or analogy.”

Mañjuśrī! If such merit as this were not dedicated toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, one would become the king of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven for as many kalpas as there are atoms [in that merit], the king of the Nirmāṇarati heaven for that same number of kalpas, the king of the Tuṣita heaven for that same number of kalpas, the king of the Yāma heaven for that same number of kalpas, and Śakra, the lord of the devas, for that same number of kalpas;
how much more so would one become a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin)?

Because they dedicate [their merit] toward *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), they are able to achieve the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). Mañjuśrī!
Throughout Jambudvīpa, srotāpannas, sakṛdāgāmins, anāgāmins, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas are as densely packed as a forest of bamboo, hemp, sugarcane, or reeds.
"If there were an evil person who killed all these worthy sages and saints— Mañjuśrī,
what do you think?"
"By reason of this, would that person incur much demerit?
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
If one kills a single sage, one will fall into the Avīci Hell for an entire kalpa;
how much more so for such a great number! Their transgressions are exceedingly many, beyond all calculation.
The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, saying:

"If there are those who slander this sūtra, their sin is heavier than that [previous one]; even a hundredth part does not equal it, nor do a thousandth, a hundred-thousandth, or ten-millionth part. Indeed, it cannot be reached even by calculation or analogy."

Mañjuśrī! Suppose the continent of Aparagoyānī were completely filled with srotāpannas, sakṛdāgāmins, anāgāmins, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas, as densely packed as a forest of bamboo, hemp, sugarcane, or reeds.
"If there were evil people, he would kill them all. Mañjuśrī,
what do you think?"
"Would this person, by reason of these causes and conditions, incur much demerit?
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"This sin is unbearable to hear, truly unbearable to hear; such a person has no prospect of escape from the Avīci Hell.
The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, saying:

"If there is someone who does not believe this sūtra, their sin is heavier than that [previous one]; even a hundredth part does not equal it, nor a thousandth, nor a hundred-thousand-millionth part, nor can it be reached by any calculation or analogy."

Mañjuśrī! Suppose the four continents were all reduced to atoms, and there were as many Buddhas, Tathāgatas, as there were those atoms. If there were an evil person who killed them all and seized their two kinds of wealth—the wealth of the Dharma and the wealth of the world.
Mañjuśrī! What do you think?
Would this person’s transgression be great?
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This transgression is inconceivable, incalculable, and beyond all measure.”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva:

"If there should be another person who obstructs this sūtra, slanders it, and does not believe in it, their sin shall be heavier than that [previous one]; even a hundredth part will not equal it, nor a thousandth, nor a hundred-thousand-millionth part, nor can it be reached by any calculation or analogy."

Even if all sentient beings throughout the three thousandfold great thousandfold world system were to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, such an evil person would still not emerge from the Avīci hell.
Mañjuśrī! Such evil persons have not failed to pass through every single Avīci hell in all worlds;
how much less so for the other hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts!
Why is this? Because it destroys the Mother of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Even if one were to escape the three miserable realms for as many eons as there are atoms mentioned before, should one be born among humans, one would contract the disease of *asādha*.

Furthermore, after passing through as many kalpas as there are atoms in those [lands], one receives the retribution of being tongueless; likewise, after passing through as many kalpas as there are atoms in those [lands], one receives the retribution of being handless. Mañjuśrī!

Even if I were to remain in the world for a full kalpa, or slightly less than a kalpa, using the spiritual power of a Buddha to describe the retributive offenses incurred by such evil persons, I could not exhaustively finish the account.
Mañjuśrī! If you seek happiness in the present and future lives, do not disparage or lack faith in this sūtra, nor create great obstacles to it.

Chapter 14: The Chapter on the Two Practices. From the *Suvikrāntavikramī-paripṛcchā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, Chapter Fourteen, "The Two Practices. At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
"When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, they should accomplish the *prajñāpāramitā* of both the preceding and the subsequent [stages]."
Why is this? Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have two kinds of practice:
the accomplishment of prajñā and the teaching and transforming of sentient beings.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva teach and transform sentient beings?”
The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, saying:

"From the initial stage of Prajñā until the ultimate limit, he expounds the Dharma without end, free from the exertion of mental effort, without interruption in the interim, in order to liberate beings from the retribution of the three realms of existence and evil destinies, and to establish all sentient beings in the good paths and enable them to attain the fruits of the three types of noble ones."
Mañjuśrī! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom to transform sentient beings. Mañjuśrī!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they accomplish the boundless and unconditioned; this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s own practice. Why is this?
"Because they have accomplished all virtues.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What dharmas are associated with the prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva? The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, saying:

"The knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is the true dharma, which transcends conceptualization; its subtle, signless principle is profoundly deep, invisible and difficult to penetrate. It is eternally abiding, quiescent, cool, and all-pervading; it is without discrimination, attachment, or obstruction. It accords with the principle and cannot be grasped; it is great tranquility and ultimate stillness, the most unsurpassed among all dharmas, with nothing equal to it."
“Mañjuśrī! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they cultivate these dharmas in correspondence with sarvajñā.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
within what sphere does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the prajñāpāramitā?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
“Mañjuśrī, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, it is a profound sphere, a vast sphere, and a sphere of merit.”

This profound realm is, in its essence, unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); it cannot be separated from [reality], does not cling to the two extremes, and is liberated from all hindrances. It is pure by nature, inconceivable, and beyond calculation; it is not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Mañjuśrī! Regarding the vast object:

when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the *prajñāpāramitā*, the body of all the merits of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, consists of two dharmas—*prajñāpāramitā* and *mahākāruṇā*. Free from the marks of conceptual discrimination and operating with effortlessness, they benefit sentient beings in accordance with their respective inclinations, never abandoning them for even a moment.

Mañjuśrī! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they are in accord with all merits. They are able to manifest all manner of physical forms—such as the thirty-two marks, the eighty minor characteristics, and the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power—in accordance with the faculties, desires, natures, and behaviors of sentient beings. They may ascend to Tuṣita Heaven or descend from it; they may manifest dwelling in the womb, or manifest birth, or manifest as a youth, or sporting in a garden, or manifest renunciation, or manifest ascetic practices, or approach the Bodhi tree, or manifest the attainment of Buddhahood, or manifest turning the wheel of Dharma, or manifest parinirvāṇa.
In these various ways, they exhaust birth and death for the sake of all sentient beings.
Mañjuśrī! This is called the sphere of activity of the bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!
This profound Prajñāpāramitā, the realm of all Buddhas, is inconceivable.”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
"So it is, so it is! It is just as you have said."
The Prajñāpāramitā is an uncommon dharma, inconceivable. Why is this?
Because all ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas cannot penetrate it; it is not within their sphere of experience.
Apart from the Buddha-Tathāgata, there is no one else who has attained it. Why is this?
Because the principle of suchness is exceedingly profound in its meaning.
Sovereign and immovable, it is subsumed within the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*);
in its transformation and teaching of sentient beings, its benefit is perfected.
For these reasons, it is called the sphere of all Buddhas.
It transcends all language and is subsumed within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
It is devoid of vitarka, vicāra, discrimination, and deliberation, and is beyond all analogies.
Among all phenomena, it is the most supreme; it dwells neither in saṃsāra nor in nirvāṇa.
Mañjuśrī! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), there are five inconceivable matters:
first, its intrinsic nature; second, its location; third, its abiding; fourth, its identity and difference; and fifth, its benefit.
Mañjuśrī! Why is self-nature inconceivable?
Form itself is suchness; it cannot be found when sought.
Apart from form, there is suchness, yet it cannot be found when sought.
It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
The earth element is itself suchness, yet it cannot be found when sought.
Seeking suchness apart from the earth element is likewise unattainable;
the same applies to the elements of water, fire, and wind.
The sense-base of the eye is itself suchness; it cannot be found by seeking.
Apart from the eye, one cannot find suchness;
it is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—all are likewise.
There is no dharma that is suchness, for though sought, it cannot be found.
Dharmatā is suchness, and it is likewise unattainable.
Whether within the desire realm, it is inconceivable;
even when apart from the desire realm, it is inconceivable.
It is thus for all things in the realms of form and formlessness.
If they are in the eastern direction, they are inconceivable;
if they are apart from the eastern direction, they are inconceivable.
In the south, west, and north, in the four intermediate directions, and above and below, it is likewise in all places.
The dwelling in inconceivable peace and happiness, the dwelling in inconceivable tranquility, the dwelling with mind, and the dwelling without mind are all inconceivable.
The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time are together in one place: the self-nature pure, untainted dharmadhātu.
Whether they are one or many is inconceivable; their wisdom and spiritual powers are identical within this single dharmadhātu.

The two aspects of *prajñā* and *upāya* are equal, capable of bringing immeasurable benefit to sentient beings. They transcend verbal expression and lie beyond the realm of language; yet, in accordance with the faculties and natures of sentient beings, they manifest various teachings and various demonstrations, appearing in such ways as the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics according to the inclinations of beings.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what are called the thirty-two marks and the eighty minor characteristics?”
The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, saying:

"The marks and embellishments of a Tathāgata are inexhaustible and boundless; they cannot be fully described. It is in accordance with worldly conventions that I have briefly explained only the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor embellishments."
First, the soles of his feet are flat and full;
second, his gait is level and upright;
third, the mark of wheels on the soles of his feet is fully adorned with hubs, rims, and a thousand spokes.
4. His fingers are slender, long, soft, and straight, with the joints and bones not being visible;
5. His body is large, expansive, and well-proportioned;
6. His fingers and toes are joined by a web-like membrane, just like those of the king of geese.
