7. His palms are like red lotuses;
8. His anklebones are not visible;
9. His calves are like those of the king of the eneya deer;
Tenth, the body is supple and straight;
eleventh, the male organ is concealed within a sheath like that of a horse;
twelfth, the limbs are perfectly proportioned, like those of the nyagrodha tree.
Thirteen, the body hairs curl to the right;
fourteen, each pore has a single hair, and the skin is so fine and smooth that it does not retain dust or grime;
fifteen, the body is golden in color.
16. A halo extending one zhang;
17. Fullness at seven places;
18. A lion-like chest.
Nineteen: His two arms are level and straight, and the area beneath his armpits is full;
twenty: His two arms are rounded and straight like the trunk of an elephant king, hanging down past his knees when he stands.
Twenty-one: His mouth has forty teeth, which are even, closely set, and connected to one another, white as jade or snow;
twenty-two: his four upper and lower canine teeth are shaped like the crescent moon;
twenty-three: he has a lion’s forehead.
Twenty-fourth, his head is perfectly round;
twenty-fifth, his throat is endowed with a thousand channels;
twenty-sixth, his breastbone is like that of Nārāyaṇa.
Twenty-seventh, the cranial bone rises up naturally;
twenty-eighth, the tongue is broad and long, like a lotus petal;
twenty-ninth, the voice is like that of the Brahma King or a celestial drum.
30. His eyes are blue, like the *utpala* flower;
31. His eyelashes are deep blue and radiant, like those of a bull king;
32. He has a white tuft of hair between his eyebrows.
Mañjuśrī! These are called the thirty-two marks.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they are able to fully accomplish such merits as these.
“Mañjuśrī! What are called the eighty minor marks?
First, the crown of the head is invisible.”
2. The cranial bone is firm and solid;
3. The forehead is broad and even;
4. The eyebrows are high and long, shaped like the crescent moon, and the color is deep blue like lapis lazuli.
5. His eyes are wide and long;
6. His nose is high, rounded, and straight, with the nostrils not visible; 7. [His lips are red like the Bimba fruit.]
8. His ears are thick, broad, and long, with well-formed lobes; 9.
His body is firm and solid, like that of Nārāyaṇa.
Ninth, his body parts are indestructible;
tenth, his joints are firm and dense;
eleventh, when he turns his whole body to look back, it is like that of an elephant king.
12. His body possesses radiance.
13. His body is well-proportioned and upright.
14. He remains perpetually youthful and does not age.
Fifteenth, the body is always moist and lustrous;
sixteenth, the body is naturally protected and guarded without depending on others;
seventeenth, the parts of the body are fully developed.
Eighteenth, the fulfillment of consciousness;
nineteenth, the perfection of dignified demeanor;
twentieth, the far-reaching resonance of majestic power.
21. Facing all directions, he does not turn his back on others;
22. His dwelling place is peaceful and secure, without danger or instability;
23. His face is proportionate, being neither too large nor too long.
Twenty-fourth, his face is broad and even;
twenty-fifth, his face is round and pure like the full moon;
twenty-sixth, he has no expression of weariness.
Twenty-seven: His advancing and retreating are like those of an elephant king;
twenty-eight: His deportment is like that of a lion king;
twenty-nine: His gait is like that of a swan king.
30. His head is like the *mātuluṅga* fruit;
31. His body is radiant and pleasing;
32. The insteps of his feet are thick.
33. His nails are like the leaves of red copper;
34. When he walks, the patterns of his footprints appear on the ground;
35. His finger-joints are beautifully adorned.
36. The lines on his fingers are clear and not obscure;
37. the lines on his hands are clear and straight;
38. the lines on his hands are long.
Thirty-nine: the lines on his palms are unbroken;
forty: his hands and feet are supple and compliant;
forty-one: his hands and feet are rosy-white, their color like that of a lotus.
42. The physical characteristics are complete according to the tradition of the gate of the sages; 43.
His gait is not diminished; 44. His gait is not excessive.
Forty-five: His gait is steady and level; forty-six:
His navel is deep and thick, shaped like a coiled snake, round and turning to the right;
forty-seven: The color of his body hair is blue-red, like the neck of a peacock.
Forty-eight: The color of his body hair is glossy and pure;
forty-nine: the body hairs curl to the right;
fifty: his mouth emits unsurpassed fragrance, as do his body and body hairs alike.
Fifty-one: The color of the lips is crimson and lustrous, like the *bimba* fruit;
fifty-two: the lips are moist and well-proportioned;
fifty-three: the shape of the tongue is thin.
Fifty-four: All views are pleasant; fifty-five:
following the inclinations of sentient beings, speaking with harmony and joy;
fifty-six: in all places, there are no words that are not virtuous.
57. If one sees a person, one speaks to them first;
58. One’s voice is neither too high nor too low, conforming to the preferences of sentient beings;
59. One preaches the Dharma according to the languages of sentient beings.
Sixty: preaching the Dharma without attachment;
sixty-one: viewing all sentient beings with equanimity;
sixty-two: observing first and then acting.
63. Emitting a single sound, he answers all voices;
64. His sequential exposition of the Dharma is always accompanied by its underlying causes and conditions;
65. No sentient being is able to perceive the exhaustion of his physical marks.
Sixty-sixth, those who behold him never tire;
sixty-seventh, he is endowed with all vocal qualities;
sixty-eighth, he manifests a sublime complexion.
69. Those who are fierce and stubborn are subdued upon seeing him; those who are terrified find peace and security upon seeing him;
70. His voice is clear and pure;
71. His body does not waver or tremble.
Seventy-two: The body is large;
seventy-three: The body is tall;
seventy-four: The body is unstained.
Seventy-five: Light radiates from his entire body, each ray extending one zhang;
seventy-six: He walks while light illuminates his body;
seventy-seven: His body is pure.
Seventy-eighth: His complexion is lustrous and moist, like a blue gem;
seventy-ninth: His hands and feet are full; eightieth:
His hands and feet bear the marks of auspicious letters.

Chapter Fifteen: Praise. From the *Suvikrāntavikramī-paripṛcchā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Chapter Fifteen: Praise. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, bowed his head to the Buddha’s feet in prostration, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
The merits of the Tathāgata are rare and peerless, inconceivable; the Buddhas of the three periods of time are one and the same, without distinction.
Those sentient beings who see the Tathāgata or hear of his merits are likewise inconceivable.
"Today we have once again seen the World-Honored One turn the Great Dharma Wheel; we are filled with joy and exultation, having attained what we have never experienced before.
At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva ascended into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees and, with palms joined, praised him, saying:
"Of all sentient beings, only the Buddha, the Great Honored One, has no equal."
How much more so for those who possess excellence.
The two emptinesses of person and phenomena are, in principle, beyond peer; only the Buddha-Tathāgata is equal to the unequaled.
The habitual tendencies of afflictions are forever exhausted without remainder; all phenomena to be known are fully and clearly understood.
Whether in wisdom or in teaching, none can equal the Buddha; throughout the great trichiliocosm, the Buddha alone is supreme.
The ten powers and fearlessnesses are certain and not in vain; they cannot be attained by either Śakra or Brahmā.
O World-Honored One, your great kindness!
Regarding all sentient beings,
this matter is inconceivable;
none are able to equal it.
"Through immeasurable skillful means and various expedients, he brings benefit to sentient beings. At that time,

there was a son of heaven in the assembly named Sulūpa Chenyan Miaose (Sulūpa of Wondrous Color), who rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, and spoke this verse in praise:
"To say in this world that anyone is equal to the Buddha—such words are called verbal transgressions;
to say that the Dharma King is most supreme—this is not false, but is the truth."
When the hosts of devas and humans pose their challenges, none are able to refute my Great Teacher;
the Sugata has subdued Māra and the non-Buddhists, leading the world toward liberation.
With pure fourfold eloquence, you preach without end; You bestow the wondrous medicine of ambrosia upon all beings.
Universally observing all phenomena with unimpeded wisdom, You never lose or diminish it amidst any thought.
With great compassion, he regards all sentient beings with equanimity; his pure mind is unstained by the world.
Skillfully understanding their faculties, desires, and natures, he teaches them according to what they wish to hear.
The distinctions among afflictions are not of a single kind;
to demonstrate the immeasurable gates of their remedies, none can skillfully explain causes and conditions like the Buddha, for he is solely intent upon benefiting sentient beings.
To encounter the Buddha and hear the Dharma yet fail to attain the Way—such sentient beings are most difficult to deliver.
One should thirstily yearn for the Great Name of the Tathāgata; to behold the World-Honored One brings boundless benefit.
The Buddha’s wisdom can purify the mind; having heard the true teaching, one transcends birth and death.
Hearing the name of the Buddha brings great auspiciousness; by recollecting the World-Honored One, one is forever joyful.
Having resolved to go to the Buddha, they give rise to wisdom and understanding; practicing diligently according to the teachings, they accomplish the knowledge of all modes.
Because their category of precepts is pure, they are free from defilement; their meditative concentration is foremost, and their minds are clear and luminous.
Because their wisdom is supreme, they are unshakable; the ocean of Dharma is as pure as nectar.
While all sentient beings delight in negligence, the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, remain detached from the world.
With equal compassion for all beings as for an only son, his kindness and virtue are so profound that none can repay them;
he first taught the Dharma for destroying the thieves of the fetters, long since crushing the illusory armies of devas and māras.
The World-Honored One has already spoken of the faults of the three realms of existence and extensively demonstrated the immeasurable virtues of nirvāṇa.

At that time, there was a son of heaven in the assembly named Sunāma (in the vernacular, "Good Name"). He rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, praising him in verse:
"The Tathāgata, World-Honored One, practices great compassion;
If he were to bestow the wisdom of deliverance upon others, He would still let Devadatta be the very first to receive it, How much more so for other classes of sentient beings."
I now feel it would be a waste to pass my time in vain; I shall cultivate right practice to repay the Buddha’s kindness.
Though some have already realized the extinction of outflows (*anāsrava-nirodha*), they have not yet repaid the Buddha’s kindness;
only those who can practice the Buddha’s true teaching may be called true sons of the Buddha.
The Buddha has long undergone diligent toil for the sake of sentient beings; this unsurpassed great kindness is rarely repaid.
With great compassion, he revealed and manifested the true Dharma, enabling people to practice it themselves while simultaneously transforming others.
If the Buddha-Tathāgata does not appear in the world, all sentient beings will undergo great suffering;
there will be no further paths of goodness, only the evil realms, where one hears only the sounds of distress in the three miserable states.
Suffering in the six realms cannot be avoided or escaped, for sentient beings are bound by afflictions;
yet the World-Honored One, who can untie the poisonous knots of others, is instead entangled by great compassion.
The Buddha is the great field of merit for the world; by practicing correctly according to his teachings, one leaves the evil realms behind.
If one violates the Buddha’s teachings and fails to practice, such a person will never be born in a fortunate realm.
Those who give rise to malice toward the Buddha, or who take no delight in hearing the profound Dharma—such sentient beings are most pitiable; they are certain to dwell forever in darkness.
As the Buddha, the World-Honored One, knows through his own wisdom—only one equal to a Tathāgata can fully comprehend it—the Buddha’s wisdom is beyond my power to measure;
with head bowed in reverence, I pay homage to the Honored One of the ten directions.
Fearlessness, wisdom, powers, and the unique qualities—these alone the Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses in perfect completeness.
Adorned with the marks and signs and possessing a subtle, wondrous voice, those who behold him never tire; his excellence transcends all other forms.
With the three kinds of lotuses in full bloom, never ceasing for a moment, I now pay homage to this pure Buddha-flower.
Only the Buddha thoroughly knows the unsurpassed path; he has emerged from all perils and hardships.
The Buddha is the supreme and foremost one; I prostrate with my head at the feet of the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings.
With the water of the merit of the True Dharma, The Buddha washes away all defilements without remainder;
The World-Honored One is primordially pure both within and without— I now prostrate to this truly pure body.

At that time, Mahābrahmā, the lord of the Sahā world, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, praising him in verse:
“The Buddha is fully endowed with merit and wisdom; He benefits sentient beings without ceasing for even a moment.
Constantly raining down ambrosia to satisfy all beings, I now prostrate to the one who is able to benefit others.”
Though he is one most supreme and venerable in the world, this person still reveres the Buddha;
all evils are exhausted and all virtues are complete. I now prostrate to the Peerless Honored One;
there is not a single practice he has not cultivated and studied, for the sake of rescuing and uplifting all sentient beings.
Causing them to cross over birth and death and attain peace and happiness, I now prostrate to the Teacher who saves the world.
Homage to the subtle and wondrous golden body!
Homage to the nectar-like Dharma that has been proclaimed!
"Homage to the pure and stainless wisdom!
Homage to the forest of all virtues!
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Great Brahmā Heaven, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!
That which the Great Brahmā has praised regarding the World-Honored One is indeed true. Why is this so?
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have cultivated various merits and wisdom throughout immeasurable kalpas; therefore, there is nothing that is not fully perfected in their fruition. Why is this so?

Fully endowed with the dāna-pāramitā, śīla-pāramitā, kṣānti-pāramitā, vīrya-pāramitā, dhyāna-pāramitā, and prajñā-pāramitā, they possess purity of body, purity of speech, and purity of mind; by means of this purity, they are able to penetrate the suchness of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
"The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, abide in this reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*); what they say is not in vain.

At that time, the Great Brahmā rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray, World-Honored One!"
"By the power of their sustaining presence, they cause this Prajñāpāramitā to remain long in the world.
The Buddha addressed the Great Brahmā, saying:
"The sustaining power of all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time protects and upholds this Prajñāpāramitā in its entirety."
In this world, whether among gods, Māras, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas, there is none who can destroy it or create obstacles for it.

Why is this? I recall that in a past life, there was a Buddha named Ratnacandra Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān; his land was named Adīna, and the eon was named Praśaṃsita.
Within this assembly of the Buddha, there were two bhikṣus who served as Dharma masters and were skilled at preaching the Dharma:
the first was named Jñānavardhana, and the second was named Satyadatta.
These two bhikṣus followed the Buddha as he turned the wheel of the Dharma for a full kalpa; the ten billion Māras of the trichiliocosm were all transformed by them and resolved to attain bodhicitta.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Śāntamati rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"Is the Tathāgata Ratnacandra still in the world,
or has he already entered parinirvāṇa?
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Saṃtānabuddhi:
“Good son! To the east of here, passing beyond ten hundred thousand billion Buddha-worlds, there is a world named Adhruva (Unassailable), where the lifespan of the Buddha is ten thousand kalpas.”
In that Buddha-land, when the Prajñāpāramitā is taught, no heavenly Māras or any heterodox teachers are able to create obstacles; all have resolved their minds toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The bhikṣu Jñānavardhana is none other than Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva; the bhikṣu Satya is none other than King Śūra.
These two, through their skillful means, provide manifold protection so that the Prajñāpāramitā may abide in the world for a long time.
Wherever the Prajñāpāramitā is being taught in the Buddha-fields of the ten directions, these two individuals come immediately to listen and receive it;
just as today I emit a great radiance, and they gather here following that light.
16. Chapter on the Entrustment. In the *Suvikrāntavikramī-paripṛcchā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the sixteenth chapter, "The Entrustment," at that time the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You should receive, uphold, and practice this *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*."

At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, addressing him:
“World-Honored One!
"How should it be received and upheld?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"There are ten kinds of dharmas for receiving and upholding this sūtra."
What are the ten? First, copying;

second, making offerings; third, circulating; fourth, listening attentively; fifth, reading for oneself; sixth, memorizing; seventh, explaining extensively; eighth, reciting aloud; ninth, reflecting; and tenth, practicing.
Ānanda! These ten kinds of dharmas are able to receive and uphold this sūtra. Ānanda!
Just as all forests, flowers, and medicinal herbs depend upon the great earth for their growth,
so too do all wholesome dharmas arise in dependence upon the Prajñāpāramitā.
Ānanda! Just as when a Wheel-Turning Sage King dwells in the world, the seven treasures are constantly manifest;
so too is it with this sūtra of the Prajñāpāramitā: if it remains in the world, the lineage of the Three Jewels will never be severed.
At that time, the great assembly all gazed upon the face of the Tathāgata simultaneously, and with one voice and different mouths, they spoke together, saying:
"O sons of good family!..."

After the Tathāgata has passed into extinction, who will be able to shoulder such a great burden for the World-Honored One—namely, that which was cultivated over immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?

At that time, there were twelve thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas within the assembly who, for the sake of protecting and upholding the Dharma, rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, placed their right knees on the ground, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and prostrated with their heads at his feet, speaking these verses of praise:
"We renounce our bodies and lives, Seeking no future reward,
To protect and uphold the profound Dharma Spoken by the World-Honored One."

At that time, five hundred devaputras within the assembly, with King Bhadrika as their leader, rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and prostrated with their heads at his feet, praising him with these verses:
“For the sake of delivering all sentient beings, You have fulfilled your vow of great compassion;
You protect and uphold the profound Dharma Spoken by the World-Honored One.”

At that time, Śakra Devānām-Indra, the Great Brahmā Śikhin, and the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees upon the ground, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and prostrated with their heads at his feet. They spoke this verse in praise:
"The subtle and wondrous medicine of Prajñā Can cure all illnesses;
We shall receive and uphold it, As taught by the World-Honored One."

At that time, the Vajrapāṇi deity rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, praising him with these verses:
“The Dharma is fundamentally without name; The Buddha speaks it by means of names.
We shall receive and uphold The Great Compassionate Teaching of the World-Honored One.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Brahmā Śikhin, saying: "Brahmā!
A Buddha possesses three things that are most unsurpassed."
What are these three?
First, being able to give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; second, protecting and upholding the true Dharma; and third, practicing according to what has been heard.
Brahmā! These three dharmas are the most unsurpassed.
If there is anyone who can practice them, that person is said to be making an offering to the Tathāgata.
Whether the Buddha remains in the world for a full kalpa or slightly less than a kalpa, one could not exhaustively describe his merits. Brahmā!
If one protects and upholds even a single four-line verse of the Tathāgata, the merit of that person is still immeasurable.
How much more so the Prajñāpāramitā, the mother of the Buddhas of the three periods of time!
Why is this? O Brahmā!
All Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are born from the Prajñāpāramitā.
To make an offering of the Dharma is to make an offering to all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas; it is not by means of material wealth that one makes an offering.
Among all offerings, the offering of the Dharma is the most supreme.
"Brahmā! If there are those who protect and uphold the True Dharma of the Tathāgata, you should know that such persons will enjoy peace and happiness in both worlds. Therefore, Brahmā!"
One must protect and uphold the profound sūtras.
Brahmā! Because Brahmā protects the Dharma, he has been able to see the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa, serving as the presiding host for them all.
"Brahmā!

To protect and uphold the True Dharma in this defiled land for even a brief moment is superior to doing so in a pure land for one kalpa or even more than a kalpa. Therefore, you should diligently apply yourself with vigor to protect and uphold the True Dharma."
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying: "Kauśika!

Wherever this Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra exists, you should know that it is precisely the place where the Tathāgata attained bodhi, the place where he turned the wheel of Dharma, and the place where he manifested nirvāṇa."
Why is this? Kauśika!
All bodhisattvas, all wholesome dharmas, and all buddhas are born from this sūtra.

Kauśika! Wherever a Dharma master circulates this sūtra, that place is the very domain where the Tathāgata walks. Toward that Dharma master, you should give rise to the thought of him being a virtuous friend and a heart of reverence, just as you would toward the Buddha himself.
Upon seeing this Dharma-preacher, one should show reverence, joy, respect, and praise. Kauśika!
Whether I were to remain in the world for a full kalpa or slightly less than a kalpa, I could not exhaustively describe the merits of the Dharma-preacher who propagates this sūtra.

Kauśika! Wherever this Dharma-preacher travels, sons and daughters of good family should prick their own blood and sprinkle it upon the ground so that dust does not rise; even such an offering as this would not be considered excessive.
"Why is this? Because the Wheel of Dharma of the Tathāgata is difficult to receive and uphold.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

In future ages, wherever this sutra is preached, I and my retinue shall protect that place and the preacher of the Dharma. Whenever we see such a place where this sutra is being taught, we shall immediately give rise to the four kinds of mental states.”
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Śakra, the Lord of Devas,
saying: “Excellent, excellent, Kauśika!”
"I entrust this sūtra to Kauśika to protect and circulate it in the future final age.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
That we gods have been born into this good realm is entirely due to this sūtra;
that we seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is likewise due to this sūtra.
"I shall disregard my own body and life to protect the True Dharma.
The Buddha said, "Kauśika!
"Excellent, excellent! Practice according to what you have heard!

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Victorious Heavenly King, the great bodhisattvas of the ten directions, the entire assembly of śrāvakas, and the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others, having heard what the Buddha taught, believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.

The Sūtra of the Prajñāpāramitā of the Victorious Heavenly King, Scroll Seven; Appendix: Preface to the Sūtra. At the beginning of the *Benevolent Kings Prajñā Sūtra*, the assembly said to one another:
"O Greatly Awakened World-Honored One!..."

Previously, for twenty-nine years, you have already expounded for me the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā*, the *Rāstrapālaparipṛcchā-prajñāpāramitā*, and the *Suvikrāntavikrāmī-paripṛcchā-prajñāpāramitā*.
Thus, the title of this sutra has long been transmitted to the Great Kingdom (China).

In the sixth month of the second year of the Taiching era of the Liang dynasty, the Khotanese śramaṇa Guṇabhadra—whose name in Chinese is De-xian—brought a single volume of the Sanskrit text consisting of sixteen chapters and first arrived at the capital.

At that time, Prince Candraprabha (Yueshouna) of the kingdom of Ujjayinī in Central India—whose innate wisdom was later made radiant, who had inherited the tradition of Śākya learning and possessed no lack of refined meaning, and who was moreover proficient in local dialects—had fled his native land to serve at the court of the Liang dynasty, where he was commissioned by imperial decree to oversee all foreign diplomatic affairs.
Suddenly seeing that De-xian possessed this scripture, he cherished it with deep reverence as if in the presence of the true Buddha; he then entreated him to propagate it until the end of his life.
Praising De-xian’s noble conduct and spiritual mind, [the Buddha] bestowed it upon Śūna.
He was then again commanded by imperial decree to seek out the envoy Gu Biao to welcome the *Saṃpuṭa-sūtra*.
Hardly had he taken his leave when he encountered the rebellion of Hou Jing and Qiu Kelou; he fled with the scripture upon his head, finding no leisure for its translation.
What the people desire, Heaven will surely follow.

Entrusted with the great mandate to manifest the destiny of the era, we have renewed the glorious light and accumulated our ancestral achievements, purifying the four seas once again. Now, chariots and books are unified, and the Chinese and the barbarians dwell in harmony.

Shuna Pinjia arrived from afar carrying the scriptures in his bosom; Huang Falan, the General of Chariots and Cavalry and Governor of Jiangzhou, who had been granted the jade scepter and governed the region of Shan, protected and upheld the True Dharma and thirstily yearned for the Mahāyāna.

On the twenty-third day, the *guǐmǎo* day, of the seventh month in the year of Yǐyǒu during the sixth year of the Tiānjiā era, I exhorted Śrīnanda to attend the assembly on the island. There, I briefly expounded upon the preface of the title and preached the Great Unrestricted Assembly (*anivārita-mahāpariṣad*), at which more than five thousand members of the fourfold assembly gathered like clouds.

Dharma Master Shi Sengguo of Kuangshan, along with renowned and virtuous masters from near and far, all topped the various schools of thought and were broadly versed in the five divisions of the canon; though each presented profound and intricate challenges, there was none that was not resolved with the clarity of water being dispersed.
On the twenty-ninth day of that month, he returned to the Xingye Monastery.

Once the gong had sounded and the assembly of monks had gathered, Śrīnanda personally took up the Sanskrit text and translated it into the Chen language. Shi Zhixin of the Ayuwang Monastery in Yangzhou, who was visiting the region of Guhui, humbly submitted to these supreme teachings; listening with his ears and recording with his pen, he did not dare to lose a single word. After revising and refining the text two or three times, he compiled it into seven fascicles, completing the work on the eighteenth day of the ninth month of that year, at which point the text and its phrasing were finalized.

The Dharma Master Shi Huigong, the Sangha Rectifier of Jiangzhou, possessed the fragrant incense of the precepts and the crystal-clear water of meditative concentration; he was a model for all to look up to, upon whom the Chen and Liang dynasties relied.
Biejia Wanyin of Yuzhang was the arm and thigh of [Hui]zhou and the cypress and paulownia among men of talent; he cultivated both faith and wisdom and employed both civil and martial arts.
Entrusting these two men with the task, they initiated the meritorious work; I have appended this to the end of the volume, briefly describing the events of the time.
It is hoped that future gentlemen may perhaps refine themselves therein.
